_comment: Per-tool curated content keyed by tool id. Replaces template/fallback plans. `merges` absorbs other ids (titles become aliases). Every entry is a CLAIM until reviewedBy names a clinician. Sources: NICE CKS topic named per tool, BNF, cited NICE NG/CG. Batch 1 = musculoskeletal, 2026-10-11.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Clinical diagnosis: heel pain worst on first steps in the morning or after rest, tender at medial calcaneal tubercle. Imaging not routinely needed.
2. Differentials: calcaneal stress fracture (pain on squeeze test, runners), Sever's disease (child 8–14), tarsal tunnel/S1 radiculopathy (paraesthesia), fat pad atrophy, spondyloarthritis (young, bilateral, inflammatory back pain, psoriasis/IBD).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rest from aggravating activity; weight loss if BMI raised; supportive footwear with cushioned heel; avoid barefoot on hard floors.
2. Plantar fascia and calf stretches 2–3× daily; ice after activity.
3. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g qds prn; ibuprofen 400 mg tds prn with food (or topical ibuprofen gel) if no contraindication.
4. Gel heel pads or off-the-shelf orthoses; night splint if morning pain dominant.
5. Not improving at 6–12 weeks: physiotherapy; corticosteroid injection (e.g. methylprednisolone 20–40 mg with lidocaine) — short-term benefit only, risk of fat-pad atrophy and fascia rupture; extracorporeal shockwave therapy (NICE IPG311) via MSK service.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Routine podiatry/MSK referral if no improvement after 3–6 months of conservative care, or diagnostic uncertainty.
2. Orthopaedic/foot & ankle referral if symptoms >12 months despite the above; surgery (plantar fascia release) is a last resort.
3. Urgent: suspected stress fracture (offload, X-ray; MRI if X-ray normal), or features of inflammatory arthritis → rheumatology.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Pain and tenderness over lateral epicondyle, worse on resisted wrist/finger extension (Cozen's test) and gripping. No imaging needed for typical presentation.
2. Exclude: radial tunnel syndrome (pain 3–5 cm distal, worse resisted supination), cervical radiculopathy C6/7, elbow OA or loose body (locking), referred shoulder pain.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Explain: self-limiting, 90% settle in 6–24 months. Modify or pause the provoking activity; check ergonomics/grip size.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol; topical NSAID (ibuprofen 5% gel qds) first line; oral ibuprofen 400 mg tds for short courses only.
3. Physiotherapy: progressive loading/eccentric wrist extensor exercises for ≥6–12 weeks; counterforce (epicondylar) brace for symptom relief.
4. Corticosteroid injection: short-term relief only and WORSE outcomes at 6–12 months — not routinely recommended; consider only for severe pain limiting work/function after shared decision.
5. Avoid repeated injections; no evidence for PRP in routine care.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Routine MSK/orthopaedic referral if persistent >6–12 months despite loading programme, or diagnostic uncertainty (consider USS/MRI).
2. Surgical options (release/debridement) only after failed conservative care.

elbow-medial-epicondylitis.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Tennis elbow — medial section; BMJ Best Practice)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Tenderness at medial epicondyle, pain on resisted wrist flexion/pronation. Check ulnar nerve: paraesthesia ring/little finger, Tinel at cubital tunnel (co-exists in up to 50%).
2. Differentials: cubital tunnel syndrome, ulnar collateral ligament injury (throwers), C8/T1 radiculopathy.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Activity modification; topical NSAID gel; paracetamol.
2. Physiotherapy: eccentric/isometric wrist flexor–pronator loading 6–12 weeks; counterforce brace.
3. Steroid injection: short-term relief only; risk of ulnar nerve injury — specialist/USS-guided if at all.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer MSK/orthopaedics if >6 months, progressive ulnar neuropathy (weakness, wasting → nerve conduction studies), or instability.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mid-portion (2–6 cm above insertion, fusiform swelling) vs insertional (at calcaneus, often Haglund's). Morning stiffness, pain on loading.
2. Exclude rupture: Simmonds/Thompson test, palpable gap, sudden 'kick' sensation → see Achilles rupture.
3. Risk factors to address: fluoroquinolones (stop and avoid), corticosteroids, hypercholesterolaemia, diabetes, sudden training increase.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Relative rest (reduce not stop); ice after activity; heel raise/cushioned shoe; avoid flat shoes and hill running.
2. Progressive loading: eccentric heel-drop programme (Alfredson, 3×15 reps bd, 12 weeks) for mid-portion; floor-level only for insertional. Expect 3–6 months.
3. Analgesia short term: paracetamol; ibuprofen 400 mg tds ≤2 weeks.
4. DO NOT inject corticosteroid into or around the tendon (rupture risk).
5. Persisting >3 months: physiotherapy review; ESWT (NICE IPG312) via MSK service.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same-day orthopaedics/ED: suspected rupture.
2. Routine orthopaedic (foot & ankle) referral if no improvement after 6 months of a supervised loading programme; USS/MRI to characterise.

ankle-achilles-rupture.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Achilles tendinopathy — rupture; BOA/BOFAS)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Sudden pain/'snap' at the heel during push-off, weak plantarflexion, palpable gap 2–6 cm above insertion, positive Simmonds (calf squeeze → no plantarflexion). Patient may still walk — do not be reassured.
2. Risk: recent fluoroquinolone, steroid injection, age 30–50 'weekend athlete'.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same-day referral to ED/orthopaedics (fracture clinic). Non-weight-bearing, equinus splint, elevation, analgesia (paracetamol ± ibuprofen).
2. Secondary care decides functional bracing (most) vs surgery (athletes, delayed presentation >2 weeks, re-rupture). VTE risk assessment and prophylaxis per local protocol while immobilised.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. All suspected ruptures same day. Missed/chronic rupture (>4 weeks): urgent orthopaedic foot & ankle referral — outcomes worse with delay.

ankle-sprain.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Sprains and strains, 2024)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Ottawa ankle rules — X-ray if: bone tenderness posterior edge/tip of either malleolus, base of 5th metatarsal, navicular, OR unable to weight-bear 4 steps immediately and in clinic.
2. Grade: I stretch (stable), II partial tear (laxity, swelling), III complete (gross instability, positive anterior drawer).
3. Also check: syndesmosis (squeeze test, pain on external rotation → high ankle sprain, longer recovery), peroneal tendon dislocation, Achilles.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. First 48–72 h: protection, relative rest, ice 15–20 min every 2–3 h, compression, elevation. Avoid heat, alcohol, massage, running (HARM) for 72 h.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g qds; ibuprofen 400 mg tds with food if needed (topical NSAID alternative).
3. Early mobilisation and weight-bearing as tolerated; functional support (lace-up brace) rather than rigid immobilisation. Grade III: short period in walking boot then brace.
4. Rehabilitation: range of movement → strengthening → proprioception/balance (wobble board) to prevent recurrence (up to 30%).

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: fracture on X-ray or Ottawa-positive with no imaging access; gross deformity; neurovascular compromise.
2. Physiotherapy if not improving at 2–4 weeks or grade III.
3. Orthopaedics: persistent instability or pain >6–8 weeks (consider osteochondral lesion, syndesmosis injury, peroneal pathology → MRI).

shoulder-pain.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Shoulder pain, 2024; BESS/BOA)

options.label: Red flags / urgent
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute trauma + loss of ACTIVE abduction/external rotation with preserved passive range → suspected acute full-thickness cuff tear: urgent X-ray and orthopaedic referral within 2–3 weeks (repair outcomes fall after 3 months), especially age <65.
2. Trauma + deformity/loss of rotation → X-ray same day (fracture, dislocation). Unreduced posterior dislocation is easily missed.
3. Systemically unwell, red hot joint → septic arthritis (same-day admission). Unexplained mass, night pain, weight loss, history of cancer → 2WW / urgent imaging.
4. Chest pain, pain unrelated to movement → consider cardiac or diaphragmatic/referred cause.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Painful arc 60–120°, pain on resisted abduction/external rotation, positive Hawkins–Kennedy → rotator cuff tendinopathy/subacromial pain. Weakness out of proportion → tear.
2. Global loss of passive external rotation → frozen shoulder or glenohumeral OA (X-ray distinguishes). Pain at ACJ with high-arc pain → ACJ.
3. Imaging: plain X-ray if trauma, age >60 with new symptoms, or not improving at 6–12 weeks. USS for suspected tear (via MSK service).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Education: most subacromial pain improves over 6–12 months; keep moving within pain; modify overhead work.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol 1 g qds; ibuprofen 400 mg tds or naproxen 500 mg bd short course (with PPI if risk); topical NSAID.
3. Physiotherapy: structured rotator-cuff and scapular strengthening ≥12 weeks is first-line.
4. Subacromial corticosteroid injection (e.g. methylprednisolone 40 mg + 1% lidocaine 4–5 ml, or triamcinolone 40 mg) for pain limiting rehabilitation; benefit ~6–8 weeks; maximum 2 injections, ≥6 weeks apart; avoid if tear suspected in young patient.
5. Calcific tendinopathy: same conservative care; USS-guided barbotage or ESWT via MSK service if persistent.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. MSK interface/physio-led service: not improving after 12 weeks of rehabilitation, or after 1–2 injections.
2. Orthopaedics: symptomatic full-thickness tear (especially traumatic, age <65), failure of 6 months conservative care (consider subacromial decompression — only after conservative care and shared decision; NICE/BESS), recurrent calcific deposits.

shoulder-frozen.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Shoulder pain — frozen shoulder, 2024)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Age 40–60; global restriction of ACTIVE and PASSIVE movement, external rotation most limited; three phases — painful (2–9 months), stiff (4–12 months), thawing (12–42 months).
2. X-ray to exclude glenohumeral OA and posterior dislocation (both mimic). Check HbA1c and TFTs (diabetes ×5 risk; thyroid disease).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Explain natural history (most recover over 1–3 years; residual stiffness in some). Keep using the arm within pain.
2. Painful phase: paracetamol + ibuprofen 400 mg tds/naproxen 500 mg bd short course; intra-articular glenohumeral corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 40 mg or triamcinolone 40 mg, ideally image-guided) gives the best early pain relief; short oral prednisolone course only in exceptional cases.
3. Stiff phase: physiotherapy — stretching within pain, pulley/pendulum exercises; avoid aggressive manipulation.
4. Optimise diabetic control.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer orthopaedics/MSK if severe pain and loss of function unresponsive to injection + physiotherapy at 3–6 months: options hydrodilatation, manipulation under anaesthesia, arthroscopic capsular release (UK FROST: similar outcomes at 1 year — shared decision).
2. Diagnostic doubt (e.g. young patient, trauma) → imaging/referral.

hand-trigger-finger.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Trigger finger, 2024; BSSH)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Catching/locking of the finger in flexion with painful nodule at A1 pulley (palm, MCP crease). Grade: I pain, II catching, III locking (releases with help), IV fixed.
2. Associations: diabetes (check HbA1c if not known), RA, carpal tunnel, Dupuytren's. Children: congenital trigger thumb → hand surgery.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mild: activity modification, avoid repetitive gripping; paracetamol/ibuprofen; night splint holding MCP in extension for 6 weeks (resolves ~50%).
2. Corticosteroid injection into the tendon sheath at A1 pulley (e.g. methylprednisolone 20–40 mg + lidocaine): effective in ~60–90%; second injection if recurs; lower success in diabetes. Warn of skin/fat atrophy and transient glucose rise.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hand surgery referral: locked digit (grade IV), failure of 2 injections, multiple digits, diabetes with poor response, children. Percutaneous or open A1 pulley release — >95% success.

hand-dupuytren-s.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Dupuytren's disease, 2024; BSSH)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Painless palmar nodules/cords, ring and little finger commonest; measure MCP and PIP flexion contracture; table-top test (cannot lay palm flat).
2. Risk: family history, Northern European, diabetes, alcohol, smoking, epilepsy drugs. Note ectopic disease (Garrod's pads, plantar fascia, Peyronie's).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Nodules without contracture: reassure, no treatment; splints, NSAIDs, physiotherapy and steroid injection do NOT alter progression.
2. Advise on smoking/alcohol; optimise diabetes. Explain variable progression; review if function declines.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Refer hand surgery when: MCP contracture ≥30°, ANY PIP contracture, positive table-top test, rapidly progressive disease, functional impairment, or first-web/thumb involvement.
2. Options: needle fasciotomy (quick, higher recurrence), limited fasciectomy (standard), dermofasciectomy for recurrence. Collagenase (Xiapex) withdrawn from UK market 2020.

hip-trochanteric-bursitis.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Greater trochanteric pain syndrome, 2024)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Greater trochanteric pain syndrome

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Lateral hip pain worse lying on that side, climbing stairs, standing on one leg; tenderness over greater trochanter; pain on resisted abduction/30-second single-leg stand. Women 40–60, often with low back pain or knee OA.
2. Exclude: hip OA (groin pain, restricted internal rotation → X-ray), lumbar radiculopathy L4/5, stress fracture femoral neck (runners, osteoporosis → urgent), septic bursitis (rare, unwell).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Education and load management: avoid lying on the affected side (pillow between knees), avoid crossing legs, sitting low, hanging on one hip; weight loss if indicated.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol; ibuprofen 400 mg tds/naproxen 500 mg bd short course; topical NSAID.
3. Physiotherapy: progressive gluteal (abductor) strengthening ≥8–12 weeks — better long-term outcomes than injection (LEAP trial).
4. Corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 40 mg + lidocaine, to point of maximal tenderness) for short-term relief if severe; max 2–3/year.
5. Persistent: ESWT via MSK service.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. MSK/orthopaedics if no improvement after 3–6 months of exercise therapy ± injection; USS/MRI for gluteal tendon tear.
2. Urgent: suspected femoral neck stress fracture or inability to weight-bear.

knee-patellofemoral.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Knee pain — assessment, 2024; BJSM consensus)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diffuse anterior/retropatellar pain worse on stairs (down > up), squatting, prolonged sitting ('theatre sign'); crepitus; no effusion or locking. Common in adolescents and runners.
2. No imaging unless red flags, trauma, effusion, locking, or failure to improve at 6–12 weeks. Differentials: patellar tendinopathy (inferior pole), Osgood–Schlatter (tibial tuberosity, adolescent), plica, OA (>50), referred hip (SUFE/Perthes in children — examine the hip).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Education; relative rest from aggravating load, then graded return.
2. Physiotherapy: quadriceps (VMO) and hip abductor/external rotator strengthening ≥12 weeks is the core treatment; patellar taping for short-term relief; foot orthoses if pronation.
3. Analgesia short term: paracetamol; ibuprofen 400 mg tds prn. Avoid steroid injection.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Physiotherapy at diagnosis. MSK/orthopaedics only if not improving after 6 months of supervised rehabilitation, recurrent patellar instability/dislocation, or diagnostic uncertainty (MRI).

knee-meniscal.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG226 Osteoarthritis 2022; NICE CKS Knee pain — assessment)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Twisting injury with delayed swelling (hours), joint-line tenderness, pain on McMurray/Thessaly, ± locking or giving way. Degenerative tears in >40s often without clear injury.
2. Ottawa knee rules for X-ray after trauma: age ≥55, isolated patellar tenderness, fibular head tenderness, cannot flex to 90°, cannot weight-bear 4 steps.
3. Immediate large haemarthrosis → think ACL/fracture (see Knee – ligament).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Degenerative tear or tear with OA: treat as OA — exercise, weight management, paracetamol/topical NSAID, physiotherapy for ≥3 months. NICE NG226: do NOT refer for arthroscopic lavage/debridement for OA; arthroscopy only for true mechanical locking.
2. Acute traumatic tear in young/active patient: protect, ice, analgesia (ibuprofen 400 mg tds), physiotherapy; early orthopaedic opinion if mechanical symptoms (repairable tears are time-sensitive).

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day/urgent: true locked knee (cannot fully extend), suspected bucket-handle tear, haemarthrosis.
2. Orthopaedics/MSK with MRI: young patient with mechanical symptoms, or failure of 3 months physiotherapy. Over 50 without locking: X-ray and OA pathway first; MRI rarely changes management.

knee-ligament.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Knee pain — assessment; BOAST)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ACL: pivot/landing injury, audible pop, immediate swelling (haemarthrosis within 1–2 h), instability; Lachman most sensitive. 50% have meniscal injury too.
2. MCL: valgus force, medial pain, laxity at 30° flexion — grade I–III. PCL: dashboard injury, posterior sag. Multi-ligament/dislocation → vascular check.
3. X-ray per Ottawa rules; Segond fracture on X-ray = ACL until proven otherwise.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute: rest, ice, compression, elevation, crutches; paracetamol + ibuprofen 400 mg tds; hinged brace for MCL grade II–III.
2. MCL grade I–II: physiotherapy, early range of movement, return to sport 2–8 weeks. Isolated PCL: physiotherapy quadriceps-focused.
3. ACL: structured physiotherapy (prehabilitation) for all; reconstruction decision with orthopaedics based on instability, age, activity and associated meniscal injury.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day ED/orthopaedics: haemarthrosis, suspected dislocation or multi-ligament injury, neurovascular compromise, locked knee.
2. Urgent orthopaedic (within 2 weeks): suspected ACL rupture, MCL grade III, PCL with instability — MRI arranged by secondary care or MSK interface.

polymyalgia-rheumatica.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Polymyalgia rheumatica, 2024; BSR 2015)

options.label: Diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Core features: age ≥50, bilateral shoulder ± pelvic girdle aching >2 weeks, morning stiffness >45 min, raised ESR/CRP, rapid (≥70%) response to prednisolone 15 mg within 1 week.
2. Before steroids: FBC, ESR + CRP, U&E, LFT, calcium, ALP, TSH, CK, RF, anti-CCP, urine dip, protein electrophoresis/light chains; chest X-ray if indicated.
3. ALWAYS ask about GCA: headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, visual symptoms → see Giant cell arteritis (same-day). Atypical features (age <60, no girdle pain, normal inflammatory markers, prominent peripheral synovitis, poor steroid response) → consider RA, myositis, malignancy, infection, hypothyroidism → rheumatology.

options.label: Treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Prednisolone 15 mg once daily (12.5–25 mg range); review at 1 week — expect dramatic improvement; if <70% improvement, reconsider diagnosis before escalating.
2. Taper (CKS): 15 mg for 3 weeks → 12.5 mg for 3 weeks → 10 mg for 4–6 weeks → then reduce by 1 mg every 4–8 weeks (or alternate-day reductions) to zero; typical course 1–2 years. Relapse: return to previous effective dose.
3. Bone protection from the start: alendronic acid 70 mg weekly + calcium/vitamin D (DEXA if <65 and no fracture). Gastroprotection (lansoprazole 15–30 mg od) if NSAID/high risk. Steroid card; sick-day rules.
4. Monitor: ESR/CRP, glucose/HbA1c, BP, weight every 3 months; warn about adrenal suppression on withdrawal.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same-day: any GCA feature.
2. Rheumatology (routine/urgent as clinically indicated): age <60, atypical features, poor or incomplete response to 15 mg, unable to reduce below 10 mg after 1 year, ≥2 relapses, steroid toxicity — consider methotrexate as steroid-sparing (specialist).

giant-cell-arteritis.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Giant cell arteritis, 2024; BSR 2020)

steps.question: Giant cell arteritis — treat as emergency

options.label: Recognise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Age ≥50 with new temporal/occipital headache, scalp tenderness, jaw or tongue claudication, visual symptoms (amaurosis, diplopia, blur), PMR symptoms, fever/weight loss, thickened tender non-pulsatile temporal artery.
2. Bloods SAME DAY: ESR, CRP, FBC (thrombocytosis), LFT (raised ALP). Normal ESR/CRP does not exclude GCA if clinical suspicion is high. Do NOT delay steroids for results.

options.label: Immediate treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. No visual symptoms: start prednisolone 40–60 mg once daily immediately (same day).
2. Visual symptoms or jaw claudication: 60 mg prednisolone and SAME-DAY ophthalmology/ED referral (IV methylprednisolone 500 mg–1 g for 3 days in secondary care). Vision loss is usually irreversible — minutes matter.
3. Add: gastroprotection (lansoprazole 30 mg od); bone protection (alendronic acid 70 mg weekly + calcium/vitamin D); aspirin 75 mg not routinely (BSR 2020) unless other indication; steroid card.
4. Ensure specialist review within 3 working days (fast-track GCA pathway where available) for temporal artery ultrasound/biopsy — steroids should not be stopped while awaiting confirmation.

options.label: Ongoing
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Specialist-led taper over 12–18 months (e.g. to 20 mg by 3 months, 10 mg by 6 months); relapse → increase. Tocilizumab (NICE TA518) for relapsing/refractory disease — rheumatology.
2. GP monitoring: BP, glucose, weight, mood, infection; relapse symptoms; long-term aortic imaging per specialist.

pseudogout.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Gout — differentials; EULAR CPPD 2011/2023)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute hot swollen joint, typically knee or wrist in older adult; may follow illness/surgery. Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray supports but does not confirm. Definitive: aspiration — positively birefringent rhomboid crystals.
2. A hot swollen joint is SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise — same-day aspiration before any steroid; admit if unwell.
3. Screen for causes if <60 or polyarticular: calcium, PTH (hyperparathyroidism), ferritin/transferrin saturation (haemochromatosis), magnesium, ALP, TSH.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rest, ice, aspiration (therapeutic).
2. NSAID: naproxen 500 mg bd or ibuprofen 400–600 mg tds with PPI, for shortest duration; OR colchicine 500 micrograms bd–qds (max 6 mg/course; reduce in renal impairment, interactions with statins/clarithromycin); OR intra-articular corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 40 mg) once infection excluded — preferred in elderly/renal impairment/anticoagulated.
3. Short oral prednisolone 15–20 mg for 3–5 days if the above are unsuitable.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: possible septic arthritis, unable to aspirate in primary care.
2. Rheumatology: recurrent attacks (consider colchicine 500 micrograms od–bd prophylaxis), chronic CPP inflammatory arthritis, young onset, metabolic cause found.

septic-arthritis-knee.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS — hot swollen joint; BSR/BOA hot swollen joint guideline)

options.label: Recognise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute (<2 weeks) hot, swollen, painful joint with restricted movement, ± fever — in a prosthetic joint, immunosuppressed, diabetic, IV drug user, or elderly, fever and leucocytosis may be ABSENT.
2. Any acutely hot swollen joint is septic until proven otherwise (mortality ~10%, cartilage destroyed within days). Gout/pseudogout can co-exist with infection.

options.label: Action
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. SAME-DAY admission (orthopaedics/ED). Do NOT start antibiotics in primary care before joint aspiration and blood cultures unless the patient is septic and transfer is delayed.
2. Secondary care: aspiration (Gram stain, culture, crystals), blood cultures, FBC, CRP, urate; IV flucloxacillin (or per local policy/MRSA risk) for 2 weeks then oral, total 4–6 weeks; washout.
3. Prosthetic joint: never aspirate in primary care — urgent orthopaedic referral.

options.label: Follow-up
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. After discharge: complete antibiotic course, monitor CRP, physiotherapy to restore range; review risk factors (diabetes control, skin infections, immunosuppression).

fibromyalgia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG193 Chronic pain 2021; EULAR fibromyalgia 2016; NICE CKS)

options.label: Diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Chronic widespread pain ≥3 months (ACR 2016 criteria: widespread pain index + symptom severity), fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive symptoms ('fibro fog'); tender points no longer required.
2. Make a POSITIVE diagnosis in primary care and explain it — avoid repeated investigation. Baseline to exclude mimics: FBC, ESR/CRP, U&E, LFT, calcium, CK, TSH, HbA1c, vitamin D, ± ferritin, coeliac serology. Normal inflammatory markers expected.
3. Screen for and treat comorbid depression, anxiety, sleep apnoea, IBS.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Non-drug first (EULAR strong recommendation): education on central sensitisation; graded aerobic exercise (walking, aquatic) built up slowly; sleep hygiene; CBT or ACT; pain management programme; social prescribing/peer support (Versus Arthritis).
2. Drugs (modest benefit, trial 4–6 weeks, stop if no benefit): amitriptyline 10 mg at night, increase by 10 mg weekly to 25–50 mg; OR duloxetine 30 mg od → 60 mg (off-label, helpful if depression); OR pregabalin 75 mg bd → 150–225 mg bd (controlled drug, dependence risk — NICE NG193 advises against starting gabapentinoids for primary chronic pain; use only if diagnosis is fibromyalgia with specialist-level rationale).
3. Do NOT start opioids, NSAIDs, benzodiazepines, or paracetamol for fibromyalgia pain (NG193). Deprescribe existing opioids gradually.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rheumatology only for diagnostic doubt (inflammatory features, raised markers, synovitis).
2. Community pain service / pain management programme for multidisciplinary support; IAPT/talking therapies for CBT; occupational health if work affected.

foot-morton-s-neuroma.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS — forefoot pain; NICE IPG; BOFAS)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Burning/shooting forefoot pain radiating to toes, 'pebble in shoe', worse in tight shoes, relieved by removing shoe; 3rd/4th web space commonest; Mulder's click on squeeze. Women 40–60.
2. Differentials: metatarsal stress fracture, MTP synovitis/plantar plate tear (2nd MTP), Freiberg's, bursitis. USS confirms if needed.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Wide, low-heeled shoes; metatarsal dome/pad or orthoses; weight loss; activity modification; paracetamol/ibuprofen 400 mg tds prn.
2. Persistent at 3 months: USS-guided corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 20–40 mg) — relief in ~50% at 3 months; max 2.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Podiatry/MSK for orthoses and injection. Orthopaedic foot & ankle if failure after 6 months conservative care: neurectomy or radiofrequency ablation.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Lateral deviation of great toe with medial prominence, pain from shoe pressure, bursitis, transfer metatarsalgia, lesser toe deformity. Weight-bearing X-ray only if surgery considered.
2. Check for hallux rigidus (OA — pain on dorsiflexion), gout, RA, diabetic/neuropathic foot (ulceration risk).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Footwear: wide, deep toe box, low heel, soft upper; bunion pads/toe spacers for comfort (do not correct deformity); orthoses if flat foot.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol; topical or oral NSAID short course for bursitis flares.
3. Diabetic/neuropathic foot: podiatry early to prevent ulceration.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Orthopaedic foot & ankle referral for pain and functional limitation despite 6 months conservative care, ulceration/skin breakdown, or progressive lesser-toe deformity. Surgery (scarf/Akin, Lapidus, minimally invasive) is NOT for cosmesis alone; warn of 6–12 week recovery and recurrence risk.

stress-fracture.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS — sports injuries; BJSM bone stress injury consensus)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Insidious activity-related bone pain after a training increase; focal bony tenderness (stress fracture) vs diffuse posteromedial tibial tenderness over ≥5 cm (medial tibial stress syndrome).
2. Risk: female athlete triad/RED-S (ask about menstrual history, energy intake), low vitamin D, osteoporosis, long-term steroids, eating disorder, prior stress fracture.
3. X-ray first (often normal for 2–3 weeks); if normal and suspicion persists → MRI. High-risk sites needing urgent care: femoral neck, anterior tibial cortex, navicular, 5th metatarsal base, talus, sesamoid.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Low-risk sites (posteromedial tibia, 2nd–4th metatarsal shaft, fibula): offload — reduce impact, walking boot/stiff shoe if painful walking, cross-train (swim/cycle) 4–8 weeks, graded return when pain-free.
2. Medial tibial stress syndrome: relative rest 2–6 weeks, ice, calf/foot intrinsic strengthening, footwear/orthoses, gradual return (<10% weekly load increase).
3. Analgesia: paracetamol; avoid NSAIDs long term (may impair bone healing).
4. Bone health: check vitamin D and replace; calcium intake; address RED-S/menstrual dysfunction (sports dietitian, gynaecology); DEXA if recurrent.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Urgent orthopaedics: high-risk site, displaced fracture, inability to weight-bear, femoral neck pain in a runner (non-weight-bearing immediately).
2. Sports medicine/physiotherapy for return-to-sport planning; endocrinology/bone clinic if recurrent or low bone density.

compartment-syndrome.curatedBy: Claude draft (BOAST 10 Diagnosis and management of compartment syndrome; NICE CKS)

options.label: Acute — emergency
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. After fracture (tibia, forearm), crush, tight cast, reperfusion or anticoagulation: pain OUT OF PROPORTION, worse on passive stretch of the compartment muscles, tense swollen compartment, paraesthesia; pulses are preserved until late — do not wait for pulselessness.
2. Action: 999/immediate ED. Remove/split any cast or dressing to skin, keep limb at heart level (do not elevate above), analgesia, nil by mouth. Fasciotomy within hours prevents permanent damage.

options.label: Chronic exertional
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Runners/military: cramping tightness in a compartment after a predictable duration of exercise, resolves with rest; normal examination at rest; may have transient numbness.
2. Management: reduce provoking load, gait retraining (forefoot strike), footwear; physiotherapy. Diagnosis by intracompartmental pressure testing in sports medicine/orthopaedics; fasciotomy if conservative care fails.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute: emergency, never outpatient.
2. Chronic: routine sports medicine/orthopaedic referral; exclude popliteal artery entrapment and tibial stress injury first.

cubital-tunnel.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS — peripheral nerve entrapment; BSSH)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Numbness/tingling in little and ring fingers, worse with elbow flexion (phone, sleeping); positive Tinel at cubital tunnel, elbow flexion test; later weakness of grip/pinch, interossei wasting, clawing (Froment's sign).
2. Differentials: C8 radiculopathy (neck pain, triceps), thoracic outlet, Guyon's canal (dorsal hand sensation spared), medial epicondylitis.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Activity modification: avoid leaning on elbow, prolonged flexion; elbow pad; night splint/towel wrap keeping elbow ≤45° flexion for 6–12 weeks.
2. Analgesia if needed: paracetamol/NSAID. Steroid injection has no proven benefit.
3. Nerve conduction studies if persistent >6–8 weeks, any motor signs, or before surgery.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Urgent hand/plastic surgery: motor weakness, muscle wasting, or constant numbness (irreversible if delayed).
2. Routine: sensory symptoms persisting >3 months despite conservative care — decompression ± transposition.

cervical-radiculopathy.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Neck pain — cervical radiculopathy, 2024; NICE NG59 for analgesic principles)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Neck pain – cervical radiculopathy

options.label: Red flags
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Cervical MYELOPATHY (same-day/urgent neurosurgery): bilateral symptoms, gait disturbance, clumsy hands, hyperreflexia, Hoffmann's, upgoing plantars, bladder/bowel change.
2. Urgent: significant trauma, cancer history/weight loss/night pain, fever/IVDU/immunosuppression (infection), progressive motor deficit, vertebral artery symptoms (dizziness, drop attacks), age <20 or >55 with new severe pain.
3. Suspected cardiac/shoulder referral if pain not dermatomal.

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Explain: most improve in 4–6 weeks, 80–90% by 3 months without surgery. Stay active; avoid collars beyond a few days.
2. Analgesia stepwise: paracetamol/NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg tds or naproxen 500 mg bd with PPI) short course; neuropathic pain if radicular (CKS): amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrate to 25–50 mg, or gabapentin 300 mg od → tds (NG59 advises against gabapentinoids for non-radicular back pain only); short course of codeine only if severe and brief.
3. Physiotherapy: neural mobilisation, posture, strengthening; manual therapy as part of a package.
4. Imaging (MRI) only if red flags, progressive deficit, or persistent >6 weeks when intervention is being considered.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: myelopathy signs. Urgent (2 weeks): progressive weakness, intractable pain.
2. Spinal/MSK interface after 6–12 weeks of conservative care: MRI, nerve root block/epidural, or surgical decompression (ACDF) for persistent radicular pain with concordant MRI.

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Fluctuant swelling over the olecranon, usually painless with full elbow movement (unlike septic arthritis where movement is restricted).
2. SEPTIC bursitis (~1/3): warmth, erythema, tenderness, overlying skin break, fever; risks — trauma, diabetes, immunosuppression, gout, RA. Aspirate for Gram stain/culture/crystals if infection or gout suspected (aseptic technique; avoid repeated aspiration).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Aseptic: avoid pressure/leaning, compression (elastic sleeve), ice, NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg tds or naproxen 500 mg bd with food) 1–2 weeks; aspiration ± corticosteroid injection (methylprednisolone 20–40 mg) only if infection excluded and persistent — risk of skin atrophy/infection.
2. Septic: aspirate (send fluid), then flucloxacillin 500 mg–1 g qds for 7 days (clarithromycin 500 mg bd if penicillin-allergic; review MRSA risk); review at 48 h; extend course if slow response.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day orthopaedics/ED: systemically unwell, spreading cellulitis, immunosuppressed, failure to improve at 48 h on antibiotics, suspected joint involvement.
2. Routine orthopaedics: recurrent/persistent aseptic bursitis >8–12 weeks (bursectomy).

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Smooth, firm, transilluminable cystic swelling, dorsal (70%) or volar wrist, flexor sheath (pea-sized at finger base) or DIP (mucous cyst with nail ridging). Usually painless; may fluctuate in size.
2. Volar ganglion: check radial artery (Allen's test) — surgery/aspiration risk. Imaging (USS) only if diagnosis unclear (solid lump, fixed, rapid growth → 2WW sarcoma pathway).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Reassure: benign, ~50% resolve spontaneously within 1–2 years; leave alone unless painful, limiting function or cosmetically distressing after discussion. Do not 'bash with a Bible'.
2. Aspiration (large-bore needle, ± steroid) — recurrence ~50%; avoid for volar wrist ganglia (artery) unless USS-guided.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hand surgery: persistent pain, nerve compression symptoms, functional limitation, recurrent after aspiration, mucous cyst with nail deformity — excision (recurrence 10–20%). Local commissioning may require pain/function criteria (procedures of limited clinical value).

iron-deficiency-anaemia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Anaemia – iron deficiency 2024; NICE NG12; BSG 2021 IDA guideline; BNF)

options.label: Confirm and find the cause
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Anaemia: Hb <130 g/L men, <120 g/L non-pregnant women, <110 g/L pregnancy. Iron deficiency: ferritin <30 micrograms/L (ferritin is an acute-phase protein — if CRP raised or chronic disease, ferritin <100 with transferrin saturation <20% still suggests deficiency). Microcytosis with normal ferritin → thalassaemia trait (check Hb electrophoresis, family origin).
2. History: diet, menstrual loss, GI symptoms, NSAID/aspirin, weight loss, family history of colorectal cancer/coeliac. Examine abdomen; PR if GI symptoms.
3. Investigations: FBC, ferritin, B12/folate, coeliac serology (tTG-IgA + total IgA), urinalysis; FIT (≥10 micrograms/g = refer).
4. NICE NG12 — 2WW colorectal referral: age ≥60 with IDA; <50 with rectal bleeding + IDA; any adult with IDA and FIT ≥10. Men of any age and post-menopausal women with IDA without obvious cause → urgent GI referral (OGD + colonoscopy). Pre-menopausal women with menorrhagia and no GI symptoms can be treated and monitored; investigate if not responding.

options.label: Treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Ferrous sulfate 200 mg (65 mg elemental iron) ONCE daily or on alternate days — better absorbed and tolerated than tds; take with vitamin C/orange juice, away from tea, calcium, PPIs. Alternatives: ferrous fumarate 210 mg od, ferrous gluconate 300 mg od–bd (less elemental iron).
2. Expect Hb to rise ≥20 g/L in 3–4 weeks; recheck FBC at 2–4 weeks, then continue for 3 months AFTER Hb normalises to replenish stores; then FBC + ferritin every 3 months for a year.
3. Intolerance: switch preparation, alternate-day dosing, take with food (reduces absorption), liquid iron (Sytron) — avoid modified-release (poorly absorbed).
4. IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose/ferric derisomaltose — secondary care/day unit): oral failure or intolerance, malabsorption (coeliac, IBD, bariatric), CKD on ESA, late pregnancy with severe anaemia, pre-operative. Not for first trimester.
5. Failure to respond: non-adherence, ongoing blood loss, malabsorption, wrong diagnosis (thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease, mixed deficiency).

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: Hb <70 g/L or symptomatic (chest pain, breathlessness at rest, heart failure) — transfusion assessment.
2. 2WW: criteria above (NG12); also coeliac-positive → gastroenterology.
3. Routine haematology: persistent unexplained IDA after normal GI work-up; consider small-bowel capsule via gastroenterology, urinary loss, menorrhagia → gynaecology.

b12-and-folate-deficiency.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG239 Vitamin B12 deficiency 2024; NICE CKS Anaemia – B12 and folate 2024; BSH 2014; BNF)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Anaemia – B12 and folate deficiency

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Test B12 when: macrocytosis (MCV >100 fL), unexplained anaemia, neurological symptoms (paraesthesia, glove-and-stocking loss, proprioception/ataxia, cognitive change), glossitis, risk factors (vegan diet, metformin >4 months, PPI/H2RA long term, bariatric or ileal surgery, Crohn's, coeliac, autoimmune disease, nitrous oxide use).
2. Interpret (NG239): total B12 <180 ng/L (133 pmol/L) = deficiency; 180–350 ng/L indeterminate → repeat with methylmalonic acid (MMA) or active B12 if symptomatic or risk factors; do not use holotranscobalamin/MMA in pregnancy or CKD without specialist advice. Check folate, FBC, film, TFTs, LFTs; coeliac serology if malabsorption suspected.
3. Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies: positive confirms pernicious anaemia (50–70% sensitive); negative does not exclude it. Anti-parietal cell antibodies not recommended.
4. Macrocytosis with normal B12/folate: alcohol (GGT), liver disease, hypothyroidism, drugs (methotrexate, azathioprine, hydroxycarbamide, zidovudine, anticonvulsants), reticulocytosis (haemolysis), myelodysplasia (older patient, other cytopenias → haematology), pregnancy.

options.label: Treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NEUROLOGICAL symptoms: hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM on alternate days until no further improvement (specialist review), then 1 mg every 2 months. Do not delay for antibody results.
2. No neurological symptoms, malabsorptive/autoimmune cause (pernicious anaemia, ileal disease, surgery): hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM 3× weekly for 2 weeks, then 1 mg every 2–3 months for life.
3. Dietary cause or indeterminate without malabsorption (NG239): oral cyanocobalamin 1 mg daily (prescribable) or dietary advice/fortified foods; recheck at 3 months. Metformin/PPI-related: oral replacement, review need for the drug.
4. Folate deficiency: folic acid 5 mg daily for 4 months (until term in pregnancy); ALWAYS treat B12 first or together if both low — folate alone can precipitate subacute combined degeneration. Check coeliac; advise diet (green vegetables), alcohol reduction.
5. Recheck FBC and reticulocytes at 7–10 days, FBC at 8 weeks; potassium may fall transiently with brisk response — check if frail/on diuretics.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: Hb <70 or severe symptoms; acute neurological deficit.
2. Haematology: no response, pancytopenia, suspected myelodysplasia, haemolysis.
3. Gastroenterology: pernicious anaemia with dyspepsia/iron deficiency (gastric cancer/NET risk — OGD), coeliac positive, suspected Crohn's. Neurology: neurological signs not resolving.

anaemia-haemolytic.title: Anaemia – other causes (chronic disease, renal, haemolysis, marrow failure)
anaemia-haemolytic.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Anaemia – iron deficiency; NICE NG203 CKD 2021; BSH haemolysis guidance; BNF)

steps.question: Anaemia — not iron, B12 or folate

options.label: Normocytic — chronic disease / renal
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Anaemia of chronic disease/inflammation: mild (Hb 90–120), normocytic or mildly microcytic, ferritin normal/raised, transferrin saturation low, raised CRP/ESR. Causes: RA, IBD, chronic infection, malignancy, heart failure, CKD. Treat the cause; iron only if functional deficiency (ferritin <100 + TSAT <20%); check B12/folate, TFTs, LFTs, U&E, myeloma screen if >60.
2. Renal anaemia (NG203): investigate when eGFR <60 and Hb <110 (or symptomatic). Exclude iron deficiency first (ferritin <100, TSAT <20% → iron, IV preferred in CKD 4–5). Refer to renal team for ESA (epoetin/darbepoetin) if Hb persistently <100–110 after iron repletion; target Hb 100–120 g/L; check BP.
3. Also consider: hypothyroidism, alcohol, drugs (chemotherapy, zidovudine, linezolid, methotrexate), early iron deficiency, mixed deficiency (normal MCV from micro + macro).

options.label: Haemolysis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect when: anaemia with raised reticulocytes, raised unconjugated bilirubin, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, jaundice, dark urine, splenomegaly, spherocytes/fragments on film. Order: FBC + film, reticulocytes, bilirubin, LDH, haptoglobin, DAT (Coombs), U&E, LFT, urine dip (haemoglobinuria).
2. DAT-positive = autoimmune (warm: idiopathic, lymphoma, CLL, SLE, drugs e.g. methyldopa, cephalosporins; cold: mycoplasma, EBV, lymphoma) → urgent haematology; prednisolone 1 mg/kg started by specialist.
3. DAT-negative: hereditary spherocytosis (family history, osmotic fragility/EMA test), G6PD deficiency (Mediterranean/African/Asian origin; crisis with fava beans, infection, drugs — avoid dapsone, primaquine, nitrofurantoin, quinolones, sulfonamides, rasburicase; supportive care, folic acid 5 mg if chronic), microangiopathic (fragments + thrombocytopenia → TTP/HUS = EMERGENCY, same-day admission), PNH (unexplained haemolysis + thrombosis + cytopenias → flow cytometry via haematology), mechanical valve, malaria (travel).
4. Folic acid 5 mg daily in any chronic haemolysis; vaccinate and penicillin V 250 mg bd if splenectomy.

options.label: Marrow failure / pancytopenia — refer
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Pancytopenia, or anaemia with neutropenia (<1.0) or thrombocytopenia (<50), or blasts/tear-drop cells on film → URGENT haematology (same day if neutrophils <0.5, fever, or bleeding).
2. Aplastic anaemia (hypocellular marrow — drugs: chloramphenicol, carbamazepine, gold, NSAIDs; hepatitis; idiopathic), MDS (older, macrocytic, dysplastic film), sideroblastic (ring sideroblasts; alcohol, isoniazid, lead, copper deficiency, congenital — check lead level if exposure; pyridoxine trial by specialist), myelofibrosis, marrow infiltration.
3. Primary care: stop suspected drugs, neutropenic sepsis advice (temperature ≥38 °C = 999/ED), avoid IM injections if platelets low, transfusion by secondary care.

anticoagulation-warfarin-vs-doac.title: Anticoagulation – choosing, dosing, monitoring and reversal
anticoagulation-warfarin-vs-doac.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation 2021; NICE NG158 VTE 2020; NICE CKS Anticoagulation – oral 2024; BSH warfarin guideline; BNF)

options.label: Choice and dosing
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. DOAC first-line for AF (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥2 women/≥1 men) and VTE. Warfarin ONLY when DOAC unsuitable: mechanical heart valve, moderate–severe mitral stenosis, antiphospholipid syndrome (triple-positive), CrCl <15 mL/min, severe hepatic impairment, drug interactions (strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors/inducers), pregnancy (neither — LMWH).
2. Dosing (use Cockcroft–Gault CrCl, actual weight):
   • Apixaban 5 mg bd; 2.5 mg bd if ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥133 micromol/L. VTE: 10 mg bd 7 days then 5 mg bd.
   • Rivaroxaban 20 mg od with food; 15 mg od if CrCl 15–49. VTE: 15 mg bd 21 days then 20 mg od.
   • Edoxaban 60 mg od; 30 mg if CrCl 15–50, weight ≤60 kg, or ciclosporin/dronedarone/erythromycin/ketoconazole. VTE: after ≥5 days LMWH.
   • Dabigatran 150 mg bd; 110 mg bd if ≥80 years, verapamil, or high bleeding risk; avoid CrCl <30. VTE: after ≥5 days LMWH.
3. Before starting: FBC, U&E/CrCl, LFT, coagulation screen, weight; HAS-BLED/ORBIT to modify bleeding risk factors (BP, alcohol, NSAIDs, falls are NOT a reason to withhold). Review annually (6-monthly if CrCl <60 or age >75): FBC, renal function, adherence, bleeding, interactions.
4. Warfarin: INR target 2.5 (range 2–3) for AF, VTE, bioprosthetic valve; 3.0 (2.5–3.5) for mechanical mitral valve/recurrent VTE on therapeutic warfarin; loading per local slow protocol (e.g. 5 mg, 5 mg, then by INR); LMWH bridging for VTE until INR ≥2 for 24 h.

options.label: Bleeding and reversal
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. MAJOR bleeding (haemodynamic compromise, intracranial, GI with drop in Hb, any requiring transfusion/intervention): 999/ED. Secondary care: warfarin → vitamin K 5–10 mg IV + 4-factor PCC (Beriplex/Octaplex) 25–50 units/kg; dabigatran → idarucizumab 5 g IV; apixaban/rivaroxaban → andexanet alfa (NICE TA697, GI bleeding only) or PCC; edoxaban → PCC.
2. Minor bleeding (epistaxis, gum, bruising, haematuria without instability): local measures; check FBC, renal function, INR; review interacting drugs/NSAIDs; consider dose reduction if DOAC over-dosed for renal function; investigate the source (haematuria → urology 2WW if age ≥45; GI → FIT/endoscopy) — bleeding on anticoagulant unmasks pathology, do not just stop the drug.
3. Warfarin high INR without bleeding (BSH): INR 5–8 → omit 1–2 doses, reduce maintenance; INR >8 → vitamin K 1–5 mg orally (phytomenadione injection solution given orally), recheck INR 24 h; any bleeding with INR >5 → urgent assessment.
4. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: platelets fall >50% 5–10 days after heparin/LMWH ± new thrombosis → stop all heparin (incl. flushes), urgent haematology, alternative anticoagulant (argatroban/fondaparinux/DOAC); never re-expose.

options.label: Peri-procedure, interactions, switching
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Dental extraction/minor skin surgery: continue warfarin if INR <4 (check within 72 h) or DOAC (omit morning dose for high-bleed-risk extractions). Endoscopy/surgery: follow BSG/local peri-operative protocol — DOAC usually stopped 24–48 h before (longer if CrCl low or dabigatran); warfarin 5 days before with bridging only for mechanical valve/recent VTE/high-risk AF.
2. Interactions: avoid NSAIDs/aspirin unless specialist indication (post-ACS/stent — dual therapy time-limited); DOAC: rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, St John's wort (reduce effect); ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir, dronedarone (increase); warfarin: antibiotics (check INR within 3–5 days of clarithromycin, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, fluconazole), amiodarone, alcohol, cranberry.
3. Switching: warfarin → DOAC when INR <2 (rivaroxaban/edoxaban <2.5–3); DOAC → warfarin: overlap with INR monitoring on days 2–3 after stopping DOAC; LMWH → DOAC: start at next due dose.
4. Patient: anticoagulant alert card, written information, what to do if a dose is missed (DOAC: take if within 6 h for bd, 12 h for od; never double).

thrombosis-unprovoked.title: VTE – duration, unprovoked clots, thrombophilia and recurrence
thrombosis-unprovoked.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG158 Venous thromboembolic diseases 2020; BSH thrombophilia 2022; NICE CKS DVT; BNF)

steps.question: VTE: how long, and who needs more tests

options.label: Duration of anticoagulation
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Provoked (major transient risk: surgery, immobility, plaster, pregnancy/COC — now stopped): 3 months then stop (NG158). Distal DVT: 3 months. Cancer-associated: DOAC (apixaban/edoxaban/rivaroxaban; LMWH if GI/GU luminal cancer) for 6 months then review while cancer active.
2. Unprovoked DVT/PE: review at 3 months — offer continued (long-term) anticoagulation unless bleeding risk outweighs benefit; recurrence 10% in year one, ~30% at 5–10 years off treatment. Options for long term: apixaban 2.5 mg bd or rivaroxaban 10 mg od after 6 months; aspirin 75 mg only if anticoagulation declined.
3. Use HAS-BLED/VTE-BLEED and shared decision; document the plan; annual review (renal function, FBC, bleeding, adherence).
4. Compression stockings: not for post-thrombotic syndrome prevention (NG158); only for symptom relief.

options.label: Unprovoked VTE — look for a cause
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Cancer screen (NG158): history, examination, FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, urinalysis, chest X-ray; do NOT routinely CT-scan — further imaging only if symptoms/signs. Age-appropriate screening up to date (FIT, mammography, cervical). PSA in men over 50 if symptoms.
2. Antiphospholipid antibodies (anticardiolipin, anti-β2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant): test in unprovoked VTE when it would change management — before starting/when choosing anticoagulant (lupus anticoagulant unreliable on DOAC/warfarin; take before treatment or via haematology). Positive twice ≥12 weeks apart = APS → WARFARIN (INR 2–3; 3–4 if arterial/recurrent) not DOAC (NICE/MHRA: DOACs not recommended, especially triple-positive).
3. Hereditary thrombophilia (factor V Leiden, prothrombin gene, protein C/S, antithrombin): NG158 — do not test routinely; consider only if a first-degree relative has had VTE AND the result would change management (e.g. stopping anticoagulation, family planning); never test while anticoagulated or during acute VTE. Testing relatives of a known carrier is not routinely recommended.
4. Other: JAK2 if raised Hb/platelets (myeloproliferative), PNH if cytopenias or unusual site (hepatic/cerebral vein), oestrogen exposure (stop COC/HRT; progestogen-only or non-hormonal alternatives).

options.label: Recurrence and referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. VTE while on anticoagulation: check adherence, dose for weight/renal function, interactions, cancer, APS; switch to LMWH (therapeutic, weight-based, e.g. enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg od) and refer haematology urgently.
2. Second unprovoked VTE: lifelong anticoagulation (unless high bleeding risk).
3. Refer haematology/thrombosis clinic: recurrence on treatment, APS, unusual-site thrombosis, pregnancy planning on anticoagulant (warfarin teratogenic — switch to LMWH pre-conception/at positive test), need for IVC filter, heavy menstrual bleeding on anticoagulant (tranexamic acid, IUS; gynaecology).

lymphoma-2ww.title: Haematological cancer – recognising and referring (2WW)
lymphoma-2ww.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG12 Suspected cancer 2015/2023; NICE CKS Haematological cancers; NICE NG35 Myeloma; BSH)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Haematological cancers – recognition and referral

options.label: Lymphadenopathy / lymphoma
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Worrying nodes: >2 cm, persistent >6 weeks, hard/rubbery/fixed/non-tender, supraclavicular or generalised, with B symptoms (fever, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss), pruritus, alcohol-induced pain, hepatosplenomegaly.
2. NG12: consider a very urgent (48-h) FBC for children/young people with unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. Adults: 2WW haematology (lymphoma) for unexplained lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly, with greater suspicion if fever, night sweats, weight loss, pruritus, alcohol-induced pain, bruising, infection.
3. Before/alongside referral: FBC + film, ESR/CRP, LFT, LDH, HIV, EBV/CMV if young and febrile, chest X-ray (mediastinal mass); do not biopsy or start steroids in primary care (steroids mask lymphoma).
4. Reactive nodes (tender, <2 cm, recent infection) → review at 2–4 weeks; refer if persisting or enlarging.

options.label: Leukaemia / blood count abnormalities
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ACUTE leukaemia (ALL/AML): pallor, fatigue, bruising/petechiae, infections, bone pain, gum hypertrophy, hepatosplenomegaly — in children/adults with these features NG12 says FBC within 48 h; blasts, pancytopenia or WBC >50 → SAME-DAY telephone referral to haematology; neutropenic sepsis (temp ≥38) = 999.
2. CLL: lymphocytosis >5 ×10⁹/L persisting, smear cells; mostly older adults, often incidental — if asymptomatic and lymphocytes <30 with no cytopenia/nodes, repeat in 3 months then routine haematology; 2WW if lymphocytes rising rapidly, cytopenias, B symptoms, bulky nodes/spleen. Watch-and-wait is standard early management; vaccinations, infection advice.
3. CML: WBC >50 with left shift (myelocytes, basophilia), splenomegaly → urgent/2WW haematology; BCR-ABL confirms; tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib) — specialist.
4. MDS/myelofibrosis: older adult with macrocytic anaemia ± other cytopenias, tear-drop cells, splenomegaly → haematology (2WW if symptomatic/progressive).
5. Isolated splenomegaly: FBC/film, LFT, viral serology (EBV, hepatitis), USS; refer if unexplained.

options.label: Myeloma
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect (NG12/NG35) in age ≥60 with: bone pain (especially back/ribs), unexplained fracture, hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, raised ESR/plasma viscosity, recurrent infections, hyperviscosity (blurred vision, headache).
2. Order: FBC, calcium, U&E/eGFR, ESR/PV, serum protein electrophoresis + serum free light chains (or urine Bence-Jones protein), LFT, LDH, beta-2 microglobulin; plain X-ray of painful sites.
3. Paraprotein present with any of CRAB (Calcium >2.6, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions) or light chains markedly raised → 2WW haematology. Hypercalcaemia >3.0 or acute kidney injury → same-day admission.
4. MGUS (paraprotein <30 g/L, no CRAB, light-chain ratio near-normal) — see MGUS tool. Waldenström (IgM paraprotein, lymphoplasmacytic, hyperviscosity, neuropathy) → haematology.
5. Treatment is specialist (bortezomib/lenalidomide-based regimens, autologous transplant if fit; bisphosphonate zoledronate for bone disease). Primary care: analgesia (avoid NSAIDs — renal), infection vigilance, vaccinations, VTE risk on lenalidomide/thalidomide, hypercalcaemia symptoms.

mgus.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG35 Myeloma 2016; BSH MGUS guideline 2009/2024 update; NICE CKS Haematological cancers)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Haematological cancers – recognition and referral

options.label: Diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Definition: serum paraprotein <30 g/L, marrow plasma cells <10%, NO myeloma-defining events (CRAB: calcium >2.6, renal impairment attributable, Hb <100 or 20 below normal, lytic bone lesions). Prevalence 3% over 50, 5% over 70. Progression to myeloma/lymphoma ~1%/year.
2. Work-up when a paraprotein is found: FBC, calcium, U&E, serum free light chains (ratio), immunoglobulins (immunoparesis), LDH, beta-2 microglobulin, urine Bence-Jones protein, plain films of symptomatic bones; bone marrow and whole-body imaging via haematology if paraprotein ≥15 g/L, non-IgG, abnormal light-chain ratio, or symptoms.
3. Risk-stratify (Mayo): paraprotein ≥15 g/L, non-IgG type, abnormal FLC ratio — 0 factors = low risk (5% progression at 20 years); 3 factors = high risk (58%).

options.label: Monitoring
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Low-risk IgG MGUS <15 g/L with normal FLC ratio and no symptoms: can be followed in primary care (shared-care protocol): paraprotein, FBC, calcium, U&E at 6 months then annually if stable.
2. Intermediate/high-risk, IgM or IgA, or any symptoms: haematology-led follow-up (3–6 monthly initially).
3. Educate: report new bone pain, fractures, infections, weight loss, fatigue, thirst/polyuria, bleeding, neuropathy, visual change (hyperviscosity). Associated conditions: peripheral neuropathy (anti-MAG in IgM), osteoporosis (consider DEXA), VTE risk slightly raised.

options.label: Refer / escalate
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. 2WW haematology: paraprotein rising >25% or by ≥5 g/L, new CRAB feature, falling immunoglobulins, FLC ratio becoming abnormal, new anaemia or renal impairment, bone pain/fracture, hyperviscosity.
2. Same day: calcium >3.0, AKI, spinal cord compression symptoms (back pain + neurology).

polycythaemia.title: Myeloproliferative neoplasms – polycythaemia and thrombocytosis
polycythaemia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Polycythaemia/erythrocytosis 2024; BSH PV 2018 and ET 2024 guidelines; NICE NG12)

options.label: Raised haemoglobin / haematocrit
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Erythrocytosis: Hb >165 g/L or Hct >0.49 (men), Hb >160 or Hct >0.48 (women). Repeat FBC unstressed/unhurried; check for dehydration, diuretics.
2. Secondary causes (commonest): smoking, COPD/hypoxia (oxygen saturations), sleep apnoea (STOP-Bang), obesity, testosterone/anabolic steroids, EPO, renal/hepatic tumours or cysts, cyanotic heart disease, high altitude. Investigate: U&E, LFT, ferritin, oxygen saturation, serum EPO, JAK2 V617F (and exon 12 if negative with high suspicion), renal USS if EPO raised.
3. Polycythaemia vera: JAK2-positive (97%), low EPO, ± raised platelets/WBC, splenomegaly, aquagenic pruritus, erythromelalgia, gout. Risks: thrombosis (arterial and venous), transformation to myelofibrosis/AML.
4. Refer haematology (2WW if Hct >0.52 men / >0.48 women persistently, JAK2-positive, thrombosis, splenomegaly): management = venesection to Hct <0.45, aspirin 75 mg daily, cardiovascular risk control; cytoreduction (hydroxycarbamide, interferon, ruxolitinib) if high risk (age >60 or prior thrombosis).

options.label: Raised platelets
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Thrombocytosis >450 ×10⁹/L: repeat in 4–6 weeks unless very high or symptomatic. Reactive (90%): iron deficiency (check ferritin), infection/inflammation (CRP), post-surgery/trauma, post-splenectomy, malignancy, chronic inflammatory disease, drugs (steroids, adrenaline), haemolysis.
2. NG12: thrombocytosis is a cancer marker — consider 2WW for lung (age ≥40 + thrombocytosis with cough/fatigue/SOB/chest pain/weight loss/appetite loss), endometrial (≥55 + thrombocytosis + visible haematuria/vaginal discharge), gastric/oesophageal (≥55 + thrombocytosis + upper GI symptoms, or ≥55 with weight loss + dyspepsia/reflux), and consider for colorectal and other cancers. Order chest X-ray, FIT, urinalysis, CA125 in women.
3. Persistent unexplained >450 for >3 months, or >600, or with splenomegaly, thrombosis/bleeding, erythromelalgia → haematology: JAK2, CALR, MPL testing; ET diagnosis by exclusion + marrow.
4. ET management (specialist): aspirin 75 mg (avoid if platelets >1000 until acquired von Willebrand excluded), hydroxycarbamide if age >60/platelets >1500/prior thrombosis; younger — interferon or anagrelide; CV risk control.

options.label: Referral summary
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: thrombosis or bleeding with extreme counts (Hct >0.60, platelets >1500), neurological symptoms (hyperviscosity/stroke).
2. 2WW haematology: persistently raised Hct beyond thresholds, JAK2-positive, thrombocytosis with splenomegaly or constitutional symptoms. 2WW per site for cancers above.
3. Routine: secondary erythrocytosis controlled by cause (stop smoking, treat OSA, review testosterone) with FBC every 3–6 months.

thrombocytopenia.title: Thrombocytopenia – causes, ITP and when to refer
thrombocytopenia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS — thrombocytopenia; BSH ITP 2024; ASH ITP 2019; BNF)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Haematological cancers – recognition and referral

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Platelets <150 ×10⁹/L: repeat in citrate tube to exclude EDTA clumping (pseudothrombocytopenia) and review film. Bleeding risk rises below 50; spontaneous bleeding usually <20–30.
2. History: drugs (heparin — HIT, quinine/tonic water, sodium valproate, carbamazepine, linezolid, co-trimoxazole, rifampicin, NSAIDs, chemotherapy, methotrexate), alcohol, viral illness (EBV, CMV, HIV, hepatitis C), pregnancy (gestational 5–8%), liver disease/splenomegaly (hypersplenism), autoimmune (SLE, APS), recent transfusion, B12/folate deficiency, family history.
3. Tests: FBC + film, reticulocytes, clotting screen + fibrinogen, U&E, LFT, B12/folate, HIV, hepatitis B/C, H. pylori (ITP), TFTs, ANA, immunoglobulins; USS spleen if indicated.
4. RED FLAGS → same-day admission: platelets <20, active bleeding, neurological symptoms with fragments (TTP), fever/sepsis, pregnancy with platelets <80 or pre-eclampsia (HELLP), DIC picture (low platelets + prolonged PT/APTT + low fibrinogen + raised D-dimer in a sick patient — sepsis, malignancy, obstetric emergency, trauma).

options.label: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnosis of exclusion: isolated thrombocytopenia, normal film otherwise, no other cause. Children: often post-viral, 80% resolve in 6 months; adults: chronic course common.
2. Observe without treatment if platelets >30 and no bleeding (both children and adults); avoid aspirin/NSAIDs/IM injections/contact sports; manage menorrhagia (tranexamic acid 1 g tds during menses, hormonal control).
3. Treat (specialist-initiated) if platelets <20–30, bleeding, or procedure needed: prednisolone 1 mg/kg (max 80 mg) for up to 2–3 weeks then taper, or dexamethasone 40 mg daily 4 days; IVIG if rapid rise needed. Second line: thrombopoietin receptor agonists (eltrombopag, romiplostim; NICE TA293/TA221), rituximab, fostamatinib; splenectomy now rarely.
4. Eradicate H. pylori if positive (may remit ITP). Vaccinations up to date before any immunosuppression.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: criteria above; platelets <20 even without bleeding.
2. Urgent/2WW haematology: platelets <50 unexplained, other cytopenias, abnormal film (blasts, fragments, tear-drops), splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, B symptoms.
3. Routine haematology: persistent 50–100 for >3 months without clear cause; pregnancy with platelets <100 → obstetric haematology. Stop/replace suspected drug and repeat FBC at 1–2 weeks (drug-induced usually recovers within a week).

neutropenia.title: White cell count – neutropenia and leucocytosis
neutropenia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG151 Neutropenic sepsis 2012/2020; NICE CKS Haematological cancers; BSH)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Haematological cancers – recognition and referral

options.label: Neutropenia
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Neutrophils <1.5 ×10⁹/L (mild 1.0–1.5; moderate 0.5–1.0; severe <0.5). Benign ethnic (Duffy-null) neutropenia in people of African/Afro-Caribbean/Middle-Eastern origin: 1.0–1.5, stable, no infections — document, no further action.
2. NEUTROPENIC SEPSIS (NG151): neutrophils <0.5 (or <1.0 and falling) with temperature ≥38 °C or signs of sepsis, especially on chemotherapy/clozapine/carbimazole/methotrexate → 999/immediate admission for IV piperacillin-tazobactam within 1 hour. Any patient on these drugs with sore throat/fever needs an URGENT FBC the same day.
3. Causes: viral infection (transient, recheck 4–6 weeks), drugs (carbimazole, clozapine, methotrexate, azathioprine, sulfasalazine, co-trimoxazole, phenytoin, NSAIDs, antipsychotics), B12/folate deficiency, alcohol, autoimmune (SLE, Felty's), hypersplenism, HIV, marrow disorder.
4. Work-up: repeat FBC + film, B12/folate, LFT, HIV, ANA/RF, immunoglobulins; stop suspected drug. Refer haematology: neutrophils persistently <1.0, other cytopenias, recurrent infections, abnormal film; same day if <0.5.

options.label: Leucocytosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. WBC >11 ×10⁹/L — identify the lineage on differential.
2. Neutrophilia: infection, inflammation, steroids, smoking, obesity, stress, pregnancy, post-splenectomy, lithium, G-CSF; >25 with left shift/basophilia/splenomegaly → CML (urgent haematology, BCR-ABL). Leukaemoid reaction in severe sepsis.
3. Lymphocytosis: viral (EBV — monospot in young), pertussis, chronic infection; persistent >5 with smear cells (age >50) → CLL: repeat 3 months, immunophenotyping via haematology; 2WW if cytopenias/nodes/B symptoms.
4. Eosinophilia >0.5: atopy/asthma, drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, allopurinol), parasites (travel — stool O&P, strongyloides serology), EGPA, lymphoma, hypereosinophilic syndrome (>1.5 persistent with organ damage → urgent haematology; cardiac screen).
5. Monocytosis >1.0: chronic infection (TB, endocarditis), IBD, CMML in older adults → haematology if persistent.
6. Blasts or WBC >50 of any type → same-day haematology.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: neutropenic sepsis, neutrophils <0.5, blasts, WBC >50, symptoms of hyperviscosity/leucostasis.
2. 2WW haematology (NG12): unexplained persistent leucocytosis/lymphocytosis with cytopenias, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, bruising, infections or B symptoms.
3. Routine: stable mild abnormalities persisting >3 months after treating reversible causes.

sickle-cell-disease-management.title: Sickle cell disease – routine care and crisis
sickle-cell-disease-management.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CG143 Sickle cell acute painful episode 2012; NICE CKS Sickle cell disease 2024; NHS Sickle Cell Society standards; BNF)

options.label: Acute painful crisis / emergencies
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Treat as an emergency (CG143): analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival — patients know their own needs; do not label as drug-seeking. Mild crisis at home: paracetamol 1 g qds + ibuprofen 400 mg tds (if renal function normal) + codeine 30–60 mg or the patient's usual plan; warmth, hydration, rest.
2. Admit same day/999 if: pain not controlled by home regimen within hours, chest pain/breathlessness/hypoxia (ACUTE CHEST SYNDROME — life-threatening), fever ≥38 °C (functional asplenia — sepsis risk; needs IV ceftriaxone), neurological symptoms (stroke), priapism >2–4 h, abdominal pain with splenic enlargement (sequestration, especially children), Hb fall >20 g/L (aplastic crisis — parvovirus), pregnancy, severe dehydration/vomiting.
3. Hospital: opioid analgesia (morphine), avoid pethidine, oxygen if saturations <95%, IV fluids if dehydrated, incentive spirometry, VTE prophylaxis, exchange transfusion for severe complications.

options.label: Routine care
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Penicillin V 250 mg bd lifelong (erythromycin 250 mg bd if allergic); folic acid 5 mg daily.
2. Vaccines: pneumococcal (PCV + PPV23 every 5 years), annual influenza, meningococcal ACWY + B, Hib, hepatitis B, COVID; malaria prophylaxis for travel (sickle trait does NOT protect against severe disease).
3. Hydroxycarbamide (specialist-initiated, 15–35 mg/kg): ≥3 crises/year, acute chest syndrome, severe anaemia — monitor FBC monthly initially; contraception required (teratogenic). Newer: crizanlizumab (NICE TA743 withdrawn 2023), voxelotor (withdrawn 2024) — check current status.
4. Annual review (haematology-led, shared with GP): FBC, reticulocytes, ferritin (transfusion iron overload), U&E (sickle nephropathy — ACE-i if proteinuria), LFT, urinalysis, BP, oxygen saturations, retinal screening from age 10 (HbSC especially), transcranial Doppler for children 2–16, pulmonary hypertension screen if breathless, leg ulcers, gallstones, avascular necrosis, mental health.
5. Triggers to avoid: cold, dehydration, hypoxia (altitude, flights — keep hydrated), infection, alcohol, strenuous exercise, stress.

options.label: Trait, contraception, pregnancy, referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Sickle cell trait (HbAS): usually asymptomatic; rare risks — exertional rhabdomyolysis, renal medullary carcinoma (haematuria → investigate), hyposthenuria; genetic counselling for partner testing before pregnancy (antenatal screening programme).
2. Contraception: progestogen-only methods and LNG-IUS preferred (UKMEC 1–2); combined hormonal methods UKMEC 2.
3. Pregnancy: high risk — joint obstetric/haematology clinic, aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks, LMWH if admitted, stop hydroxycarbamide 3 months pre-conception.
4. All patients should have a named haematology specialist centre, an individual care plan and a crisis plan; refer if not under follow-up.

thalassaemia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Anaemia – iron deficiency (differential); UK Thalassaemia Society standards 2016; NHS Sickle Cell and Thalassaemia Screening Programme; BNF)

options.label: Trait — recognise and advise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect: microcytosis (MCV <75–80 fL) and hypochromia out of proportion to a mild anaemia, with NORMAL ferritin; raised RBC count; Mediterranean, Middle-Eastern, South Asian, South-East Asian or African family origin. Mentzer index (MCV/RBC) <13 suggests thalassaemia.
2. Confirm: Hb electrophoresis/HPLC — HbA2 >3.5% = beta thalassaemia trait; normal HPLC with persistent microcytosis and normal iron → alpha thalassaemia trait (DNA analysis if needed for family planning). Check ferritin first — co-existing iron deficiency lowers HbA2 and masks trait.
3. Do NOT give iron unless ferritin is low (risk of iron loading). Reassure: trait is not a disease; MCV will always be low — annotate the record so future microcytosis is not re-investigated.
4. Genetic counselling: partner testing before/early in pregnancy (NHS screening programme by 10 weeks); if both carriers → refer for prenatal diagnosis counselling. Alpha-trait (two gene deletions in cis, --/αα, common in SE Asian origin) risks Hb Bart's hydrops — specialist advice.

options.label: Thalassaemia intermedia / major
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Major: transfusion-dependent from infancy; intermedia: variable anaemia (Hb 70–100), splenomegaly, bone changes, extramedullary haematopoiesis. All should be under a specialist haemoglobinopathy centre with an annual review and care plan.
2. Specialist-led: regular transfusion to pre-transfusion Hb 95–105; iron chelation (deferasirox, deferiprone, desferrioxamine) guided by ferritin and MRI T2* (cardiac/liver iron); folic acid 5 mg; splenectomy rarely; luspatercept (NICE TA-pending/approved for transfusion-dependent beta thalassaemia — check current TA); stem cell transplant in children; gene therapy emerging.
3. GP role: vaccinations (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, influenza, hepatitis B — especially if splenectomised, plus penicillin V 250 mg bd), monitor complications — endocrine (diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypogonadism, hypoparathyroidism from iron), cardiac, liver, osteoporosis (DEXA), gallstones, leg ulcers, VTE; avoid iron supplements; fertility/pregnancy planning via specialist.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Haematology/haemoglobinopathy centre: any thalassaemia beyond simple trait; trait with unexplained anaemia or Hb <100; couples at risk for counselling.
2. Same day: transfusion-dependent patient with fever (sepsis/splenectomy), chest pain/arrhythmia (cardiac iron), severe anaemia symptoms.

von-willebrand.title: Bleeding disorders – von Willebrand disease and haemophilia carriers
von-willebrand.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG88 Heavy menstrual bleeding 2018; BSH von Willebrand 2014/2021; UKHCDO; NICE CKS Bruising)

options.label: When to suspect and test
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Bleeding history (use a bleeding assessment tool, e.g. ISTH-BAT): easy bruising >5 cm, epistaxis >10 min or needing packing, prolonged bleeding after dental extraction/surgery/childbirth, heavy menstrual bleeding since menarche (NG88: test for coagulation disorder if HMB since menarche AND personal or family history of bleeding), gum bleeding, haemarthrosis/muscle bleeds (haemophilia), family history.
2. Exclude: drugs (aspirin, NSAIDs, SSRIs, anticoagulants), liver disease, renal failure, thrombocytopenia, vitamin K deficiency, non-accidental injury in children/vulnerable adults (safeguarding).
3. First-line tests: FBC + film, PT, APTT, fibrinogen, ferritin, U&E, LFT. Note APTT may be NORMAL in mild vWD/mild haemophilia — a normal screen does not exclude a bleeding disorder if history is strong → request von Willebrand screen (vWF antigen, vWF activity/ristocetin cofactor, factor VIII) and factor IX; blood group O lowers vWF levels (interpret with haematology). Avoid testing in acute illness/pregnancy/on COC (raise vWF).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. All confirmed bleeding disorders are registered with a haemophilia comprehensive care centre (UKHCDO) with a care plan, alert card and emergency contact; GP should not start treatment unsupervised.
2. von Willebrand (type 1 commonest, 70%): tranexamic acid 1 g tds–qds for mucosal bleeding/menorrhagia/dental work (started by GP per care plan); desmopressin (DDAVP) 0.3 micrograms/kg IV/SC or 300 micrograms intranasal (Octim) for type 1 responders — trial dose at centre first; fluid restriction after dose (hyponatraemia); vWF/FVIII concentrate for major surgery or type 2B/3. Heavy menstrual bleeding: tranexamic acid, LNG-IUS or combined pill (also raises vWF) — gynaecology/haematology joint care.
3. Haemophilia carriers: factor VIII/IX levels can be low (<40 IU/dL) — carriers can bleed; check level, give a care plan; genetic counselling, antenatal planning (male fetus 50% affected; avoid ventouse/fetal scalp electrodes); daughters/sisters offered testing at an appropriate age.
4. Avoid aspirin/NSAIDs (paracetamol, COX-2 only on advice), IM injections (give vaccines SC or with pressure 5 min), contact sports in severe disease; dental care with centre liaison; hepatitis A/B immunisation.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: any significant bleed (head injury, haemarthrosis, GI, post-operative, trauma) in a known bleeding disorder — contact the haemophilia centre/ED; give the patient's usual factor if they self-treat.
2. Routine haematology: positive bleeding history with abnormal screen, or strong history with normal screen; before surgery/pregnancy in known carriers; children with unexplained bruising after safeguarding assessment.

bite-animal.title: Bites – animal and human
niceRefs: NICE CKS Bites – human and animal

options.label: Wound care and assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Irrigate thoroughly with warm running water/saline; remove foreign material; do not close puncture wounds or hand bites primarily. Assess depth, tendon/joint/bone involvement, neurovascular status. X-ray if fracture, foreign body (tooth) or joint involvement suspected.
2. Tetanus: give booster (Td/IPV) if >10 years since last dose or incomplete course; tetanus immunoglobulin if high-risk wound and incomplete immunisation.
3. Rabies: any bite abroad in a rabies-endemic country, or any bat contact in the UK → same-day UKHSA advice for post-exposure vaccine ± immunoglobulin.
4. Human bite: assess blood-borne virus risk (hepatitis B vaccination/HBIG, HIV PEP if source high-risk — see Needlestick); consider safeguarding/assault documentation.

options.label: Antibiotics
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Cat bite or human bite that has broken skin and drawn blood: prophylactic antibiotics. Dog bite: prophylaxis only if broken skin AND (drawn blood, deep/puncture, hand/foot/face/genitals, prosthetic joint/valve, immunosuppressed, diabetes, asplenia, cirrhosis).
