2. First line: co-amoxiclav 625 mg tds for 3 days (prophylaxis) or 5–7 days (infected). Penicillin allergy: doxycycline 200 mg stat then 100 mg bd + metronidazole 400 mg tds. Children: co-amoxiclav by weight; co-trimoxazole + metronidazole if allergic.
3. Review at 24–48 h for hand bites and infected wounds.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day plastics/orthopaedics/ED: hand or face bites with tendon/joint involvement, deep puncture, devitalised tissue, foreign body, spreading infection, systemic illness, immunosuppressed, bites to genitals, uncontrolled bleeding.
2. Plastics: cosmetic facial wounds needing closure (within 24 h).
3. Infection not responding at 48 h → admit for IV antibiotics.

bite-animal.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

lyme-disease.title: Lyme disease and tick bites

options.label: Tick bite without symptoms
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Remove tick promptly with fine tweezers/tick tool, straight out, no twisting/burning; clean. Transmission risk rises after 24–36 h attachment.
2. NG95: NO prophylactic antibiotics and NO testing after an asymptomatic bite. Advise to watch for erythema migrans (expanding rash ≥5 cm, 3 days–3 months) and flu-like symptoms for up to 3 months; prevention advice (repellent, cover skin, tick checks).

options.label: Diagnosis and treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Erythema migrans = clinical diagnosis: treat immediately, do NOT test. Other presentations (facial palsy, radiculopathy, arthritis, carditis, lymphocytoma) → ELISA; if negative but <4 weeks since symptoms, repeat at 4–6 weeks; positive/equivocal ELISA → immunoblot.
2. Adults — erythema migrans or non-focal: doxycycline 100 mg bd (or 200 mg od) for 21 days; alternatives amoxicillin 1 g tds 21 days, azithromycin 500 mg od 17 days. Lyme arthritis/acrodermatitis: doxycycline 28 days. Cranial nerve/peripheral nerve involvement: doxycycline 21 days. CNS (meningitis, encephalitis): IV ceftriaxone 2 g od 21 days (admit). Carditis with haemodynamic compromise: admit, IV ceftriaxone.
3. Children <12: amoxicillin 30 mg/kg tds 21 days (doxycycline over 12 or specialist advice). Pregnancy: amoxicillin.
4. Jarisch–Herxheimer reaction possible in first 24 h — warn.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: Lyme carditis (syncope, heart block), meningitis/encephalitis.
2. Specialist (infectious diseases/neurology/rheumatology/paediatrics): focal symptoms, persistent symptoms after a completed course (second course only once — do not repeat indefinitely), diagnostic uncertainty, pregnancy with disseminated disease. Persistent fatigue after treatment is NOT ongoing infection — supportive management.

lyme-disease.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

tb-suspect.title: Tuberculosis – suspect, latent, active and contacts

options.label: When to suspect and investigate
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect: cough >3 weeks, haemoptysis, fever, night sweats, weight loss, fatigue; risk — born in/travel to high-incidence country, close contact, HIV, immunosuppression (anti-TNF, steroids, transplant), diabetes, homelessness, prison, alcohol/drug dependence, silicosis.
2. Pulmonary: chest X-ray (upper-lobe infiltrates, cavitation, nodes); 3 sputum samples (one early morning) for AFB smear, culture and NAAT; HIV test, FBC, LFT, U&E. Extrapulmonary (lymph node, spine, CNS, GU, bone, abdominal): imaging ± biopsy/aspirate for culture — refer.
3. Suspected TB is a notifiable disease on clinical suspicion; refer to the local TB service the same week (same day if unwell, haemoptysis, suspected CNS/spinal TB, or infectious risk in a congregate setting). Do NOT start antibiotics with anti-TB activity (fluoroquinolones) for undifferentiated pneumonia if TB possible.

options.label: Active TB (specialist-led) — GP role
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Standard regimen: rifampicin + isoniazid + pyrazinamide + ethambutol 2 months, then rifampicin + isoniazid 4 months (6 months total); CNS TB 12 months (plus dexamethasone); spinal TB 6 months ± surgery for instability/neurology; pyridoxine 10 mg daily with isoniazid.
2. GP: support adherence (DOT/VOT via TB nurse); monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity — stop and contact TB team if ALT >3× with symptoms or >5×); visual symptoms on ethambutol (stop, urgent review); rifampicin interactions — COC ineffective (use IUD/injectable), warfarin, DOAC, anticonvulsants, HIV drugs, orange secretions; peripheral neuropathy (isoniazid).
3. Infectiousness: smear-positive pulmonary TB usually non-infectious after 2 weeks of treatment; off work/school until TB team advises. Contact tracing by TB service/UKHSA.

options.label: Latent TB and contacts
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Screen (NG33): close contacts of pulmonary/laryngeal TB, new entrants from high-incidence countries (≥40/100,000) aged 16–65 (test if <35 for treatment; HIV-positive any age), before anti-TNF/biologics, transplant, dialysis, HIV. Test: IGRA (adults) or Mantoux (children <2 and BCG-naive); chest X-ray to exclude active disease before treating latent TB.
2. Treatment (TB service): 3 months rifampicin + isoniazid (3HR) or 6 months isoniazid (6H); offer to under-65s (balance hepatotoxicity risk over 35). Baseline and monthly LFT if risk.
3. Contacts: refer all household/close contacts to TB service; children <2 in contact with smear-positive case need urgent assessment (prophylaxis). BCG for unvaccinated under-16 contacts if Mantoux negative.

shingles.title: Shingles and chickenpox in adults

options.label: Shingles
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Antiviral within 72 h of rash (or later if new vesicles still forming, ophthalmic, immunocompromised, or severe): aciclovir 800 mg 5×/day 7 days, or valaciclovir 1 g tds 7 days (better adherence), or famciclovir 500 mg tds. Offer to all ≥50, any ophthalmic/non-truncal, moderate–severe pain or rash, immunocompromised.
2. Analgesia: paracetamol ± codeine; neuropathic pain early — amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte or gabapentin 300 mg titrated; no evidence steroids prevent PHN. Keep rash covered, avoid contact with pregnant women, neonates, immunocompromised until crusted.
3. Post-herpetic neuralgia (>3 months): amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin/pregabalin per NICE CG173; topical lidocaine 5% plaster or capsaicin 0.075% cream; pain clinic if refractory.
4. Shingles vaccine (Shingrix, 2 doses): offered at 65 (phased to 60) and 70–79, and immunocompromised ≥50 — check eligibility.

options.label: Red flags and referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Ophthalmic zoster (V1 dermatome, especially tip of nose — Hutchinson's sign), red eye, visual symptoms → same-day ophthalmology + oral antiviral.
2. Ramsay Hunt (ear vesicles + facial palsy) → antiviral + prednisolone 60 mg 7 days, ENT review. Disseminated zoster (>2 dermatomes), immunocompromised, motor involvement, severe systemic illness → admit for IV aciclovir.
3. Shingles in under-40s with no cause: consider HIV test.

options.label: Chickenpox in adults
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Adults (≥14): aciclovir 800 mg 5×/day for 7 days if within 24 h of rash (reduces severity); paracetamol (NOT ibuprofen — necrotising fasciitis risk), calamine, chlorphenamine for itch; fluids; exclude from work until lesions crusted (~5 days).
2. Admit: pneumonitis (cough, breathlessness, chest pain — smokers, pregnancy), encephalitis, haemorrhagic rash, immunocompromised.
3. PREGNANCY: non-immune woman exposed (face-to-face/15 min same room) → check VZV IgG urgently; if negative, oral aciclovir prophylaxis day 7–14 post-exposure (UKHSA 2022 — VZIG now reserved for those who cannot take aciclovir) and inform obstetrics; chickenpox in pregnancy → oral aciclovir if ≥20 weeks and within 24 h, obstetric review, fetal medicine referral (<28 weeks for fetal varicella syndrome risk). Neonates of mothers with chickenpox 7 days before to 7 days after delivery → VZIG/aciclovir via paediatrics.

influenza-antiviral.title: Influenza and COVID-19 – antivirals, vaccination, long COVID

options.label: Influenza
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Antivirals only when UKHSA has confirmed flu is circulating AND patient is in an at-risk group (≥65, chronic heart/lung/renal/liver/neuro disease, diabetes, immunosuppressed, pregnant, BMI ≥40, care home) or severely unwell: oseltamivir 75 mg bd for 5 days within 48 h of symptoms (dose-adjust CrCl <60); zanamivir inhaled if oseltamivir resistance/intolerance. Post-exposure prophylaxis (oseltamivir 75 mg od 10 days) for at-risk contacts within 48 h, especially care-home outbreaks (UKHSA advice).
2. Otherwise supportive: paracetamol/ibuprofen, fluids, rest; safety-net — breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, haemoptysis, failure to improve after 1 week → review/admit.
3. Vaccination annually (Sept–Dec): ≥65, at-risk groups, pregnant women (any trimester), carers, health/social care workers, children 2–17 (nasal LAIV; inactivated if egg allergy/immunosuppressed contact), care home residents; adjuvanted (aQIV) for ≥65.

options.label: COVID-19
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Highest-risk patients (NICE TA878 eligibility: e.g. Down's syndrome, solid organ/stem cell transplant, haematological malignancy, immunosuppressed, CKD 4–5, advanced HIV, certain lung/liver/neurological conditions, ≥70 or ≥85 with risk factors — check current list) with positive test and symptoms ≤5 days: nirmatrelvir/ritonavir (Paxlovid) 300/100 mg bd 5 days (check interactions — statins, DOACs, antiplatelets, immunosuppressants; CrCl 30–60 half dose; avoid <30), or molnupiravir 800 mg bd 5 days if Paxlovid unsuitable, or remdesivir IV via CMDU. Refer to the local CMDU/COVID treatment pathway the same day.
2. All others: supportive; antibiotics only for bacterial complication; admit if saturations <92% (or 3% below baseline), RR >30, confusion, chest pain. Dexamethasone only for hospitalised hypoxic patients.
3. Vaccination: spring/autumn boosters for ≥75, care home residents, immunosuppressed ≥6 months; autumn for at-risk groups per Green Book.

options.label: Long COVID (NG188)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Ongoing symptomatic COVID 4–12 weeks; post-COVID syndrome >12 weeks not explained by another diagnosis. Common: fatigue, breathlessness, cognitive 'fog', palpitations, chest pain, anosmia, anxiety/depression, sleep disturbance.
2. Exclude alternatives: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, CRP, ferritin, HbA1c, BNP; ECG; chest X-ray at 12 weeks if respiratory symptoms; oxygen saturations/exercise desaturation test; PHQ-9/GAD-7; orthostatic BP/HR (POTS).
3. Management: self-paced return to activity (avoid graded exercise if post-exertional malaise), breathing retraining, sleep, olfactory training for anosmia, occupational health/fit note with phased return; refer post-COVID assessment service if symptoms >12 weeks affecting function; cardiology/respiratory if abnormal tests.

helicobacter-eradication.title: Helicobacter pylori – testing and eradication
niceRefs: NICE CKS Dyspepsia – proven GORD/unidentified cause

options.label: Testing
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Test and treat for uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features (after 4 weeks PPI trial or first line if high-prevalence background), proven peptic ulcer, MALT lymphoma, before long-term NSAID, unexplained iron deficiency after GI work-up, ITP.
2. Test: carbon-13 urea breath test or stool antigen — patient must be OFF PPI for 2 weeks and antibiotics for 4 weeks. Serology not recommended (remains positive after cure).
3. Retest for eradication (breath test, 4 weeks post-treatment) only if: ulcer, MALT lymphoma, persistent symptoms, family history gastric cancer, or patient preference.

options.label: First-line eradication (7 days, all tds bd as listed)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. PPI (omeprazole 20 mg bd / lansoprazole 30 mg bd / esomeprazole 20 mg bd) + amoxicillin 1 g bd + clarithromycin 500 mg bd OR metronidazole 400 mg bd — choose metronidazole if clarithromycin exposure in past year, clarithromycin if metronidazole exposure.
2. Penicillin allergy: PPI + clarithromycin 500 mg bd + metronidazole 400 mg bd. Penicillin allergy with prior clarithromycin: PPI + bismuth subsalicylate 525 mg qds + metronidazole 400 mg bd + tetracycline 500 mg qds (bismuth quadruple).
3. Counsel: adherence (failure usually = resistance or non-adherence), metallic taste, avoid alcohol with metronidazole, diarrhoea; interactions — clarithromycin with statins (hold simvastatin), warfarin, DOACs.

options.label: Second line and failure
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Second line (7 days): PPI + amoxicillin 1 g bd + whichever of clarithromycin/metronidazole was NOT used first; if both used before: PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin 250 mg bd (or tetracycline 500 mg qds). Penicillin allergy: PPI + metronidazole + levofloxacin; or bismuth quadruple.
2. Third line: refer gastroenterology for culture-guided therapy (OGD with biopsies for sensitivities); rifabutin-based regimen by specialist.
3. Persistent symptoms after confirmed eradication → manage as functional dyspepsia; OGD if alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, haematemesis, anaemia, age ≥55 with persistent symptoms — NG12).

dengue.title: Fever in the returning traveller – dengue, typhoid and other imported infections
niceRefs: NICE CKS Fever in returning travellers (via UKHSA/NaTHNaC)

options.label: First actions — exclude malaria
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Fever within 12 months of travel to the tropics = MALARIA until proven otherwise: same-day blood film ×3 (and rapid antigen) via ED/acute medicine; do not wait for GP results if unwell. Falciparum can kill within 24–48 h.
2. Also same day: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, blood cultures, urinalysis, glucose; dengue NS1/PCR, typhoid cultures (blood ± stool), HIV test. Ask: countries, dates, rural/urban, mosquito bites, food/water, freshwater exposure, animal contact, sexual contact, vaccinations/prophylaxis, onset relative to return (incubation).
3. Admit if unwell, bleeding, dehydration, confusion, jaundice, pregnancy, or any positive malaria test. Notifiable diseases: malaria, typhoid, dengue (suspected), leptospirosis, brucellosis.

options.label: Arboviruses — dengue, chikungunya, Zika
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Dengue (S/SE Asia, Americas, Africa; incubation 4–10 days): fever, severe myalgia/'breakbone', retro-orbital headache, rash day 3–5, thrombocytopenia, raised ALT. Supportive: paracetamol, oral fluids — AVOID NSAIDs/aspirin (bleeding). WARNING signs (days 3–7, as fever settles): abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, lethargy, fluid accumulation, rising haematocrit with falling platelets → admit (dengue shock). Daily FBC until recovery.
2. Chikungunya: fever + severe symmetrical polyarthralgia (hands/feet), may persist months; supportive, NSAIDs once dengue excluded; rheumatology if chronic arthritis.
3. Zika: mild rash/conjunctivitis/arthralgia; PREGNANCY — fetal microcephaly risk: refer obstetrics/fetal medicine; avoid conception for 2 months (women) / 3 months (men) after travel; barrier contraception. Testing via UKHSA RIPL.

options.label: Bacterial — typhoid, leptospirosis, brucellosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Typhoid/paratyphoid (South Asia; incubation 6–30 days): sustained fever, headache, abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhoea, relative bradycardia, rose spots, leucopenia. Blood cultures before antibiotics; treat in secondary care/ID: IV ceftriaxone 2 g od (fluoroquinolone resistance in South Asia; azithromycin 500 mg–1 g od 7 days for uncomplicated oral treatment). Exclude from food handling until clearance stools.
2. Leptospirosis (freshwater exposure, rats, Weil's disease): fever, myalgia (calves), conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage; serology/PCR via UKHSA; doxycycline 100 mg bd 7 days (mild) or IV benzylpenicillin/ceftriaxone (admit if jaundice/AKI). Prophylaxis doxycycline 200 mg weekly for high-risk exposure.
3. Brucellosis (unpasteurised dairy, Middle East/Mediterranean): undulant fever, sweats, arthralgia, sacroiliitis, epididymo-orchitis; serology; doxycycline 100 mg bd 6 weeks + rifampicin 600–900 mg od 6 weeks (or + gentamicin/streptomycin) — ID-led. Notify.

hepatitis-a.title: Hepatitis A and E

options.label: Diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Prodrome (malaise, nausea, anorexia, fever) then jaundice, dark urine, pale stool, RUQ pain; ALT often >1000. Hepatitis A: travel, shellfish, MSM, outbreaks, household contact (incubation 2–6 weeks). Hepatitis E: UK pork products (genotype 3 — autochthonous, older men), travel (genotype 1), may be anicteric; neurological complications (Guillain–Barré, neuralgic amyotrophy).
2. Tests: LFT, INR, FBC, U&E, hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis E IgM/IgG + HEV RNA, hepatitis B surface antigen/core IgM, hepatitis C antibody, EBV/CMV, paracetamol level if relevant, autoimmune screen if persisting. Both are NOTIFIABLE on suspicion (UKHSA arranges contact prophylaxis).

options.label: Management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Supportive: rest, fluids, antiemetics (cyclizine), avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs (review paracetamol dose ≤2 g/day, statins, methotrexate); itch — chlorphenamine/colestyramine. Most recover in 2–8 weeks; hepatitis A never chronic; hepatitis E chronic only if immunosuppressed (ribavirin via hepatology).
2. Hygiene: hand washing, no food handling/preparation for others until 1 week after jaundice onset; exclude from school/work 7 days from onset.
3. Repeat LFT/INR weekly until improving; check pregnancy (hepatitis E in pregnancy carries 20% mortality in genotype 1 — specialist care).

options.label: Referral and prevention
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Admit: INR >1.5, encephalopathy (confusion, drowsiness), bilirubin rising with falling ALT, vomiting/unable to maintain hydration, pregnancy with hepatitis E, immunosuppressed, age >60 with hepatitis E.
2. Hepatitis A prevention: vaccine for travellers to endemic areas, MSM, PWID, chronic liver disease, haemophilia, occupational risk; post-exposure — vaccine within 14 days to household/close contacts (UKHSA), HNIG in addition for >60, chronic liver disease, immunosuppressed. No hepatitis E vaccine in UK — cook pork thoroughly.

hepatitis-a.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

options.label: Immediate
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Encourage bleeding (do not suck), wash with soap and running water, cover; eyes/mouth — irrigate with water. Record: time, type of injury (hollow-bore, depth, visible blood), source (known/unknown, HIV/HBV/HCV status, viral load).
2. Occupational: contact occupational health/ED within 1 hour — HIV PEP is most effective <24 h and not given after 72 h. Community (discarded needle): risk very low but assess same day.

options.label: Post-exposure prophylaxis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. HIV PEP (via ED/GUM/OH): tenofovir-emtricitabine 1 od + raltegravir 400 mg bd (or dolutegravir 50 mg od) for 28 days — start within 72 h if source HIV-positive with detectable viral load, or unknown source in high-prevalence setting; NOT needed if source on ART with undetectable viral load (U=U). Baseline HIV test, repeat at 6 weeks and 12 weeks.
2. Hepatitis B: test exposed person's anti-HBs; if vaccinated responder (≥10 mIU/mL) — booster only if ≥5 years; non-immune/unvaccinated — accelerated vaccine course (0, 1, 2 months) ± HBIG within 48 h (72 h max) if source HBsAg-positive/high risk.
3. Hepatitis C: no PEP; test HCV antibody/RNA at baseline, 6 weeks (RNA) and 12 weeks/6 months; early treatment with DAAs if seroconverts.

options.label: Follow-up and tetanus
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Tetanus booster if >10 years or unknown; TIG for heavily contaminated wounds.
2. Advise barrier contraception and no blood donation until final testing; document incident (RIDDOR if occupational); support/counselling; source testing with consent via the treating team.

necrotising-fasciitis.title: Severe and unusual soft-tissue infections – necrotising fasciitis, lymphadenitis, cat-scratch

options.label: Necrotising fasciitis — recognise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Pain OUT OF PROPORTION to skin findings, rapidly spreading erythema/oedema, skin anaesthesia, bullae, dusky/grey discolouration, crepitus, systemic toxicity (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion), rapid progression over hours; risk — diabetes, immunosuppression, IV drug use, recent surgery/trauma, chickenpox, NSAID use.
2. 999/immediate surgical admission — this is a surgical emergency (debridement within hours; mortality 20–30%). Do not delay for imaging or GP antibiotics; if transfer delayed, IV benzylpenicillin + clindamycin per sepsis protocol in secondary care. Mark the edge of erythema and time it.

options.label: Lymphadenitis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute tender enlarged node(s) with overlying erythema, usually bacterial (Staph aureus, group A strep) from a skin/throat source; children common. Examine for source; FBC/CRP if unwell; USS if fluctuant.
2. Flucloxacillin 500 mg–1 g qds (child by weight) for 7 days, or clarithromycin 500 mg bd if penicillin-allergic; review at 48 h; aspiration/I&D if abscess.
3. Admit: systemically unwell, neck swelling with airway concern/trismus, <3 months old, immunocompromised, no response at 48 h. Persistent (>4–6 weeks), non-tender, >2 cm, supraclavicular → see Haematological cancer 2WW; consider TB, atypical mycobacteria (child, violaceous skin), cat-scratch, toxoplasmosis, HIV.

options.label: Cat-scratch disease
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Bartonella henselae: papule at scratch site 3–10 days, then tender regional lymphadenopathy (axilla/neck) 1–3 weeks, low-grade fever, malaise; usually self-limiting over 2–4 months. Serology (Bartonella IgG/IgM) if diagnosis unclear.
2. Mild: no antibiotics needed; analgesia; warm compress; avoid I&D (sinus) — needle aspiration if painful.
3. Azithromycin 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg days 2–5 (child 10 mg/kg then 5 mg/kg) for bulky/painful nodes or immunocompromised. Refer: neuroretinitis (visual loss), encephalopathy, hepatosplenic disease, endocarditis, HIV (bacillary angiomatosis) → ID/ophthalmology.

niceRefs: NICE CKS Boils, carbuncles and staphylococcal carriage

options.label: Who to screen and decolonise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Screen (nose, throat, perineum/groin, wounds, catheter sites) before elective surgery per hospital policy, on admission to high-risk units, care-home residents with wounds/catheters, and in recurrent furunculosis (also screen household contacts).
2. Decolonise: known MRSA carriers before surgery/admission; recurrent staphylococcal skin infections (MSSA or MRSA) after acute infection treated.

options.label: Decolonisation regimen (5 days)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mupirocin 2% nasal ointment to the inner surface of each nostril tds for 5 days (if mupirocin-resistant: naseptin — contains peanut oil — qds 10 days, or octenidine nasal gel).
2. Chlorhexidine 4% body wash (or octenidine wash) daily for 5 days, including hair on days 1 and 5; dry with clean towel; clean clothes, bedding and towels daily; hot wash.
3. Treat skin conditions (eczema) that harbour carriage; nail hygiene; do not share razors/towels. Re-screen ≥48 h after finishing if required by the surgical pathway; repeat course once if still positive (limit to 2 courses — resistance).

options.label: Treating MRSA infection
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mild skin/soft tissue infection with MRSA on culture: doxycycline 100 mg bd (or 200 mg od) 7 days, or clindamycin 300–450 mg qds, or co-trimoxazole 960 mg bd — per sensitivities and local microbiology advice.
2. Admit for IV vancomycin/teicoplanin/linezolid: systemic illness, deep infection, bacteraemia, prosthetic material, failure of oral therapy. Inform hospital of MRSA status on any referral.

cytomegalovirus.title: CMV and toxoplasmosis

options.label: Immunocompetent adults
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Both cause a glandular-fever-like illness (fever, fatigue, lymphadenopathy, atypical lymphocytes, mild hepatitis) with negative monospot. Tests: CMV IgM/IgG (± avidity), toxoplasma IgM/IgG (IgG avidity to time infection), LFT, FBC/film, EBV serology, HIV test.
2. Management supportive — no antivirals in immunocompetent adults; toxoplasma chorioretinitis or severe disease → ophthalmology/ID (pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid, or co-trimoxazole).
3. Toxoplasma exposure advice: avoid undercooked meat, wash fruit/veg, gloves for gardening/cat litter.

options.label: Pregnancy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Primary CMV in pregnancy (commonest congenital infection): if suspected (seroconversion, symptoms, fetal USS findings) → refer fetal medicine urgently; high-dose valaciclovir 8 g/day in first trimester seroconversion reduces transmission (specialist); amniocentesis for fetal PCR after 21 weeks. Hygiene advice for all pregnant women with toddlers: hand washing after nappies/saliva contact, do not share utensils.
2. Toxoplasmosis in pregnancy: confirm with reference lab (IgG avidity); spiramycin 1 g tds to reduce transmission until fetal infection excluded; if fetal infection (amniotic PCR) — pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/folinic acid from 18 weeks; fetal medicine.
3. Congenital CMV in neonate: urine/saliva CMV PCR within 21 days of birth; valganciclovir 6 months for symptomatic infants (hearing/neurology) — paediatric ID.

options.label: Immunocompromised
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. HIV (CD4 <50–100), transplant, chemotherapy: CMV retinitis (floaters, visual loss → same-day ophthalmology; valganciclovir 900 mg bd induction), colitis, pneumonitis, encephalitis; toxoplasma encephalitis (focal neurology, seizures, ring-enhancing lesions → emergency admission; pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine or co-trimoxazole).
2. Prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole 480–960 mg od for toxoplasma-seropositive HIV patients with CD4 <200; CMV monitoring/pre-emptive valganciclovir per transplant protocol. All managed with the specialist team; GP checks FBC (neutropenia on valganciclovir).

presbyacusis.title: Hearing loss and tinnitus
niceRefs: NICE NG98 Hearing loss in adults
NICE CKS Hearing loss in adults

options.label: Red flags — urgent
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. SUDDEN sensorineural hearing loss (over ≤72 h, Weber lateralises to the good ear, Rinne positive/normal in affected ear, no wax): same-day ENT/ED — oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (max 60 mg) for 7 days started within 24–72 h plus audiology; MRI IAM to exclude acoustic neuroma.
2. Also urgent (NG98): unilateral hearing loss with focal neurology, head injury, fluctuating loss with vertigo, immunocompromised with otalgia/discharge (malignant otitis externa — same day), suspected cholesteatoma. 2WW ENT: unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus with other cranial nerve signs, or in a person of Chinese/SE Asian origin (nasopharyngeal carcinoma).
3. Pulsatile tinnitus (synchronous with heartbeat): examine for bruit, check BP, FBC, TFT; refer ENT for imaging (MRA/CT) — glomus tumour, carotid stenosis, dural AV fistula, idiopathic intracranial hypertension (obese young woman, headache, papilloedema).

options.label: Age-related and conductive loss
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Presbyacusis: bilateral, gradual, high-frequency sensorineural; otoscopy normal. Refer audiology directly (no ENT needed) for hearing aids — NG98: offer hearing aids to anyone whose hearing loss affects communication; NHS hearing aids free. Review ototoxic drugs (aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, cisplatin, high-dose aspirin, quinine); check for depression/cognitive effects of untreated loss.
2. Conductive loss (Rinne negative, Weber to affected ear): wax (olive oil 3–5 days then irrigation/microsuction), glue ear, otosclerosis (young adult, family history, worse in pregnancy, normal drum, Carhart's notch on audiogram → ENT: hearing aid or stapedectomy), chronic otitis media, ossicular disruption after trauma.
3. Asymmetric sensorineural loss (>15 dB difference at two frequencies) → ENT for MRI (vestibular schwannoma).

options.label: Tinnitus (NG155)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Assess: hearing (audiology for all persistent tinnitus), otoscopy, drugs (NSAIDs, aspirin, loop diuretics, SSRIs, quinine), noise exposure, TMJ, anxiety/depression (PHQ-9/GAD-7), sleep, impact (Tinnitus Handicap Inventory).
2. Explain: common (10% adults), usually benign, habituation expected; avoid silence (sound enrichment/white noise), manage caffeine/alcohol, sleep hygiene. Hearing aids if any hearing loss — often the best tinnitus treatment. Psychological: CBT-based tinnitus therapy via audiology/IAPT; tinnitus retraining therapy; British Tinnitus Association resources. No drugs are effective for tinnitus itself; treat insomnia/depression.
3. Refer ENT: unilateral, pulsatile, associated vertigo or neurology, objective tinnitus, severe distress not improving with audiology-led care, suicidal ideation (urgent mental health).

presbyacusis.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

glue-ear.title: Middle ear – glue ear, Eustachian tube dysfunction, CSOM, cholesteatoma, barotrauma, foreign body
niceRefs: NICE NG233 Otitis media with effusion in under 12s 2023
NICE CKS Otitis media – chronic suppurative
NICE CKS Otitis media with effusion

options.label: Glue ear (OME) and ETD
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Glue ear (children 2–7, dull retracted drum, fluid level/bubbles, conductive loss, speech/behaviour/balance effects): NG233 — audiology/tympanometry at diagnosis; active observation 3 months (most resolve); do NOT use antibiotics, steroids, antihistamines, decongestants or mucolytics; autoinflation (Otovent balloon) for ≥3 years during watchful waiting.
2. Persistent >3 months with hearing loss ≥25–30 dB or impact → ENT: grommets (± adenoidectomy if recurrent) or hearing aids as an alternative. Down's syndrome/cleft palate: refer early, hearing aids first-line.
3. Adults with unilateral glue ear → ENT 2WW to exclude nasopharyngeal carcinoma (nasendoscopy). Adult ETD (fullness, popping, after URTI/flight): Valsalva/autoinflation, treat rhinitis (intranasal steroid 6 weeks), decongestant ≤5 days; ENT if >3 months (balloon dilatation).

options.label: CSOM and cholesteatoma
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. CSOM: painless persistent discharge >2 weeks through a perforation, conductive loss. Aural toilet (microsuction), keep dry; topical quinolone drops (ciprofloxacin 0.3% ear drops — licensed, non-ototoxic; or ofloxacin) 2–4 drops bd for 7–14 days; avoid aminoglycoside drops with perforation; oral antibiotics not helpful unless cellulitis. Refer ENT if persisting >2 weeks after treatment, recurrent, or hearing loss (tympanoplasty).
2. Cholesteatoma: offensive discharge, attic/posterosuperior crust or pearly mass, retraction pocket, progressive hearing loss ± vertigo/facial weakness → URGENT ENT (CT temporal bone; surgery). Complications (facial palsy, vertigo, meningism, mastoid swelling) → same day.
3. Dry perforation after AOM/trauma: avoid water in ear, review at 6 weeks; most heal in 2 months; ENT if >3 months.

options.label: Barotrauma and foreign body
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Barotrauma (flying/diving): pain, fullness, haemotympanum, serous effusion; usually resolves 1–3 weeks — analgesia, decongestant (pseudoephedrine 60 mg) pre-descent on future flights, autoinflation; ENT if persistent effusion >6 weeks or sensorineural loss/vertigo (perilymph fistula — urgent).
2. Ear foreign body: insects — kill with olive oil/lidocaine then remove/irrigate; organic matter (beans) — do NOT irrigate (swells); button battery → same-day ENT (necrosis within hours); otherwise attempt removal only with direct vision, good lighting, cooperative patient and appropriate instrument; one attempt — then ENT (same day if pain, bleeding, battery, or failed attempt). Children: ENT if not easily removable.

glue-ear.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

rhinosinusitis-chronic.title: Nose – chronic rhinosinusitis, polyps, septal deviation, fracture, foreign body, smell disorders

options.label: Chronic rhinosinusitis and polyps
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. CRS = ≥12 weeks of nasal blockage/discharge ± facial pressure ± reduced smell. Examine with speculum/otoscope for polyps (pale, insensate, mobile — vs turbinates). Ask about aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (asthma + polyps + NSAID reactions).
2. Treat: saline irrigation (large-volume, e.g. NeilMed) bd; intranasal corticosteroid long term (mometasone 2 sprays each nostril od, or fluticasone furoate; drops — betamethasone/fluticasone nasules in head-down position for polyps for 4–6 weeks then spray); avoid smoking; treat allergic rhinitis (antihistamine). Short course prednisolone 25–30 mg 5–7 days for severe polyps (specialist advice/limited repeats). Long-term macrolide (clarithromycin 250 mg od 12 weeks) for CRS without polyps — ENT-led.
3. Refer ENT (routine) if no improvement at 12 weeks of maximal medical therapy — CT sinuses, FESS/polypectomy; biologics (dupilumab, mepolizumab) for severe recurrent polyps via specialist. URGENT/2WW: unilateral polyp or bloodstained discharge (tumour), orbital symptoms (periorbital swelling, diplopia, reduced vision — same day), severe frontal headache/meningism.

options.label: Septal deviation, fracture, foreign body
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Septal deviation: blockage (often unilateral), snoring; trial intranasal steroid + saline 6–8 weeks (treats coexisting rhinitis); refer ENT for septoplasty if persistent symptomatic obstruction (commissioning criteria apply).
2. Nasal fracture: X-ray not needed; check for septal haematoma (bilateral boggy septal swelling — SAME DAY ENT: abscess/saddle nose), CSF rhinorrhoea, epistaxis, eye signs. Ice, analgesia; ENT review at 5–7 days once swelling settled if deformity/obstruction (manipulation within 2 weeks).
3. Nose foreign body (child): try 'parent's kiss' (occlude other nostril, blow into mouth); button battery or magnet → same-day ENT; otherwise ENT if not easily removed with direct vision (do not probe blindly — posterior displacement/aspiration).

options.label: Smell disorders
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Causes: post-viral (COVID — most recover within 6 months), CRS/polyps (conductive — treat and smell returns), head injury, neurodegenerative (Parkinson's, Alzheimer's — early sign), drugs, smoking, idiopathic. Phantosmia (smelling things not there): post-viral, migraine, temporal lobe epilepsy, psychiatric.
2. Examine nose (polyps), neurology; MRI if unilateral, with neurology, head injury, phantosmia persisting or in the absence of a clear cause.
3. Olfactory training: sniff 4 odours (rose, lemon, clove, eucalyptus) for 20 seconds each, twice daily for ≥12 weeks (Fifth Sense/AbScent kits). Treat CRS; stop smoking; safety — gas detectors, food dates, smoke alarms. Refer ENT/smell clinic if >6–12 months or diagnostic uncertainty; steroids only if CRS.

rhinosinusitis-chronic.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

tonsillitis-recurrent.title: Throat – recurrent tonsillitis, quinsy, adenoids, stridor

options.label: Recurrent tonsillitis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute episode: FeverPAIN ≥4 or Centor ≥3 → phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg qds (or 1 g bd) 5–10 days (child by weight); clarithromycin 250–500 mg bd 5 days if allergic. No antibiotics for FeverPAIN 0–1. Avoid amoxicillin (EBV rash). Consider EBV (monospot) if exudate, posterior nodes, splenomegaly — avoid contact sports 4–8 weeks.
2. Tonsillectomy criteria (SIGN/NHS England): ≥7 documented episodes in 1 year, or ≥5/year for 2 years, or ≥3/year for 3 years, each disabling and preventing normal function — refer ENT. Also refer: 2 or more quinsies, obstructive sleep apnoea from tonsillar hypertrophy (children), suspected malignancy.

options.label: Quinsy and deep neck infection
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Quinsy: unilateral severe sore throat, trismus, 'hot potato' voice, drooling, uvula deviated away, unilateral peritonsillar swelling, fever. SAME-DAY ENT/ED for aspiration/incision + IV antibiotics (benzylpenicillin + metronidazole, or co-amoxiclav) and dexamethasone; usually day-case.
2. Red flags for deep neck space infection/airway: stridor, drooling, neck swelling/stiffness, trismus, septic — 999.
3. Adenoid hypertrophy (children): mouth breathing, snoring, hyponasal voice, recurrent otitis media/glue ear, OSA (witnessed apnoeas) → trial intranasal steroid (mometasone) 6–8 weeks; refer ENT for adenoidectomy if OSA, recurrent otitis media with effusion, or persistent obstruction; sleep study if OSA suspected.

options.label: Stridor — emergency
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Stridor = upper airway obstruction. Acute stridor with drooling, fever, toxic appearance, tripod position → suspected EPIGLOTTITIS/supraglottitis (adults too): 999, do not examine throat, do not lie flat, keep calm, oxygen; anaesthetics/ENT at hospital.
2. Child with barking cough and mild stridor at rest = croup: dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg oral single dose (or prednisolone 1 mg/kg); admit if stridor at rest, recession, saturations <95%, <6 months, or poor response. Foreign body (sudden onset while eating/playing) → choking algorithm/999.
3. Chronic/progressive stridor (adult): laryngeal tumour, bilateral cord palsy, subglottic stenosis → urgent ENT (2WW if smoker/hoarseness). Infant chronic stridor: laryngomalacia (worse supine/feeding, resolves by 2 years) — refer paediatric ENT if feeding difficulty, failure to thrive, cyanosis, apnoea.

tonsillitis-recurrent.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

hoarse-voice.title: Hoarseness – laryngitis, vocal cord nodules and 2WW

options.label: 2WW and red flags
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: 2WW ENT (laryngeal cancer) for persistent unexplained hoarseness in people aged ≥45, or an unexplained lump in the neck. Also refer urgently if hoarseness with stridor, dysphagia, odynophagia, haemoptysis, otalgia (referred), weight loss, smoker/heavy alcohol at any age.
2. Any hoarseness >3 weeks without an obvious cause → ENT laryngoscopy (routine if <45 and no red flags).

options.label: Acute laryngitis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Viral URTI with hoarseness <3 weeks: voice rest (no whispering — strains cords), steam/humidification, fluids, avoid smoking/alcohol/caffeine, paracetamol. Antibiotics not indicated unless bacterial features (persistent purulent sputum, fever >5 days). Reflux laryngitis: PPI trial 8 weeks (lansoprazole 30 mg od) if reflux symptoms.
2. Steroid inhaler users: rinse mouth, spacer, consider dose reduction (dysphonia from inhaled steroid). Hypothyroidism, ACE-inhibitor cough, allergic rhinitis with post-nasal drip — treat cause.

options.label: Vocal cord nodules / functional dysphonia
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Nodules (singers, teachers, children who shout): bilateral, symmetrical; vocal cord polyps/cysts (unilateral); muscle tension dysphonia; cord palsy (breathy weak voice — recurrent laryngeal nerve: lung/thyroid/oesophageal tumour, post-thyroid surgery — needs chest/neck imaging).
2. Refer ENT (laryngoscopy) then speech and language therapy: voice therapy (hydration, vocal hygiene, resonance exercises) is first-line for nodules and functional dysphonia; microlaryngeal surgery for polyps/cysts or persistent nodules. Cord palsy: CT skull base to chest; injection laryngoplasty/thyroplasty.

hoarse-voice.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

oral-cancer-2ww.title: Head and neck cancer – oral, tonsil and salivary gland (2WW)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Head and neck cancers

options.label: Oral cavity and tongue
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: 2WW oral surgery/ENT for unexplained ulceration in the oral cavity lasting >3 weeks, or a persistent unexplained lump in the neck. 2WW via dentist/oral surgery for a lump on the lip or in the oral cavity consistent with cancer, or a red (erythroplakia) or red-and-white (erythroleukoplakia) patch. White patch (leukoplakia) → urgent dental/oral surgery assessment.
2. Risk: smoking, alcohol, betel/paan, HPV, poor dentition, age >45. Examine: lift tongue, floor of mouth, lateral tongue, soft palate, tonsils; palpate neck nodes.
3. Benign tongue lesions: geographic tongue (migratory map pattern — reassure), black hairy tongue (smoking, antibiotics — brush tongue), lichen planus (white lacy — refer oral medicine if erosive/persistent, small malignant risk), aphthous ulcers (heal <2 weeks; chlorhexidine, hydrocortisone buccal tablets 2.5 mg qds; check ferritin, B12, folate, coeliac if recurrent), traumatic ulcer from sharp tooth (dental).

options.label: Tonsil and oropharynx
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect: unilateral tonsil enlargement, asymmetry, ulceration, persistent unilateral sore throat/otalgia, dysphagia, neck node (often first sign in HPV-positive disease — younger non-smokers), trismus, blood-stained saliva.
2. 2WW ENT: unilateral tonsillar enlargement or any of the above >3 weeks; neck lump. Do not treat a unilateral tonsil mass as recurrent tonsillitis.
3. HPV vaccination (Gardasil) for boys and girls age 12–13 and MSM ≤45 prevents oropharyngeal cancer.

options.label: Salivary glands
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Salivary stone (submandibular 80%): intermittent painful swelling at mealtimes; palpate floor of mouth; sialogogues (lemon drops), hydration, massage, warm compress; NSAID; antibiotics (flucloxacillin or co-amoxiclav) if infected (pus from duct, cellulitis). Refer ENT/oral surgery if stone palpable in duct (removal), recurrent, or persistent (USS; sialendoscopy; gland excision).
2. Persistent salivary gland swelling: 2WW ENT (NG12: unexplained persistent salivary gland swelling, or a lump in the gland) — pleomorphic adenoma (parotid, slow, mobile), Warthin's, malignancy (fixed, facial nerve palsy, pain, rapid growth, skin involvement = red flags). USS + FNA via specialist.
3. Bilateral diffuse swelling: Sjögren's (dry eyes/mouth — check ANA, anti-Ro/La), mumps (notify), sialadenosis (diabetes, alcohol, bulimia), HIV, sarcoid, drugs.

oral-cancer-2ww.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

facial-palsy.title: Facial palsy – Bell's palsy and when it is not

options.label: Is it Bell's palsy?
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Bell's: acute (<72 h) unilateral LOWER motor neurone weakness — forehead involved (cannot raise eyebrow), eye closure weak, mouth droop; ± ear pain, hyperacusis, altered taste. Diagnosis of exclusion.
2. NOT Bell's — refer same day: forehead SPARED (upper motor neurone → stroke: FAST/999), other neurology (limb weakness, diplopia, dysarthria), bilateral palsy (Lyme, GBS, sarcoid), vesicles in ear/palate (Ramsay Hunt → aciclovir 800 mg 5×/day + prednisolone, ENT), parotid mass or progressive onset >72 h (tumour — 2WW), trauma, otitis media/cholesteatoma (ENT), rash/tick exposure (Lyme serology — treat with doxycycline), pregnancy (higher risk, still treat), children (consider Lyme, otitis, leukaemia — paediatrics).

options.label: Treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Prednisolone within 72 h of onset: 50 mg daily for 10 days (or 60 mg 5 days then taper 10 mg/day) — adults; children: specialist advice (steroids not routinely). Antivirals alone are not effective; add aciclovir/valaciclovir only for severe/complete palsy or Ramsay Hunt (shared decision).
2. EYE CARE is essential: lubricating drops hourly (hypromellose) + ointment at night (Lacri-Lube), tape eye closed at night, sunglasses; refer ophthalmology urgently if red eye, pain, or incomplete closure not protected.
3. Reassure: 70% full recovery untreated, 80–85% with steroids; improvement usually starts by 3 weeks; facial exercises/physio; avoid electrical stimulation.

options.label: Follow-up and referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Review at 3 weeks and 3 months. Refer ENT/neurology if no improvement by 3 weeks, incomplete recovery at 3 months, recurrent palsy (consider sarcoid, Lyme, tumour — MRI), or atypical features.
2. Long-term sequelae (synkinesis, contracture, crocodile tears): facial therapy/physio, botulinum toxin via specialist; psychological support (Facial Palsy UK).

facial-palsy.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

vertigo-and-bppv.title: Vertigo – BPPV, vestibular neuritis/labyrinthitis, Ménière's
niceRefs: NICE CKS Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo

options.label: Is it central? (red flags)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same-day stroke pathway if: sudden persistent vertigo with any of — new headache/neck pain, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, ataxia/unable to stand, limb weakness/numbness, vertical or direction-changing nystagmus, abnormal HINTS (normal head impulse test in acute vestibular syndrome = central), hearing loss with vertigo (AICA stroke or labyrinthitis), age >60 with vascular risk factors and first episode.
2. Also urgent: vertigo with fever/otalgia/discharge (suppurative labyrinthitis, cholesteatoma), head injury, sudden hearing loss (see Hearing loss).
3. Chronic/non-rotatory dizziness: cardiovascular (orthostatic BP, arrhythmia), medication (antihypertensives, sedatives), anxiety/PPPD, anaemia, hypoglycaemia.

options.label: BPPV and vestibular neuritis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. BPPV: brief (<1 min) rotatory vertigo on turning in bed/looking up, no hearing loss. Dix–Hallpike positive (torsional upbeat nystagmus after latency, fatigable) → Epley manoeuvre in clinic (cures 80% after 1–2 attempts); teach Brandt–Daroff exercises if Epley unavailable; no medication; avoid driving until symptom-free. Refer ENT/balance clinic if persistent after 3–4 weeks, atypical nystagmus, or recurrent (>3 episodes/year).
2. Vestibular neuritis (vertigo days, no hearing loss) / labyrinthitis (with hearing loss/tinnitus): acute — prochlorperazine 5 mg tds (or buccal 3 mg bd) or cyclizine 50 mg tds for ≤3 days ONLY (prolonged use delays compensation); short course prednisolone (specialist); early mobilisation and vestibular rehabilitation exercises (Cawthorne–Cooksey); improvement over 2–6 weeks. Refer if not improving at 2–4 weeks, hearing loss (urgent — audiology/ENT), or recurrent.

options.label: Ménière's disease
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Episodic vertigo 20 min–12 h with fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and aural fullness in the same ear. Diagnosis requires audiometry — refer ENT for confirmation and MRI (exclude schwannoma).
2. Acute attack: prochlorperazine (buccal 3 mg) or cyclizine; lie still; admit if dehydrated/prolonged.
3. Prevention: salt restriction (<2 g/day), limit caffeine/alcohol, stress; betahistine 16 mg tds (up to 48 mg tds) — limited evidence but commonly tried for 3–6 months; ENT options — intratympanic steroids/gentamicin, hearing aid, vestibular rehab. Inform DVLA (must not drive during attacks; notify for Group 1 if recurrent sudden disabling vertigo); Ménière's Society support.

vertigo-and-bppv.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

migraine-acute.title: Migraine – acute treatment, prophylaxis, menstrual and vestibular

options.label: Diagnosis and acute treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Migraine: recurrent headache 4–72 h, unilateral/pulsating, moderate–severe, worse on activity, with nausea/vomiting or photo/phonophobia; aura (visual/sensory, 5–60 min, fully reversible) in 25%. Headache diary (frequency, triggers, menstrual relation, analgesic days). Examination normal; imaging only if red flags (see Other headaches).
2. Acute (CG150): oral triptan + NSAID or triptan + paracetamol at onset — sumatriptan 50–100 mg (nasal 10–20 mg or SC 6 mg if vomiting; rizatriptan 10 mg wafer; zolmitriptan 2.5 mg) + ibuprofen 400–600 mg or naproxen 500 mg or aspirin 900 mg; add antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or prochlorperazine buccal 3 mg) even without nausea. Repeat triptan after 2 h if recurrence (max 2 doses/24 h); try a different triptan if first fails on 3 attacks. Avoid opioids and ergots. Limit acute treatment to <10 days/month (triptans) / <15 days (simple analgesia) to prevent medication-overuse headache. Rimegepant 75 mg (gepant) if ≥2 triptans failed/unsuitable (TA919).
3. Triptan contraindications: ischaemic heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, previous stroke/TIA, hemiplegic/basilar migraine; caution with SSRIs (serotonin syndrome rare). Children 12–17: nasal sumatriptan + ibuprofen.

options.label: Prophylaxis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Offer if ≥4 migraine days/month, or attacks disabling/poorly responsive, or acute medication overuse risk. Trial each for 8–12 weeks at target dose; aim ≥50% reduction; review at 6 months for withdrawal.
2. First line: propranolol 80–160 mg/day (avoid asthma, depression), or topiramate 50–100 mg/day (teratogenic — effective contraception; cognitive side effects, kidney stones, weight loss; MHRA 2024: Pregnancy Prevention Programme now required), or amitriptyline 10–75 mg at night (useful if sleep/tension component). Candesartan 16 mg od is a well-evidenced off-label alternative. Second line: flunarizine (unlicensed), sodium valproate (NOT in women of childbearing potential), pizotifen.
3. Riboflavin 400 mg daily, magnesium, acupuncture (10 sessions, CG150) are options. Chronic migraine (≥15 headache days/month with ≥8 migraine) after ≥3 failed prophylactics → neurology/headache clinic: botulinum toxin A (TA260), CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab) for ≥4 migraine days/month after 3 preventives, atogepant/rimegepant prophylaxis.

options.label: Menstrual, vestibular, contraception, pregnancy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Menstrual migraine (attacks day −2 to +3 of ≥2 of 3 cycles): standard acute treatment; if predictable cycles — frovatriptan 2.5 mg bd or zolmitriptan 2.5 mg bd–tds from 2 days before to 3 days after onset (short-term prophylaxis); or continuous combined hormonal contraception (no aura only) / continuous desogestrel to suppress cycles; naproxen 500 mg bd perimenstrually.
2. Contraception: migraine WITH aura = combined hormonal contraception contraindicated (UKMEC 4, stroke risk) — use progestogen-only (desogestrel, implant, LNG-IUS), copper IUD. Without aura: CHC UKMEC 2 (3 if ≥35).
3. Vestibular migraine: episodic vertigo minutes–72 h with migraine features/history, normal hearing; treat as migraine (prophylaxis — propranolol/amitriptyline/topiramate; acute — antiemetic ± triptan); vestibular rehab; ENT/neurology if diagnostic doubt.
4. Pregnancy: paracetamol first; sumatriptan acceptable; ibuprofen avoid in third trimester; prophylaxis — propranolol (preferred) or amitriptyline; avoid topiramate/valproate. Breastfeeding: sumatriptan, ibuprofen, propranolol compatible.

migraine-acute.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

headache-tension.title: Headache – red flags, tension-type, medication overuse, cluster, cervicogenic, thunderclap/SAH

options.label: Red flags — same day / 2WW
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. THUNDERCLAP (maximal within 5 min, 'worst ever'): subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise → 999/ED for CT within 6 h (± LP at 12 h); also cervical artery dissection, RCVS, pituitary apoplexy, venous sinus thrombosis.
2. Same-day assessment: headache with fever/neck stiffness/rash (meningitis — IM benzylpenicillin 1.2 g if non-blanching rash and transfer delayed), new focal neurology, reduced consciousness, seizure, papilloedema, head injury on anticoagulants or with vomiting/amnesia, new headache in immunosuppressed/HIV/cancer, age >50 with jaw claudication/scalp tenderness (GCA — see GCA tool), pregnancy >20 weeks with headache + BP/proteinuria (pre-eclampsia), acute angle-closure (red eye, halos, vomiting).
3. NG12 urgent direct-access MRI/CT (within 2 weeks) for progressive subacute headache with features of raised ICP (worse lying/coughing/morning, vomiting, visual obscurations), new cognitive/personality change, or new headache with a history of cancer. Obese young woman with headache + papilloedema/pulsatile tinnitus → IIH: same-day ophthalmology/neurology.

options.label: Tension-type and medication-overuse
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Tension-type: bilateral, pressing/tightening, mild–moderate, no nausea, not worse on activity; episodic (<15 days/month) — aspirin 600–900 mg, paracetamol 1 g, or ibuprofen 400 mg at onset; NOT opioids; address stress, sleep, posture, screen use, eye strain, caffeine. Chronic (≥15 days/month >3 months): amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrated to 25–75 mg for 3–6 months; acupuncture (CG150, up to 10 sessions); CBT/relaxation; physiotherapy for neck.
2. Medication-overuse headache: headache ≥15 days/month in someone using triptans/opioids/combination analgesics ≥10 days/month or simple analgesics ≥15 days/month for >3 months. Explain and STOP all acute analgesia abruptly for ≥1 month (expect worsening for 1–2 weeks); start migraine prophylaxis at the same time (amitriptyline/topiramate/propranolol); review at 4–8 weeks; naproxen 500 mg bd for 2–3 weeks can bridge (then stop). Refer if opioid overuse or failure.

options.label: Cluster, cervicogenic
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Cluster headache: excruciating unilateral orbital/temporal pain 15–180 min, 1–8×/day, often nocturnal, with ipsilateral lacrimation, nasal congestion, ptosis/miosis, restlessness; bouts of weeks–months. Acute: subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg (up to 2/day) or nasal zolmitriptan 5 mg + high-flow oxygen 12–15 L/min via non-rebreathe mask for 15–20 min (prescribe via HOOF form) — NOT paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/oral triptans. Transitional: prednisolone 60 mg 5 days then taper, or greater occipital nerve block (specialist). Prophylaxis: verapamil 80 mg tds titrated (up to 960 mg/day) with ECG monitoring (PR interval) — start via neurology/headache clinic (CG150: refer all cluster headache at first diagnosis); lithium second line. Alcohol/smoking avoidance during bouts.
2. Cervicogenic headache: unilateral, starts in the neck, restricted cervical range, provoked by neck movement/pressure; physiotherapy (manual therapy, strengthening), posture, NSAID short course, amitriptyline; imaging only if red flags; pain clinic for facet/GON blocks if refractory.

headache-tension.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

parkinson-s-diagnosis.title: Parkinson's disease and tremor
niceRefs: NICE NG71 Parkinson's disease in adults

options.label: Recognise and refer
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Parkinsonism = bradykinesia + rigidity and/or rest tremor (4–6 Hz, pill-rolling, asymmetric), plus reduced arm swing, shuffling, hypomimia, micrographia, hypophonia; prodrome — anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation, depression.
2. NG71: refer UNTREATED to a specialist (neurology/geriatrics PD clinic) within 6 weeks (2 weeks if later stages) — do NOT start levodopa in primary care; diagnosis is clinical (DaTscan only if uncertain). Review drug causes first: antipsychotics, metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, valproate, lithium, flunarizine — withdraw if possible (drug-induced parkinsonism may take months to resolve).
3. Red flags for atypical parkinsonism (specialist): early falls, symmetrical onset, poor levodopa response, early dementia/hallucinations (DLB), autonomic failure (MSA), vertical gaze palsy (PSP), cerebellar signs.

options.label: Treatment and GP role
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Specialist-initiated: levodopa (co-careldopa/co-beneldopa) first line if motor symptoms affect quality of life; dopamine agonist (ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine patch), MAO-B inhibitor (rasagiline, selegiline) if not. Adjuncts for wearing-off: COMT inhibitor (entacapone), amantadine for dyskinesia; advanced — apomorphine, Duodopa, deep brain stimulation.
2. GP must-dos: never stop PD drugs abruptly (neuroleptic malignant-like syndrome); in hospital/NBM ensure 'Get It On Time' (dispersible co-beneldopa/rotigotine patch); NEVER prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, haloperidol — use domperidone 10 mg tds (ECG/QT caution) for nausea, quetiapine or clozapine (specialist) if antipsychotic needed; monitor impulse-control disorders on agonists (gambling, hypersexuality — ask every review), orthostatic hypotension (midodrine/fludrocortisone via specialist), driving — must inform DVLA.
3. Non-motor: constipation (macrogol, fluid, fibre), depression (SSRI — sertraline; avoid with rasagiline caution), anxiety, dementia (rivastigmine licensed in PD dementia), psychosis (reduce agonists first; quetiapine/pimavanserin via specialist), sleep (RBD — clonazepam/melatonin; daytime sleepiness — modafinil specialist), drooling (glycopyrronium, botulinum), pain, urinary urgency (avoid oxybutynin — anticholinergic; mirabegron), sexual dysfunction (sildenafil). Physiotherapy, OT, SLT (swallow, speech), dietitian (protein redistribution if fluctuations), PD nurse specialist, advance care planning.

options.label: Essential and other tremor
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Essential tremor: bilateral postural/kinetic (4–12 Hz) hands ± head/voice, improves with alcohol, family history (50%), no bradykinesia/rigidity; worsens with age. Enhanced physiological tremor: anxiety, thyrotoxicosis (TFT), caffeine, drugs (salbutamol, SSRIs, lithium, valproate, amiodarone, steroids), alcohol withdrawal, hypoglycaemia.
2. Treat if functionally limiting: propranolol 40 mg bd–tds up to 240 mg/day (avoid asthma/bradycardia) or primidone 25 mg nocte titrated to 250–750 mg/day (sedation, start low); second line topiramate, gabapentin; occasional-use propranolol 40 mg 1 h before stressful event. Refer neurology if atypical (unilateral, rest tremor, dystonic posturing, young onset <40 with other signs — Wilson's: caeruloplasmin), poor response — focused ultrasound thalamotomy (NICE IPG617), DBS, botulinum for head/voice tremor.
3. Cerebellar (intention) tremor, dystonic tremor, functional tremor (variable, distractible, entrainable) → neurology.

parkinson-s-diagnosis.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

trigeminal-neuralgia.title: Cranial neuralgias – trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, occipital

options.label: Trigeminal neuralgia — diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Paroxysms of severe unilateral electric-shock/stabbing pain in V2/V3 (rarely V1) lasting seconds–2 min, triggered by touch, chewing, talking, cold wind; pain-free between attacks (or background ache in TN with concomitant continuous pain). Examination normal.
2. Red flags → urgent neurology/MRI: age <40, bilateral, sensory loss or other cranial nerve signs, optic neuritis history (MS), hearing loss (CPA tumour), poor response to carbamazepine. MRI brain (with trigeminal protocol) for all new cases is now standard to exclude secondary causes and assess neurovascular compression — refer at diagnosis (routine) if typical.
3. Dental causes (cracked tooth, pulpitis) mimic — dental review if pain is dull/throbbing/tooth-localised.

options.label: Trigeminal neuralgia — treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Carbamazepine 100 mg bd, increase by 100–200 mg every 2–3 days to control (usual 200–400 mg tds; max 1600 mg/day); modified-release reduces side effects. Check FBC, U&E (hyponatraemia), LFT at baseline and 2–4 weeks; HLA-B*15:02 screen before starting in Han Chinese/Thai/SE Asian origin (SJS risk). Interactions: enzyme inducer — COC ineffective, warfarin, DOACs, antipsychotics.
2. Intolerant/ineffective: oxcarbazepine 300 mg bd titrated to 600–1200 mg/day (off-label, better tolerated, hyponatraemia); lamotrigine, gabapentin/pregabalin, baclofen as add-ons via neurology. Opioids and simple analgesics do not work.
3. Refer neurology/neurosurgery early if pain not controlled on carbamazepine within weeks, side effects, or remission not achieved: microvascular decompression (best long-term), gamma knife, percutaneous rhizotomy/balloon compression. Taper and trial withdrawal after 1 month pain-free (natural remissions).

options.label: Glossopharyngeal and occipital neuralgia
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Glossopharyngeal neuralgia: stabbing pain in throat/tonsil/ear/base of tongue triggered by swallowing, coughing, talking; may cause syncope/bradycardia (vagal). ENT examination to exclude oropharyngeal tumour (2WW if any mass/ulcer); MRI; treat as trigeminal neuralgia (carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine); neurosurgery if refractory.
2. Occipital neuralgia: paroxysmal shooting pain in greater/lesser occipital nerve distribution (back of head to vertex), scalp allodynia, tenderness over nerve at nuchal line, relieved by nerve block. Exclude cervical spine pathology/cervicogenic headache (imaging if red flags). Treat: NSAID/paracetamol, heat, physiotherapy, amitriptyline 10–50 mg or gabapentin; greater occipital nerve block (lidocaine ± methylprednisolone) by trained clinician/pain clinic is both diagnostic and therapeutic; pulsed radiofrequency if recurrent.

trigeminal-neuralgia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

bell-s-palsy.title: Bell's palsy

options.label: Diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute unilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness including the forehead, onset <72 h, no other neurology; ± postauricular pain, hyperacusis, taste change. Exclude: forehead sparing (UMN → stroke, 999), vesicles (Ramsay Hunt), bilateral/tick exposure (Lyme), parotid mass, otitis media/cholesteatoma, trauma, progressive >72 h (tumour), other cranial nerve signs (brainstem, GBS, sarcoid). See the ENT Facial palsy tool for the full differential.

options.label: Treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Prednisolone 50 mg daily for 10 days (adults) within 72 h of onset; aciclovir/valaciclovir only for severe/complete palsy or Ramsay Hunt (then prednisolone + aciclovir 800 mg 5×/day 7 days + ENT).
2. Eye protection: hourly lubricant drops, ointment and taping at night, glasses; urgent ophthalmology if red/painful eye.
3. Reassure (85% recover with steroids), facial exercises; review 3 weeks and 3 months.

options.label: Referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Same day: stroke features, Ramsay Hunt with eye involvement, severe eye exposure. ENT/neurology: no improvement at 3 weeks, incomplete at 3 months, recurrence, atypical features (MRI). Facial Palsy UK and specialist facial therapy for synkinesis.

bell-s-palsy.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

peripheral-neuropathy.title: Peripheral neuropathy, radiculopathy and entrapment
niceRefs: NICE CG173 Neuropathic pain in adults

options.label: Assessment and causes
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Length-dependent symmetrical 'glove and stocking' sensory loss, paraesthesia, burning, absent ankle jerks ± distal weakness, foot ulceration risk. Ask: diabetes, alcohol, drugs (chemotherapy, isoniazid, nitrofurantoin, amiodarone, metronidazole, phenytoin, statins rarely), B12/metformin, HIV, renal failure, hypothyroidism, family history (CMT — pes cavus), paraprotein.
2. First-line bloods: HbA1c, B12/folate, TFT, U&E, LFT/GGT, FBC, ESR, serum protein electrophoresis + free light chains, HIV; add ANA/ANCA, hepatitis B/C, lead/heavy metals, Lyme if indicated. 10 g monofilament/vibration for foot risk.
3. URGENT neurology: rapidly progressive (days–weeks) ascending weakness (Guillain–Barré — same day), asymmetric/multifocal (vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex), prominent motor or autonomic involvement, proximal weakness, no cause found with disabling symptoms. Routine neurology/NCS: unclear cause, before immunosuppression, CMT suspected.

options.label: Neuropathic pain (CG173)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Offer one of: amitriptyline 10 mg nocte → 25–75 mg; duloxetine 60 mg od (first choice in diabetic neuropathy; up to 120 mg); gabapentin 300 mg od → 600 mg tds (max 3600 mg; CD Schedule 3; renal dose); pregabalin 75 mg bd → 300 mg bd. If no benefit at adequate dose/4–8 weeks, switch to another of the four; combinations by specialist. Tramadol only as short-term rescue; NOT strong opioids/carbamazepine (except TN). Capsaicin 0.075% cream for localised pain if oral drugs unsuitable; lidocaine 5% plaster for post-herpetic neuralgia.
2. Diabetic neuropathy: optimise glycaemic control (slows progression), foot care/podiatry, annual foot screen; autonomic (gastroparesis, erectile dysfunction, postural hypotension) — diabetes team. B12 neuropathy: urgent hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM alternate days until no further improvement (see B12 tool) — may be irreversible if delayed.
3. Refer pain clinic if uncontrolled after two agents; CBT/pain programme; review driving (sensory loss in feet — DVLA).

options.label: Radiculopathy and ulnar/entrapment neuropathy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Lumbar radiculopathy (sciatica — NG59): dermatomal leg pain ± weakness/reflex loss; most improve in 6–12 weeks; stay active, physiotherapy, NSAID short course; NG59 — do NOT offer gabapentinoids/opioids/benzodiazepines/antiepileptics for sciatica; epidural steroid via spinal service for severe acute radicular pain; MRI only if considering intervention or red flags. CAUDA EQUINA (bilateral sciatica, saddle numbness, urinary retention/incontinence, faecal incontinence, sexual dysfunction) → 999/same-day MRI. Cervical radiculopathy: see Cervical radiculopathy tool.
2. Ulnar neuropathy at elbow (cubital tunnel — see tool) or wrist (Guyon's canal); carpal tunnel (median: nocturnal paraesthesia thumb–ring finger, Phalen's/Tinel's; pregnancy, hypothyroidism, diabetes, RA — treat cause; night wrist splint 6–8 weeks; corticosteroid injection 20–40 mg methylprednisolone; NCS if diagnostic doubt or pre-surgery; refer hand surgery for decompression if thenar wasting, constant numbness, or failed conservative care 8–12 weeks). Peroneal neuropathy (foot drop after leg crossing/weight loss — NCS, ankle-foot orthosis, neurology if no recovery 3 months). Meralgia paraesthetica (lateral thigh numbness — weight loss, loose clothing, reassurance).

restless-legs.title: Sleep disorders – restless legs, narcolepsy, REM sleep behaviour disorder

options.label: Restless legs syndrome
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnosis (all four): urge to move legs with unpleasant sensation; worse at rest; relieved by movement; worse evening/night. Check ferritin (treat if <75 micrograms/L — ferrous sulfate 200 mg od/alternate days, recheck 3 months; IV iron via haematology if <30 and oral fails), U&E (CKD), B12/folate, glucose, TFT, pregnancy; review drugs that worsen (antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines, metoclopramide, lithium).
2. Mild/intermittent: sleep hygiene, avoid caffeine/alcohol/nicotine, exercise, stretching, hot/cold bath, distraction; levodopa 100 mg (co-careldopa) occasional use.
3. Daily moderate–severe: gabapentin 300 mg nocte → 600–1800 mg (or pregabalin 75–300 mg) now preferred FIRST line (no augmentation); dopamine agonists — ropinirole 0.25 mg → 0.5–2 mg nocte, pramipexole 88 micrograms → 540 micrograms, rotigotine patch 1–3 mg/24 h — effective but AUGMENTATION risk (symptoms earlier/worse, spreading) in up to 50% long term: use lowest dose, counsel impulse-control disorders. Refractory/augmentation → neurology/sleep clinic (oxycodone–naloxone MR, iron infusion, rotation).

options.label: Narcolepsy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Excessive daytime sleepiness >3 months with sleep attacks, cataplexy (sudden loss of tone with emotion — pathognomonic for type 1), sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations, fragmented night sleep; onset teens–20s; Epworth score >10. Exclude OSA (STOP-Bang, see OSA tool), sedating drugs, depression, insufficient sleep.
2. Refer sleep medicine/neurology for polysomnography + multiple sleep latency test (± CSF hypocretin). Treatment specialist-initiated: scheduled naps, sleep hygiene; modafinil 200–400 mg (contraception — reduces COC efficacy), pitolisant (TA776), solriamfetol, sodium oxybate (cataplexy, nocturnal sleep), methylphenidate/dexamfetamine; venlafaxine/clomipramine for cataplexy.
3. DVLA: must notify; no driving until symptoms controlled; safety at work/heights/machinery. GP: monitor BP/HR on stimulants, mood, misuse.

options.label: REM sleep behaviour disorder
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Dream-enactment (shouting, punching, kicking, falling out of bed) with loss of normal REM atonia; usually men >50; bed-partner injury. Strongly predicts alpha-synucleinopathy (Parkinson's, DLB, MSA — >80% convert within 10–15 years) — examine for parkinsonism, anosmia, orthostatic hypotension, cognition; review antidepressants (SSRIs, venlafaxine, mirtazapine can cause/worsen), alcohol withdrawal.
2. Safety: remove sharp objects, mattress on floor/bed rails, partner sleeps separately if injured.
3. Refer sleep clinic/neurology for video polysomnography (distinguish from sleepwalking/night terrors/OSA arousals/seizures) and counselling about prognosis; treatment — melatonin 2–12 mg (MR, first line, well tolerated) or clonazepam 0.25–1 mg nocte (caution falls/OSA/cognition). Annual review for emerging neurodegeneration.

restless-legs.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

subdural-haematoma.title: Subdural haematoma and hydrocephalus (including normal-pressure hydrocephalus)
niceRefs: Society of British Neurological Surgeons guidance

options.label: Subdural haematoma
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute (within 72 h of trauma): 999 — reduced GCS, focal deficit, seizure, vomiting, severe headache. NG232 head injury: same-day CT within 1 h if GCS <13, focal neurology, suspected skull fracture, seizure, >1 vomit, or (within 8 h) on anticoagulant/antiplatelet regardless of symptoms, age ≥65 with LOC/amnesia, dangerous mechanism, retrograde amnesia >30 min.
2. CHRONIC subdural (elderly, alcohol, anticoagulants/antiplatelets, falls, often trivial or forgotten injury weeks before): fluctuating confusion, headache, drowsiness, gait disturbance, unilateral weakness, 'possible stroke/dementia/UTI' that doesn't fit → same-day CT head (direct access or acute medicine). Suspected in any older patient with new cognitive/gait decline on anticoagulant.
3. Management by neurosurgery: burr-hole drainage if symptomatic/large; conservative with repeat CT if small; reverse anticoagulation; dexamethasone no longer recommended (Dex-CSDH trial). Restart anticoagulation after 4–8 weeks per neurosurgical/stroke advice (AF with high CHA2DS2-VASc usually resumes). Falls assessment, alcohol review.

options.label: Hydrocephalus and shunts
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Raised-pressure hydrocephalus (tumour, SAH, meningitis, congenital): headache worse lying/morning, vomiting, papilloedema, visual obscurations, drowsiness, gait disturbance, sunset eyes/increasing head circumference in infants → same-day neurosurgery/paediatrics; CT/MRI.
2. Patient with a VP shunt presenting with headache, vomiting, drowsiness, fever, abdominal pain, swelling along shunt tract → treat as shunt blockage/infection: same-day neurosurgical unit (not routine ED antibiotics) — low threshold; carry shunt alert card.

options.label: Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Triad in older adults: gait apraxia ('magnetic', wide-based, short steps — usually first), urinary urgency/incontinence, subcortical cognitive impairment (slowed, apathetic) over months; reversible cause of 'dementia'.
2. MRI/CT: ventriculomegaly disproportionate to atrophy (Evans index >0.3), with no obstruction. Differentiate from vascular dementia, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's (memory-dominant), cervical myelopathy.
3. Refer neurology/neurosurgery (NPH clinic) for lumbar tap test or extended lumbar drainage — gait improvement predicts response to VP shunt (improves 60–80%, best if gait is dominant and symptoms <2 years). Meanwhile: falls prevention, continence support, do not label as irreversible dementia.

motor-neurone-disease.title: Neuromuscular and movement disorders – MND, myasthenia, Lambert–Eaton, Guillain–Barré, dystonia, ataxia, Huntington's

options.label: Motor neurone disease (NG42)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect: progressive painless asymmetric weakness with wasting and fasciculation (LMN) PLUS brisk reflexes/spasticity (UMN) in the same limb; bulbar — dysarthria, dysphagia, tongue fasciculation; no sensory loss; falls, foot drop, hand weakness, emotional lability, frontotemporal cognitive change. Red flags with cramps/fasciculations alone are NOT MND if no weakness (benign fasciculation).
2. Refer neurology URGENTLY (suspected MND — most centres see within 2–4 weeks); do not wait for investigations (CK, TFT, B12, NCS/EMG, MRI to exclude cervical myelopathy done by neurology). Median survival 2–4 years — early MDT (MND care centre).
3. Specialist-led: riluzole 50 mg bd (LFT monitoring); tofersen for SOD1-MND (NHS 2025); non-invasive ventilation (respiratory function/overnight oximetry every 3 months — refer if FVC <80% or orthopnoea/morning headache); gastrostomy early when swallow/weight declines; saliva (glycopyrronium, hyoscine patch, botulinum); spasticity (baclofen); cramps (quinine); emotional lability; advance care planning, DNACPR discussions, palliative care involvement from diagnosis. GP: coordinate, review respiratory symptoms, DS1500/SR1 (benefits), carers.

options.label: Myasthenia, Lambert–Eaton, Guillain–Barré
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness — ptosis, diplopia (variable), dysarthria/dysphagia, neck/limb weakness worse end of day; no reflex/sensory change. Bloods AChR antibodies (85%), MuSK if negative; TFT; CT thorax (thymoma). Refer neurology (urgent). MYASTHENIC CRISIS (breathlessness, weak cough, cannot count to 20 in one breath, dysphagia with choking) → 999 — needs ITU (IVIG/plasma exchange). Specialist drugs: pyridostigmine 30–60 mg 4–6×/day, prednisolone (start low — may worsen initially), azathioprine, thymectomy. GP: AVOID/caution drugs that worsen MG — aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta-blockers, magnesium, penicillamine, lithium, phenytoin, statins (monitor), botulinum; check the MG drug list before any prescription; vaccinate.
2. Lambert–Eaton: proximal weakness improving briefly with exercise, autonomic (dry mouth), areflexia; 50% paraneoplastic (small-cell lung cancer) — urgent CT chest; VGCC antibodies; amifampridine (3,4-DAP) via neurology.
3. Guillain–Barré: ascending symmetrical weakness + areflexia over days (post-infection — Campylobacter, flu, COVID, Zika), back pain, paraesthesia, facial/bulbar weakness, autonomic instability → SAME-DAY admission (respiratory failure in 25%: monitor FVC); IVIG/plasma exchange; recovery months; rehabilitation; Miller Fisher variant (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia).

options.label: Dystonia, ataxia, Huntington's
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Dystonia: sustained/patterned muscle contractions causing twisting postures — cervical (torticollis, head tremor; sensory trick), blepharospasm, writer's cramp, oromandibular; secondary — drugs (acute dystonic reaction to antipsychotics/metoclopramide: procyclidine 5–10 mg IM/IV, tardive dystonia), Wilson's (young — caeruloplasmin, copper), cerebral palsy, dopa-responsive dystonia (child/young — levodopa trial). Refer neurology/movement disorder clinic: botulinum toxin injections every 12 weeks (first line for focal dystonia), trihexyphenidyl, clonazepam, baclofen, DBS for generalised. Physiotherapy, Dystonia UK.
2. Ataxia: acute (hours–days) → same day: stroke/cerebellar haemorrhage, drug toxicity (phenytoin, carbamazepine, lithium, alcohol), Wernicke's (give IV thiamine — Pabrinex — before glucose in alcohol misuse), MS relapse, infection. Subacute/chronic: alcohol, hypothyroidism, B12/vitamin E deficiency, coeliac (gluten ataxia — tTG), paraneoplastic (anti-Yo etc.), MSA, hereditary (SCA, Friedreich's — genetics); MRI brain, neurology referral; physiotherapy/OT; Ataxia UK.
3. Huntington's: autosomal dominant CAG repeat (HTT) — chorea, impulsivity/irritability, depression, cognitive decline, weight loss, onset 30–50; family history (may be hidden). Do NOT order genetic test in primary care — refer regional genetics/HD clinic for counselled predictive/diagnostic testing; neurology-led: tetrabenazine or deutetrabenazine/olanzapine/risperidone for chorea (tetrabenazine — depression/suicide risk), SSRIs, antipsychotics for behaviour; SLT, dietitian (high calorie), OT, mental health, driving (DVLA), advance care planning; Huntington's Disease Association specialist advisers; genetic counselling for relatives (predictive testing from 18, prenatal/PGT).
