dysmenorrhoea.title: Menstrual problems – dysmenorrhoea, PMS, IMB/PCB, amenorrhoea, adenomyosis

options.label: Dysmenorrhoea and adenomyosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Primary (onset 6–12 months after menarche, cramping with periods, normal examination): NSAID first line — ibuprofen 400 mg tds or naproxen 500 mg stat then 250 mg tds, or mefenamic acid 500 mg tds — started at onset/1 day before; paracetamol add-on; heat; TENS; combined hormonal contraception (continuous/extended), LNG-IUS, desogestrel or implant if contraception also wanted.
2. Secondary (onset after years of painless periods, pain before/throughout period, dyspareunia, heavy bleeding, bulky uterus): endometriosis (NG73 — transvaginal USS; refer gynaecology if suspected/not responding to 3–6 months of treatment; laparoscopy is diagnostic), adenomyosis (USS/MRI 'globular' uterus; LNG-IUS first line, CHC, tranexamic acid for bleeding, GnRH analogue via gynaecology; hysterectomy definitive), fibroids, PID (test chlamydia/gonorrhoea), copper IUD, cervical stenosis.
3. Refer: pain not controlled after 3–6 months of NSAID + hormonal therapy, suspected endometriosis/adenomyosis affecting fertility, abnormal examination/USS.

options.label: PMS / PMDD
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnose with a prospective symptom diary over 2 cycles (symptoms in luteal phase, resolve by end of menstruation, symptom-free week). PMDD = severe with functional impairment; screen for depression/anxiety which worsen premenstrually (not the same).
2. Lifestyle: exercise, sleep, reduce alcohol/caffeine/smoking; CBT (first line for moderate PMS, RCOG); vitamin B6 ≤10 mg (MHRA limit), calcium/vitamin D.
3. Drug options: continuous or extended combined pill containing drospirenone (Yasmin/Lucette — licensed evidence) first-line hormonal; SSRI — sertraline 50–100 mg or fluoxetine 20 mg either continuously or luteal-phase only (day 14 to menses), effective within days; escitalopram 10–20 mg. Severe/refractory → gynaecology: GnRH analogue with add-back HRT, LNG-IUS + transdermal oestrogen, bilateral oophorectomy as last resort. Avoid progesterone-only treatments (worsen mood).

options.label: Intermenstrual / post-coital bleeding
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. History: contraception (breakthrough bleeding common in first 3 months of CHC/POP/implant/IUS), missed pills, STI risk, smear status, pregnancy (test), anticoagulants. Examine: speculum (cervical ectropion, polyp, cervicitis, visible lesion), bimanual; swabs — chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT; smear only if due.
2. NG12: 2WW gynaecology if cervix looks suspicious (do not wait for smear); refer colposcopy for persistent PCB (>4 weeks) with normal-looking cervix in women ≥35 or with risk factors; endometrial cancer 2WW if ≥55 with postmenopausal bleeding (consider if <55); transvaginal USS for persistent IMB ≥45 or with risk factors (obesity, PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch).
3. Benign: ectropion (reassure; cryotherapy/silver nitrate if troublesome), polyp (remove via gynaecology/hysteroscopy), infection (treat), hormonal contraception (change method if >3–6 months), perimenopausal anovulation (see HMB tool).

options.label: Amenorrhoea
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Primary: no menses by 15 with secondary sexual characteristics (or by 13 without) → FSH/LH, oestradiol, prolactin, TFT, karyotype (Turner's), pelvic USS (Müllerian agenesis, imperforate hymen); refer paediatric/adolescent gynaecology or endocrinology.
2. Secondary (≥3–6 months absent after previous cycles): PREGNANCY test first. Then: FSH/LH, oestradiol, prolactin, TFT, testosterone/SHBG/free androgen index, HbA1c; pelvic USS; ask about weight loss/exercise/eating disorder (functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea — low LH/FSH/oestradiol; restore energy balance; DEXA if >6 months), stress, drugs (antipsychotics → prolactin; depot medroxyprogesterone; opioids), hot flushes.
3. Causes and actions: PCOS (Rotterdam: oligo/anovulation + hyperandrogenism ± polycystic ovaries) — induce withdrawal bleed every 3–4 months (medroxyprogesterone 10 mg 10 days) or CHC/LNG-IUS to protect endometrium, metformin for metabolic features, weight, fertility (letrozole via gynaecology); hyperprolactinaemia (>1000 mU/L after repeat → pituitary MRI, endocrinology; cabergoline); premature ovarian insufficiency (<40, FSH >25 on two samples 4 weeks apart → HRT/CHC until 51, DEXA, fertility counselling, endocrinology/gynaecology); thyroid disease; Asherman's/cervical stenosis after instrumentation (hysteroscopy); hypopituitarism (Sheehan's).

dysmenorrhoea.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

ovarian-cancer-2ww.title: Gynaecological cancer – ovarian, endometrial, cervical, vulval (2WW)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Gynaecological cancers – recognition and referral

options.label: Ovarian
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12/CG122: measure CA125 in any woman (especially ≥50) with persistent or frequent (>12×/month) bloating, early satiety/loss of appetite, pelvic/abdominal pain, urinary urgency/frequency, new IBS-type symptoms (IBS rarely starts >50), unexplained weight loss, fatigue, or change in bowel habit. Examine abdomen/pelvis.
2. CA125 ≥35 IU/mL → urgent pelvic/abdominal USS; USS suggestive of cancer → 2WW gynaecology (RMI = USS score × menopausal score × CA125 calculated in secondary care). Ascites and/or pelvic/abdominal mass (not fibroids) on examination → 2WW directly, no need to wait for CA125/USS. Normal CA125 with persistent symptoms → USS anyway or reassess; keep safety-net (CA125 raised in endometriosis, PID, fibroids, pregnancy, any peritoneal irritation; normal in 50% of early-stage cancer).
3. Management (specialist): staging CT, surgery (TAH/BSO/omentectomy) ± platinum/taxane chemotherapy; PARP inhibitors (olaparib, niraparib) for BRCA/HRD; germline BRCA testing offered to all high-grade serous cases — cascade testing for relatives. GP: symptom control, bowel obstruction awareness, palliative care liaison. Family history (two first-degree relatives, BRCA) → genetics referral; risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy.

options.label: Endometrial
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: 2WW for women ≥55 with POSTMENOPAUSAL BLEEDING (any bleeding >12 months after last period); consider 2WW if <55 with PMB. Consider direct-access transvaginal USS for ≥55 with unexplained vaginal discharge (new, thrush treated, or with thrombocytosis/haematuria) or visible haematuria with low Hb/thrombocytosis/high glucose.
2. Premenopausal risk (obesity, PCOS/anovulation, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome, unopposed oestrogen): persistent IMB/HMB → TVUSS ± hysteroscopy/biopsy. Endometrial thickness ≥4 mm postmenopausal → hysteroscopy and biopsy. Bleeding on HRT: see HRT tool.
3. Management: hysterectomy + BSO ± lymph node assessment; radiotherapy/chemotherapy by stage; Lynch screening (MMR immunohistochemistry) on all tumours — refer genetics if deficient. Prevention counselling: weight, LNG-IUS/CHC protect in PCOS.

options.label: Cervical
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: 2WW if the cervix LOOKS abnormal/suspicious of cancer on speculum (friable, ulcerated, mass, contact bleeding from a lesion) — do not take a smear (delays referral, smear is a screening not diagnostic test). Symptoms prompting speculum: post-coital bleeding, IMB, PMB, persistent offensive discharge, pelvic pain. Persistent PCB with a normal cervix → colposcopy referral (routine/urgent by age — see Menstrual tool).
2. Screening (NHS CSP): HPV primary screening every 3 years 25–49, 5 years 50–64 (moving to 5-yearly for HPV-negative in England from 2025); abnormal results managed per programme (colposcopy for HPV+ with abnormal cytology or persistent HPV at 24 months). HPV vaccination 12–13.
3. Management: LLETZ/cone for CIN/early; radical hysterectomy or chemoradiation by stage; fertility-sparing trachelectomy. Avoid smears in pregnancy unless overdue high-risk.

options.label: Vulval
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: 2WW gynaecology for an unexplained vulval lump, ulceration or BLEEDING. Also refer persistent vulval itch/soreness not responding to 6–12 weeks of treatment for lichen sclerosus/candida, pigmented or raised plaque (VIN/melanoma), non-healing ulcer.
2. Lichen sclerosus (white atrophic plaques, 'figure of eight', architectural change; 2–5% lifetime SCC risk): clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment once daily 4 weeks, alternate days 4 weeks, twice weekly 4 weeks then as needed; emollient/soap substitute; avoid irritants; annual review — biopsy any thickened/persistent/eroded area (vulval dermatology/gynaecology). Lichen planus, Paget's disease, VIN (HPV-related, young smokers) → vulval clinic for biopsy.
3. Management: wide local excision ± sentinel node/groin dissection; radiotherapy. Smoking cessation (VIN); lifelong follow-up.

ovarian-cancer-2ww.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

chlamydia.title: Vaginal discharge and STIs – chlamydia, gonorrhoea, BV, trichomonas, candidiasis
niceRefs: BASHH guidelines (chlamydia 2018/2023, gonorrhoea 2019, BV 2022, TV 2021, VVC 2019)

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. History: colour/odour/itch, new partner, condom use, symptoms in partner, contraception, pregnancy, douching, last smear, abdominal pain/dyspareunia/fever (PID — see below). Examine if symptoms persistent, pain, PCB/IMB, pregnancy, or age <25 with risk (speculum, bimanual, pH of discharge).
2. Tests: self-taken vulvovaginal swab NAAT for chlamydia + gonorrhoea (first-void urine in men); high vaginal swab (charcoal) for BV/TV/candida only if symptoms atypical/recurrent/pregnant; HIV + syphilis serology with any STI (window: HIV 45 days 4th-gen, syphilis 12 weeks). Offer full screen at GUM/sexual health (also hepatitis B/C if risk, rectal/pharyngeal swabs by exposure). Mycoplasma genitalium NAAT if urethritis/PID/PCB not explained.
3. Pattern: thin grey fishy (pH >4.5) = BV; frothy yellow-green, itch, strawberry cervix = trichomonas; thick white curdy, itch, pH <4.5 = candida; mucopurulent cervicitis/PCB = chlamydia/gonorrhoea; physiological — clear/white, no odour, cyclical.
4. PID (lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, cervical motion tenderness, discharge, fever): swabs then treat empirically WITHOUT waiting — ceftriaxone 1 g IM stat + doxycycline 100 mg bd 14 days + metronidazole 400 mg bd 14 days; admit if pregnant, severe, tubo-ovarian abscess, or not improving 72 h; remove IUD only if no improvement; partner treatment.

options.label: Chlamydia and gonorrhoea
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Chlamydia: doxycycline 100 mg bd for 7 days (first line, also covers M. genitalium poorly — avoid azithromycin single dose now except pregnancy). Pregnancy/breastfeeding: azithromycin 1 g stat then 500 mg od 2 days (or amoxicillin 500 mg tds 7 days; erythromycin). Test of cure only in pregnancy, rectal infection, or persistent symptoms (at ≥3 weeks). Re-test at 3 months (reinfection). Abstain 7 days after both partners treated. Partner notification (all partners in 6 months) — GUM/health adviser; opportunistic screening <25.
2. Gonorrhoea: ceftriaxone 1 g IM stat (if sensitivities unknown); ciprofloxacin 500 mg stat only if cipro-sensitive on culture. ALWAYS take culture (charcoal swab) before treatment for resistance; test of cure for ALL at 2 weeks (NAAT) — BASHH; refer to GUM preferably (resistance surveillance, pharyngeal/rectal sites, partner notification). Disseminated (arthritis, pustular rash) → admit.
3. Notify HIV/syphilis results; hepatitis B vaccination for MSM/risk; advise condoms; consider PrEP referral for HIV-negative at ongoing risk.

options.label: BV, trichomonas, candidiasis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. BV (treat if symptomatic, pregnant with symptoms, or before gynaecological procedures/TOP): metronidazole 400 mg bd 5–7 days (or 2 g stat — not in pregnancy), or metronidazole 0.75% vaginal gel od 5 days, or clindamycin 2% cream nocte 7 days; avoid alcohol with metronidazole; avoid douching/scented products. Recurrent (≥4/year): confirm diagnosis, treat, then suppressive metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4–6 months (BASHH), consider lactic acid gel/probiotics (weak evidence), change contraception from copper IUD; partners not treated (male).
2. Trichomonas (STI): metronidazole 400 mg bd 5–7 days (or 2 g stat; 2 g avoided in pregnancy — 400 mg bd); treat partner; test of cure not routine; full STI screen; GUM referral for partner notification.
3. Candidiasis: clotrimazole 500 mg pessary stat (or 200 mg 3 nights) ± clotrimazole 1% cream for vulva, or fluconazole 150 mg oral stat (not pregnancy — use topical 7 days). Avoid tight synthetic clothing, soaps; manage diabetes, antibiotics. RECURRENT (≥4 episodes/year, confirmed by culture): induction fluconazole 150 mg every 72 h ×3 then maintenance 150 mg weekly for 6 months (BASHH); check HbA1c, HIV, iron; non-albicans (C. glabrata) → GUM — nystatin pessaries 14 days/boric acid; consider stopping oestrogen-containing contraception; no need to treat asymptomatic partners.

pelvic-pain.title: Chronic pelvic pain, vulvodynia, vaginismus and breast pain

options.label: Chronic pelvic pain
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ≥6 months intermittent/constant lower abdominal/pelvic pain not exclusively with menstruation/intercourse. Causes often overlap: endometriosis/adenomyosis, PID sequelae/adhesions, IBS, interstitial cystitis/painful bladder, musculoskeletal (pelvic floor myalgia, hernia, nerve entrapment — pudendal), psychosocial (abuse history, depression — ask sensitively), post-surgical.
2. Work-up: pregnancy test, STI screen (chlamydia/gonorrhoea), urinalysis/MSU, FBC/CRP, transvaginal USS; pain diary (cyclical pattern suggests endometriosis — NG73); examine for trigger points, pelvic floor tenderness.
3. Management: explain pain mechanisms early; NSAID/paracetamol; hormonal suppression trial 3–6 months (CHC continuous, desogestrel, LNG-IUS) if cyclical even with normal USS; IBS treatment (antispasmodic, low FODMAP, linaclotide); pelvic floor physiotherapy; amitriptyline 10–50 mg or gabapentin for neuropathic component; CBT/pain management programme. Refer gynaecology if suspected endometriosis, no response at 3–6 months, or abnormal USS; laparoscopy for diagnosis/treatment; MDT pelvic pain clinic for refractory. Red flags → 2WW (mass, ascites, PMB, weight loss).

options.label: Vulvodynia and vaginismus
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Vulvodynia (burning vulval pain ≥3 months, no visible cause; provoked at entrance — Q-tip test — or unprovoked/generalised): exclude candida (swab), lichen sclerosus/planus, dermatitis (irritants, soaps), atrophy (menopause), herpes, neuropathy. Management: vulval skin care (emollient/soap substitute, cotton underwear, avoid wipes/panty liners), topical lidocaine 5% ointment 15–20 min before intercourse (or overnight), amitriptyline 10 mg → 25–75 mg or gabapentin, pelvic floor physiotherapy (first line for provoked), CBT/psychosexual counselling (Relate/COSRT), vaginal dilators; vulval pain clinic/dermatology if persistent; vestibulectomy rarely.
2. Vaginismus (involuntary pelvic floor spasm preventing penetration; often fear/pain cycle; may follow painful first experiences, trauma, vulvodynia): explain, examine only with consent/with the woman in control; graded self-exploration and dilator programme with pelvic floor physiotherapist; psychosexual therapy; treat underlying vulvodynia/atrophy; botulinum toxin via specialist in refractory cases. Local lubricant; avoid blaming partner dynamics. Refer psychosexual service.

options.label: Breast pain
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Cyclical (bilateral, diffuse, luteal phase, premenopausal, examination normal): reassure — not cancer (pain alone <1% cancer risk); supportive bra (day and night), paracetamol/ibuprofen or topical NSAID (diclofenac gel), reduce caffeine (weak evidence), review HRT/CHC (consider lower oestrogen, progestogen change or stopping); evening primrose oil no longer recommended. Persistent severe cyclical pain >6 months affecting life → breast clinic for danazol/tamoxifen (specialist, off-label).
2. Non-cyclical: localised — costochondritis (Tietze — tender costal cartilage; NSAID), trauma, cysts (USS/aspiration), periductal mastitis (smokers; co-amoxiclav), mastitis/abscess (lactational — flucloxacillin 500 mg qds 10–14 days, continue feeding, USS if not settling 48 h → aspiration), herpes zoster, cervical/thoracic referred pain, cardiac (if exertional/left-sided).
3. NG12: 2WW breast clinic for any unexplained lump (age ≥30), skin change, nipple change/discharge (≥50 unilateral), or any lump with pain; pain with no lump and normal examination does NOT need 2WW — reassure and review in 6–8 weeks; consider routine breast clinic if persistent unilateral non-cyclical pain.

ectopic-pregnancy.title: Pregnancy in general practice – early pregnancy, hyperemesis, antenatal care, pre-eclampsia, VTE, mental health, postnatal bleeding
niceRefs: NICE NG126 Ectopic pregnancy and miscarriage
NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health

options.label: Early pregnancy bleeding / pain — ectopic and miscarriage
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, shoulder-tip pain, collapse, or PV bleeding → pregnancy test. Positive test + pain or bleeding (or risk: previous ectopic, tubal surgery, IUD, IVF, PID) → refer EARLY PREGNANCY ASSESSMENT UNIT (same day if pain, haemodynamically unstable, shoulder-tip pain, or >6 weeks; 999 if collapse/severe pain). Do NOT do a bimanual to 'check for ectopic'.
2. NG126: EPAU does TVUSS ± serial hCG (48 h rise <63% suggests ectopic/non-viable); ectopic — expectant (hCG <1000 falling), methotrexate 50 mg/m² IM (hCG <1500–5000, no pain, unruptured, able to follow up; avoid conception 3 months), or laparoscopic salpingectomy/salpingotomy. Anti-D 250 IU for rhesus-negative women after surgical management (not for threatened/complete miscarriage <12 weeks or medical management).
3. Miscarriage: expectant (7–14 days), medical (misoprostol 800 micrograms PV/oral ± mifepristone 200 mg 48 h before — NG126 2023 update), or surgical (MVA/ERPC); bleeding/pain advice, pregnancy test 3 weeks after; Miscarriage Association support; recurrent (≥3) → recurrent miscarriage clinic (antiphospholipid antibodies, karyotype, pelvic USS).

options.label: Hyperemesis and antenatal care
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Nausea/vomiting of pregnancy (PUQE score): first line — ginger, acupressure, small frequent meals; antiemetics (RCOG/UKTIS): cyclizine 50 mg tds, prochlorperazine 5–10 mg tds (buccal 3–6 mg bd), promethazine 25 mg nocte, or doxylamine/pyridoxine (Xonvea) 10/10 mg; second line metoclopramide 10 mg tds (max 5 days) or ondansetron 4–8 mg bd–tds (small orofacial cleft risk <10 weeks — informed decision); third line prednisolone (specialist). Hyperemesis gravidarum (weight loss >5%, ketonuria, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance) → day-unit/admission for IV fluids (Hartmann's/saline + KCl, NOT dextrose first), thiamine (Wernicke's prevention), VTE prophylaxis; check TFT (gestational thyrotoxicosis), USS (molar/multiple). PPI/H2RA for reflux. Pregnancy Sickness Support.
2. Booking (NG201): by 10 weeks — refer to midwife at first contact; folic acid 400 micrograms (5 mg if previous NTD, diabetes, epilepsy, BMI ≥30, sickle/thalassaemia, antiepileptics) until 12 weeks; vitamin D 10 micrograms throughout; stop smoking/alcohol; review medications (stop ACE-i/ARB, statins, warfarin→LMWH, valproate/topiramate, methotrexate, isotretinoin, lithium with specialist); aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks if pre-eclampsia risk (see below); screening offered — bloods (FBC, group/antibodies, HIV, hepatitis B, syphilis, haemoglobinopathy), combined screening 11–14 weeks, anomaly scan 18–20+6, gestational diabetes OGTT 24–28 weeks if risk (BMI ≥30, previous GDM/macrosomia, family history, South Asian/Black Caribbean/Middle Eastern). Vaccines: pertussis from 16 weeks, influenza, COVID, RSV from 28 weeks (2024). Antenatal infections: asymptomatic bacteriuria MSU at booking (treat — nitrofurantoin avoid at term, trimethoprim avoid first trimester); chickenpox/parvovirus/rubella contact → check serology; listeria/toxoplasma food advice; group B strep — no routine screening; genital herpes first episode in third trimester → GUM/obstetrics (aciclovir, consider CS).

options.label: Pre-eclampsia, VTE, mental health, postnatal bleeding
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Pre-eclampsia (NG133): new hypertension ≥140/90 after 20 weeks with proteinuria (ACR ≥8 mg/mmol or PCR ≥30) or organ dysfunction; symptoms — headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain, oedema, reduced fetal movements. SAME-DAY obstetric assessment (maternity triage) for BP ≥140/90 with proteinuria or symptoms; ≥160/110 is severe → urgent admission (labetalol 200 mg oral, or nifedipine MR). Aspirin 75–150 mg nightly from 12 weeks for high risk (previous pre-eclampsia, chronic hypertension, CKD, diabetes, autoimmune disease) or ≥2 moderate factors (first pregnancy, age ≥40, BMI ≥35, family history, multiple pregnancy, interval >10 years). Chronic hypertension: labetalol/nifedipine/methyldopa (stop methyldopa within 2 days postnatal — depression). Postnatal: BP check day 3–5 and 2 weeks; pre-eclampsia doubles later cardiovascular risk — annual BP, lifestyle.
2. VTE (RCOG 37a): assess risk at booking, each admission and postnatally; LMWH (enoxaparin 40 mg od; weight-adjusted) antenatally if score ≥4 (≥3 from 28 weeks), 6 weeks postnatal if ≥2 or caesarean/other risk; previous VTE → LMWH throughout + 6 weeks. Suspected DVT/PE in pregnancy → same-day obstetric/medical assessment (D-dimer unreliable; duplex/CTPA or V/Q); start LMWH while awaiting imaging. Warfarin and DOACs contraindicated.
3. Mental health (CG192): ask about mood/anxiety at booking and postnatally (Whooley questions, EPDS); previous bipolar/psychosis/severe depression → refer perinatal mental health team pre-conception/at booking (postpartum psychosis risk 25–50%); suicidal ideation, psychosis, thoughts of harming baby, rapid deterioration → same-day perinatal/crisis team. Medication: sertraline preferred SSRI in pregnancy/breastfeeding; do not stop antidepressants abruptly; lithium/valproate — specialist; CBT/IAPT fast-track for perinatal women. Postnatal depression: EPDS ≥13 → treat (CBT, sertraline), health visitor, partner support.
4. Secondary postpartum haemorrhage (abnormal/excessive bleeding 24 h–12 weeks after birth): endometritis (offensive lochia, fever, tender uterus — co-amoxiclav 625 mg tds 7 days, or clindamycin + gentamicin if admitted) or retained products (USS — ERPC); heavy bleeding/unwell → same-day maternity assessment/999 if soaking pads hourly or faint. Also: perineal wound infection, mastitis, VTE, pre-eclampsia up to 6 weeks, anaemia (ferritin; iron), contraception from day 21 (LARC; avoid CHC <6 weeks if breastfeeding or VTE risk), 6–8 week check (mood, BP, contraception, smear if due, pelvic floor).

ectopic-pregnancy.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

menopause-symptoms.title: Menopause – HRT choice, risks, bleeding on HRT, non-hormonal options

options.label: Diagnosis and HRT prescribing
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnose clinically in women >45 (vasomotor symptoms + irregular/absent periods); FSH only if 40–45 with atypical symptoms, <40 (suspect POI — two FSH >25 IU/L 4–6 weeks apart), or on hormonal contraception. Also assess: sleep, mood, joint pain, cognition, libido, genitourinary symptoms, cardiovascular risk, bone risk (FRAX), contraception needs (until 2 years after LMP if <50, 1 year if >50; or 55).
2. HRT first line for vasomotor symptoms (and low mood/anxiety due to menopause — NG23 2024: do not offer SSRIs for low mood in menopause without depression). Oestrogen: transdermal preferred (patch 25–50 micrograms/24 h, gel 0.5–1 mg/2 pumps, spray) — no VTE/stroke increase, use if BMI >30, migraine, VTE/CVD risk, gallbladder disease, on enzyme inducers; oral estradiol 1–2 mg otherwise. Progestogen for endometrial protection if uterus: micronised progesterone (Utrogestan) 200 mg nocte 12 days/cycle (sequential, if periods within 12 months) or 100 mg daily (continuous combined, ≥12 months after LMP or ≥54), or LNG-IUS (Mirena, 5 years for HRT — also contraception), or combined patches/tablets. Start low; review at 3 months then annually (BP, weight, bleeding, breast awareness, symptoms); no arbitrary limit on duration — continue while benefits outweigh risks; taper or stop abruptly when stopping (same recurrence rate).
3. Vaginal oestrogen (estradiol 10 microgram pessary, estriol cream/gel, Gina OTC) for genitourinary syndrome — can be used long term, with or without systemic HRT, and in most women with breast cancer history (specialist advice). Vaginal moisturisers (Replens/YES), lubricants. Testosterone gel (Testogel/Tostran, ~5 mg/day off-label) for low libido after optimising HRT — check total testosterone baseline/3 months.

options.label: Risks, contraindications and bleeding on HRT
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Breast cancer: oestrogen-only — little/no increase; combined HRT — small increase (about 4 extra cases per 1000 women over 5 years at 50–59, similar to 2 units alcohol/day or obesity), declining after stopping; micronised progesterone/dydrogesterone lower risk than synthetic progestogens. No increase in all-cause mortality in NG23 analyses. Contraindicated: current/past breast cancer (specialist), oestrogen-dependent cancer, undiagnosed PV bleeding, active VTE/thrombophilia (transdermal possible via haematology), active liver disease, uncontrolled hypertension (control first). Migraine with aura: transdermal OK. Diabetes, hypertension, previous MI/stroke: transdermal with specialist advice; starting <60 or within 10 years of menopause is cardioprotective/neutral.
2. VTE: oral HRT ~2× risk (absolute low); transdermal no increase — use transdermal in BMI >30, previous VTE, thrombophilia, smokers, immobility. Stroke: oral slight increase >60; transdermal none. Gallbladder disease: oral increases.
3. Bleeding on HRT: sequential — expect monthly withdrawal bleed; investigate if heavy, prolonged, >6 months of irregular bleeding, or bleeding after 6 months on continuous combined, or any bleeding after amenorrhoea on continuous combined → TVUSS (endometrial thickness threshold on HRT ~5 mm) ± hysteroscopy/biopsy; 2WW if ≥55 and postmenopausal bleeding not clearly HRT-related. Check adherence, missed progestogen, drug interactions (enzyme inducers, St John's wort), weight. Unscheduled bleeding in first 3–6 months is common — reassure and review.

options.label: Non-hormonal and lifestyle options
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Lifestyle: regular exercise, weight management, reduce alcohol/caffeine/spicy food, layered clothing/fans, sleep hygiene, stop smoking; CBT (NG23 2024 — recommended for vasomotor symptoms, sleep and mood; group/online — Menopause: Stress, Mood etc.).
2. Drugs when HRT declined/contraindicated: fezolinetant 45 mg od (NICE TA1033 2024, neurokinin-3 antagonist — LFT monitoring); SSRI/SNRI — venlafaxine 37.5–75 mg, citalopram/escitalopram 10–20 mg, paroxetine 10 mg (avoid with tamoxifen), desvenlafaxine (not UK) — modest vasomotor benefit; gabapentin 300 mg nocte–900 mg/day (night sweats, sleep); clonidine 50–75 micrograms bd (limited, hypotension); oxybutynin 2.5–5 mg (off-label). Not recommended: black cohosh/isoflavones (unregulated, interactions), compounded 'bioidentical' hormones.
3. Breast cancer survivors: vaginal moisturisers first; low-dose vaginal oestrogen with oncology agreement (not with aromatase inhibitors without discussion); CBT, fezolinetant, venlafaxine/gabapentin for flushes. Bone health: calcium/vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, FRAX/DEXA if risk; HRT is first-line for osteoporosis prevention in women <60 with POI/early menopause.

generalised-anxiety-disorder.title: Anxiety disorders – GAD, panic disorder, medication choice, benzodiazepine withdrawal
niceRefs: NICE CG113 Generalised anxiety disorder and panic disorder
NICE CKS Benzodiazepine and z-drug withdrawal

options.label: Assessment and stepped care
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. GAD: excessive worry most days ≥6 months, restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability, muscle tension, sleep disturbance (GAD-7 ≥10 moderate, ≥15 severe). Panic disorder: recurrent unexpected attacks + ≥1 month anticipatory fear/avoidance. Screen for depression (PHQ-9), alcohol/substance use, physical causes (TFT, FBC, glucose; ECG/caffeine/beta-agonists/decongestants in palpitations), suicide risk.
2. Step 1: psychoeducation, active monitoring, sleep hygiene, exercise, reduce caffeine/alcohol, self-help (NHS Every Mind Matters, Overcoming Anxiety). Step 2: low-intensity — guided self-help/CBT-based (NHS Talking Therapies self-referral), psychoeducational groups. Step 3 (marked impairment or no response): high-intensity CBT (12–15 sessions) OR drug treatment — equal evidence; patient choice. Step 4: refer secondary care if severe, self-neglect, suicide risk, treatment-resistant.
3. Panic: CBT first line (interoceptive exposure); SSRI if preferred/CBT unavailable; do NOT prescribe benzodiazepines for panic disorder; breathing/grounding techniques for acute attacks; ECG/thyroid only if clinically indicated.

options.label: Medication
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. First line: SSRI — sertraline 25–50 mg → 100–200 mg (best cost-effectiveness, off-label for GAD but NICE-preferred), or escitalopram 10 → 20 mg / paroxetine 20 → 50 mg (licensed). Warn: initial jitteriness in first 1–2 weeks (start half dose; short course of propranolol 10–40 mg tds for somatic symptoms if no asthma), full effect 4–6 weeks, review 2 weeks (1 week if <30 — suicidality warning), then monthly. Continue ≥12 months after remission (relapse prevention), taper over 4+ weeks.
2. Second line: alternative SSRI, or SNRI — venlafaxine MR 75 → 225 mg (BP check), duloxetine 60 → 120 mg. Third line: pregabalin 75 mg bd → 300 mg bd (licensed for GAD; CD; dependence/misuse risk; avoid with opioids). Do NOT use antipsychotics in primary care for GAD. Hydroxyzine 25–50 mg for short-term relief only (QT). Buspirone 5 mg tds (slow onset) as an option.
3. Benzodiazepines: only short-term crisis (≤2–4 weeks, diazepam 2–5 mg prn) — not for GAD/panic maintenance (CG113). Social anxiety (CG159): CBT first; SSRI (escitalopram/sertraline) second; propranolol for performance anxiety only. Nightmares (esp. PTSD): sleep hygiene, image rehearsal therapy (CBT-based), prazosin 1 mg nocte → 2–10 mg (off-label; postural hypotension), treat underlying PTSD/depression; stop beta-blockers/SSRIs if causing.

options.label: Benzodiazepine / z-drug reduction
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Engage: explain dependence after >2–4 weeks' use, benefits of stopping (cognition, falls, mood); patient-led pace; address underlying insomnia/anxiety first (CBT-I, SSRI). Do not withdraw abruptly (seizures).
2. Convert to diazepam (long half-life) where possible: diazepam 5 mg ≈ lorazepam 0.5 mg ≈ temazepam 10 mg ≈ nitrazepam 5 mg ≈ zopiclone 7.5 mg ≈ clonazepam 0.5 mg ≈ oxazepam 15 mg ≈ chlordiazepoxide 15 mg. Switch stepwise over 1–2 weeks for high doses.
3. Reduce diazepam by about 1/10 of the daily dose (1–2 mg) every 1–2 weeks; slow to 0.5 mg steps below 5 mg; pause (not increase) if withdrawal symptoms (anxiety, insomnia, tremor, perceptual change); typical course 2–6 months, up to a year. Review fortnightly; written plan; no 'top-ups'. Avoid substituting with pregabalin/antipsychotics/alcohol. Propranolol for autonomic symptoms if needed; NHS Talking Therapies/Bristol & District Tranquilliser Project resources. Refer community drug service if high dose (>30 mg diazepam equivalent), polysubstance use, or alcohol dependence; involve mental health team if severe anxiety unmasked.

generalised-anxiety-disorder.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

obsessive-compulsive-disorder-management.title: OCD, body dysmorphic disorder and hoarding

options.label: OCD — recognise and treat
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Obsessions (intrusive unwanted thoughts/images/urges — contamination, harm, symmetry, sexual/religious/aggressive) and/or compulsions (washing, checking, counting, mental rituals, reassurance seeking) taking >1 h/day or causing distress/impairment. Screen with 5 questions (Do you wash or clean a lot? Check things a lot? Any thought that keeps bothering you that you would like to get rid of? Daily activities take a long time? Concerned about putting things in a special order / upset by mess?). Intrusive harm thoughts are NOT intent — do not misinterpret as risk; Y-BOCS for severity.
2. Mild (CG31): low-intensity CBT including exposure and response prevention (ERP) ≤10 h — NHS Talking Therapies self-referral, guided self-help. Moderate: choice of SSRI OR high-intensity CBT/ERP (>10 h). Severe: SSRI + CBT/ERP. SSRI doses are HIGHER and response SLOWER than depression: fluoxetine 20 → 60–80 mg, sertraline 50 → 200 mg, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, escitalopram 20 mg; trial 12 weeks at maximum tolerated dose; continue ≥12 months after remission; taper slowly. Second line: clomipramine 25 → 150–250 mg (ECG, overdose risk; specialist advice). Augmentation (specialist): antipsychotic (aripiprazole/risperidone low dose).
3. Refer secondary care/specialist OCD service: severe (Y-BOCS >24), inadequate response to 2 SSRIs + CBT, significant risk/self-neglect, comorbid psychosis/severe depression, children (CAMHS — CBT/ERP first, sertraline/fluvoxamine). Family: reduce accommodation of rituals; OCD-UK/OCD Action.

options.label: Body dysmorphic disorder
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Preoccupation with perceived defect(s) in appearance not visible/slight to others (skin, hair, nose, muscles), repetitive behaviours (mirror checking, camouflage, skin picking, comparing, reassurance seeking, cosmetic procedures), ≥1 h/day, significant distress; high suicide risk (ask directly); often hidden — ask about appearance concerns in depression, social anxiety, dermatology/cosmetic requests. Screen: 'Do you worry a lot about the way you look and wish you could think about it less?'
2. Treatment (CG31): CBT specifically for BDD (with ERP, mirror retraining) ± SSRI at high dose (fluoxetine 60–80 mg) for moderate–severe; clomipramine second line; antipsychotic augmentation specialist only. Advise against cosmetic surgery/dermatological procedures (symptoms persist or shift; dissatisfaction) — refer to mental health first; liaise with dermatology/plastics.
3. Refer specialist BDD/OCD service if severe, suicidal, housebound, not responding; BDD Foundation.

options.label: Hoarding disorder
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Persistent difficulty discarding possessions regardless of value, cluttered living areas unusable, distress/impairment; onset often adolescence, worse with age/loss; assess insight (often poor), depression, OCD, ADHD, dementia, psychosis, physical disability, self-neglect, fire/fall risk, animal hoarding, safeguarding of dependents.
2. Management: build trust — do not force clear-outs (traumatic, ineffective, relapse); specialised CBT for hoarding (motivational interviewing, skills in organising/decision-making, graded discarding, home visits) via mental health team/NHS Talking Therapies where offered; SSRI/venlafaxine for comorbid depression/anxiety (modest effect on hoarding); harm reduction — fire service safe-and-well visit, clear pathways/exits, pest control, environmental health as last resort with support.
3. Refer: adult social care (self-neglect under Care Act 2014 safeguarding), community mental health team (severe/poor insight), OT home assessment, Hoarding UK/Help for Hoarders; multi-agency approach (housing, fire service).

obsessive-compulsive-disorder-management.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

post-traumatic-stress-disorder-managemen.title: PTSD and complex PTSD

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. After exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury or sexual violence (directly, witnessed, learned of, repeated occupational exposure): re-experiencing (intrusions, nightmares, flashbacks), avoidance, negative mood/cognition, hyperarousal (sleep, irritability, hypervigilance, startle) for >1 month with impairment. Screen with PC-PTSD-5 or 'In the past month have you had nightmares/avoided reminders/been on guard/felt numb?'; Trauma Screening Questionnaire ≥6; assess at 1 month post-trauma (acute stress reaction before then — watchful waiting, practical support; single-session debriefing is NOT recommended). Complex PTSD (ICD-11): core PTSD + affect dysregulation, negative self-concept, relationship difficulties — prolonged/repeated trauma (childhood abuse, domestic violence, trafficking, torture).
2. Ask about: substance/alcohol use, depression, suicide/self-harm, dissociation, ongoing safety (domestic abuse — safeguarding/MARAC; refugees — Freedom from Torture), sleep, pain, physical injury, driving, employment/benefits, veterans (Op COURAGE).
3. Children/young people: CAMHS; trauma-focused CBT age-appropriate; EMDR 7+.

options.label: Treatment (NG116)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. First line (within 1 month if symptoms severe; otherwise from 1 month): trauma-focused CBT (8–12 sessions, 90 min, e.g. cognitive processing therapy, prolonged exposure, narrative exposure therapy for refugees) OR EMDR (if trauma >3 months ago; 8–12 sessions) — via NHS Talking Therapies (self-referral; ask for trauma pathway) or secondary care for complex/multiple trauma. Do not offer non-trauma-focused interventions alone (relaxation, supportive counselling). Computerised TF-CBT for mild cases.
2. Drugs (only if preferred, psychological therapy declined/unavailable, or comorbid depression): venlafaxine 75 → 225 mg or an SSRI (sertraline 50 → 200 mg — licensed; paroxetine); review 4–8 weeks, continue ≥12 months; do NOT use benzodiazepines (impair recovery, dependence). Nightmares/sleep: prazosin 1 mg → up to 10 mg nocte (off-label), sleep hygiene, image rehearsal. Antipsychotics (risperidone) only for severe hyperarousal/psychotic symptoms under specialist supervision.
3. Complex PTSD: phased approach — stabilisation (safety, emotion regulation skills — DBT-informed/STAIR), then trauma processing, then reintegration; longer therapy via secondary care/specialist trauma service; peer support.

options.label: Referral and support
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Urgent mental health: active suicidal ideation/plan, psychosis, severe self-neglect, risk to others, severe dissociation.
2. Secondary care/specialist trauma service: complex PTSD, multiple/prolonged trauma, severe comorbidity (substance dependence — treat concurrently, do not delay trauma therapy), failure of first-line therapy, personality disorder features.
3. Signposting: Op COURAGE (NHS veterans mental health), Combat Stress, Rape Crisis, Survivors UK, Victim Support, Freedom from Torture, Refugee Council, Mind, PTSD UK; occupational health/fit note with phased return; Access to Work; DVLA only if symptoms affect driving.

psychosis-first-episode.title: Psychosis and bipolar disorder – first episode, maintenance, lithium and clozapine monitoring
niceRefs: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults

options.label: First episode psychosis and mania — act now
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Psychosis: hallucinations (usually auditory), delusions, disorganised speech/behaviour, negative symptoms (withdrawal, flat affect, self-neglect), often prodrome of decline over months (age 15–35). Refer EARLY INTERVENTION IN PSYCHOSIS (EIP) team URGENTLY — self/GP referral, assessment within 2 weeks (NHS standard), any age ≥14; do not start antipsychotics in primary care unless advised (EIP chooses: aripiprazole/risperidone/olanzapine/quetiapine low dose, CBTp, family intervention). Same day/crisis team/999 if risk to self/others, severe self-neglect, command hallucinations, catatonia, or no insight with refusal of help (Mental Health Act assessment via AMHP).
2. Exclude organic/drug causes: urine drug screen (cannabis, stimulants, synthetic cannabinoids, ketamine), alcohol withdrawal, steroids, levodopa, delirium (fluctuating consciousness — see Delirium), epilepsy, thyroid, B12, HIV/syphilis, autoimmune encephalitis (rapid onset, seizures, movement disorder → neurology), head injury; FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, glucose/HbA1c, lipids, ECG (baseline for antipsychotics), prolactin.
3. Mania (elevated/irritable mood ≥1 week with grandiosity, reduced sleep, pressured speech, risky spending/sex, psychosis) → same-day secondary care (crisis team/home treatment or admission; MHA if needed); stop antidepressants; hypomania (≥4 days, no severe impairment) → urgent CMHT. Bipolar II/cyclothymia (chronic mood swings not meeting criteria): refer CMHT for diagnosis — never start an antidepressant alone in suspected bipolar (switch risk); mood diary; psychoeducation.

options.label: Maintenance and physical health (GP role)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Schizophrenia: antipsychotic continued 1–2 years after first episode, often long term; depot (paliperidone, aripiprazole, risperidone LAI) if adherence poor; clozapine if 2 antipsychotics failed (treatment-resistant). Bipolar maintenance (CG185): lithium first line (most effective, anti-suicidal); alternatives — valproate (NOT in women of childbearing potential), olanzapine, quetiapine, lamotrigine (bipolar depression); bipolar depression — quetiapine, fluoxetine + olanzapine, lamotrigine; do not use antidepressant monotherapy. Psychological: CBT, family intervention, psychoeducation, relapse signature/crisis plan.
2. ANNUAL PHYSICAL HEALTH CHECK (SMI register, QOF): weight/BMI/waist, BP, HbA1c, lipids, smoking (offer varenicline/NRT — bupropion caution), alcohol/drugs, ECG if indicated, prolactin/sexual dysfunction (switch to aripiprazole), extrapyramidal/tardive dyskinesia (AIMS), constipation (clozapine — serious), dental, cervical/bowel/breast screening uptake, flu/COVID/pneumococcal vaccines, contraception/pregnancy planning (valproate/lithium/carbamazepine teratogenic; refer perinatal team early). Life expectancy 15–20 years shorter — treat CVD risk aggressively (statin, metformin for antipsychotic weight gain with specialist agreement).
3. Relapse signs: sleep loss, withdrawal, paranoia, stopping medication → contact CMHT/crisis team early; carers' support and assessment; employment (IPS); benefits; driving (DVLA rules for psychosis/bipolar).

options.label: Lithium and clozapine monitoring
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. LITHIUM: baseline U&E/eGFR, calcium, TFT, FBC, weight, ECG if CVD risk; target serum level 0.6–0.8 mmol/L (0.8–1.0 if previously relapsed/mania), sampled 12 h post-dose; levels weekly until stable, then every 3 months for first year and every 6 months thereafter (3-monthly if >65, renal impairment, interacting drugs, poor adherence); U&E, calcium, TFT every 6 months; weight annually. Lithium pack/alert card/record book. Toxicity (>1.5, or symptoms at any level): coarse tremor, GI upset, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, seizures → stop, same-day level and U&E, admit if >2.0 or symptomatic. Interactions: NSAIDs, ACE-i/ARB, thiazides, dehydration, low-salt diets, carbamazepine → avoid or monitor; never stop lithium abruptly (relapse) — taper over ≥4 weeks (3 months ideally) if discontinuing. Pregnancy: specialist review (Ebstein's small risk; do not stop abruptly). Long-term: nephrogenic DI, CKD, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.
2. CLOZAPINE (specialist-initiated, registered monitoring service — Clozaril/Denzapine/Zaponex): FBC weekly for 18 weeks, fortnightly to 1 year, then 4-weekly — neutrophils <1.5 = stop and urgent haematology/psychiatry; GP: never prescribe without a valid green blood result; flag fever/sore throat (agranulocytosis), chest pain/tachycardia/fever in first 2 months (myocarditis — ECG, troponin, CRP, same-day), CONSTIPATION (treat aggressively — macrogol; fatal ileus risk), hypersalivation (hyoscine), seizures (dose-related), weight/diabetes/lipids, smoking changes alter levels (stopping smoking ↑ level by up to 50% — inform team), interactions (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin ↑ levels; carbamazepine ↓). Missed doses >48 h → re-titration by team. Annual: ECG, lipids, HbA1c, weight, prolactin.

eating-disorders-when-to-refer.title: Eating disorders and gambling harm – recognition and referral

options.label: Eating disorders — recognise and assess risk
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect with: low BMI or rapid weight loss, dieting/food rules, fear of weight gain, bingeing, purging (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics, over-exercise), amenorrhoea, GI symptoms, dental erosion, calluses on knuckles (Russell's sign), lanugo, fainting, bradycardia, electrolyte disturbance; athletes, type 1 diabetes (insulin omission — 'diabulimia'), autism (ARFID — restricted range without weight/shape concerns). SCOFF ≥2 screen; do not rely on BMI alone (normal-weight bulimia/binge eating; atypical anorexia).
2. Assess (MEED): weight, BMI/centile, rate of loss (>1 kg/week = high risk), BP (postural), pulse (<40 high risk), temperature (<35.5), sit-up/squat-stand test, ECG (QTc, bradycardia), bloods — FBC, U&E, Mg, phosphate, glucose, LFT, CK, TFT, bone profile; blind weighing if preferred.
3. NG69: refer IMMEDIATELY (same week) to community eating disorder service (CEDS/FREED for 16–25) at first suspicion — do not wait for weight thresholds; children/young people to CYP-ED (assessment within 1 week urgent/4 weeks routine). Same-day medical admission (MEED red): BMI <13 (adult) or <70% median for age, pulse <40, BP <90/60, postural drop >20, QTc >450, K <3.0, Na <130, phosphate low, glucose <3, temperature <35.5, unable to stand from squat, suicidal, acute food refusal. Refeeding risk — do not start aggressive feeding in community; dietitian/specialist.

options.label: Treatment pathways
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Anorexia (NG69): individual eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-ED, up to 40 sessions), MANTRA, SSCM; children — family therapy (FT-AN) first line. No drugs for anorexia itself; treat comorbidity cautiously (SSRIs less effective at low weight; avoid bupropion/QT-prolonging drugs); bone — DEXA after 1 year, weight restoration is the treatment (not HRT/bisphosphonates routinely); dental advice (fluoride, no brushing after vomiting); contraception discussion (fertility returns unpredictably).
2. Bulimia: guided self-help CBT-ED first (4–16 weeks), then CBT-ED (up to 20 sessions); fluoxetine 60 mg (licensed) reduces bingeing — adjunct, not alone; monitor K, dental erosion, oesophageal tears (haematemesis), laxative withdrawal plan.
3. Binge eating disorder: guided self-help CBT-ED, then group/individual CBT-ED; lisdexamfetamine (specialist, off-label UK); do NOT offer weight-loss as the goal of therapy; treat obesity-related comorbidity separately and sensitively; avoid stigma. ARFID: CEDS/paediatric MDT (dietitian, SLT, OT). Diabetes + eating disorder: urgent joint diabetes/ED team review. Carers: Beat helpline, carer skills training (NG69).

options.label: Gambling harm (NG248)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Ask routinely in: depression/anxiety, suicidality (gambling-related suicide risk high), alcohol/drug misuse, debt/financial stress, relationship breakdown, ADHD, young men, those on dopamine agonists/aripiprazole (impulse-control — review drug). Screen: 'Have you ever had an issue with gambling?' / PGSI short form; Lie/Bet questions.
2. Harm reduction now: self-exclusion — GamStop (online, free, 6 months–5 years), MOSES (betting shops), gambling blocks on bank cards (most UK banks), Gamban software, remove apps; involve a trusted person for finances; debt advice (StepChange, Citizens Advice, breathing space scheme); safeguard dependants; assess suicide risk directly.
3. Treatment: refer NHS Gambling Treatment Service (regional clinics, self-referral; National Gambling Helpline 0808 8020 133 / GamCare — CBT, group, family support), Gamblers Anonymous; CBT for gambling disorder is first line; naltrexone 50 mg (off-label, via specialist) for urges; treat comorbid depression/ADHD; relapse prevention; affected others — GamAnon, GamCare family support.

delirium-causes.title: Delirium, functional neurological/dissociative disorders, factitious disorder, acute agitation and de-escalation

options.label: Delirium (CG103)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute (hours–days) fluctuating inattention, altered consciousness/arousal (hyperactive, hypoactive — often missed — or mixed), disorganised thinking, perceptual change; 4AT ≥4 or CAM. Risk: age >65, dementia, frailty, hip fracture, sensory impairment, severe illness. Delirium = medical emergency with an underlying cause.
2. Find and treat cause(s) — PINCH ME: Pain, Infection (UTI only if symptomatic/positive culture — avoid the 'UTI' reflex: urine dip unreliable >65), Nutrition/dehydration, Constipation/urinary retention (bladder scan), Hypoxia/hypoglycaemia/hypo-/hypernatraemia/hypercalcaemia/thyroid, Medication (anticholinergics, opioids, benzodiazepines, steroids, recent changes — anticholinergic burden score), Environment/sleep, alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal (CIWA; chlordiazepoxide + Pabrinex), stroke/subdural (if focal signs/head injury/anticoagulant → CT), sepsis. Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, calcium, glucose, CRP, TFT, B12; ECG; CXR; MSU if symptoms.
3. Manage: orientate (clock, calendar, glasses, hearing aids, family), lighting, sleep, mobilise, hydration, avoid catheters/restraint/moves; no drugs unless severe distress/danger — haloperidol 0.5 mg oral (max 2 mg/day short term; NOT in Parkinson's/DLB — use lorazepam 0.5 mg) or lorazepam 0.5–1 mg; stop within 1 week. Admit if cause needs hospital treatment, unsafe at home, or no improvement; inform family (delirium can take weeks–months to resolve; increases dementia risk — review cognition at 3 months); document 'delirium' in the record.

options.label: Functional neurological and dissociative disorders
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. FND (formerly conversion): functional limb weakness (Hoover's sign positive, give-way), functional/dissociative seizures (eyes closed, long duration, side-to-side movements, no post-ictal confusion, rapid recovery, triggered by stress — do not call 'pseudoseizures'), functional tremor (entrainable/distractible), gait disorder, sensory symptoms, cognitive symptoms. Diagnosis is POSITIVE (rule-in signs), not by exclusion; comorbid organic disease is common. Dissociative disorders (depersonalisation/derealisation, amnesia, identity) — trauma-linked.
2. Explain the diagnosis clearly and without blame (neurosign.org/FND Hope/neurosymptoms.org): 'the brain's software not hardware', reversible, common. Avoid repeated investigation/opioids/'nothing wrong with you'. Refer neurology for confirmation of FND; then physiotherapy (FND-specific), psychological therapy (CBT for FND/dissociative seizures, trauma-focused if PTSD), OT, SLT; treat comorbid depression/anxiety/PTSD; involve psychiatry/liaison if dissociation severe or self-harm.
3. Dissociative seizures: stop AEDs if no epilepsy (neurology-led, video-EEG); safety plan; DVLA — must notify (Group 1: 3 months seizure-free criteria differ — check); carers/ambulance crews — not status epilepticus, avoid lorazepam/intubation; sign 'dissociative seizure' in notes/alert.

options.label: Factitious disorder and acute agitation/de-escalation
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Factitious disorder (imposed on self — 'Munchausen's'): deliberate production/feigning of symptoms for the sick role, not for external gain (malingering); patterns — multiple admissions/surgeries, inconsistent history, symptoms only when observed, insisting on invasive tests, self-induced infection/hypoglycaemia (sulfonylurea/insulin screen), unexplained wounds, discharge against advice when confronted; often healthcare background, personality disorder, trauma. Factitious disorder imposed on another (FII, child/vulnerable adult) → SAFEGUARDING referral (children's social care/named doctor) — do not confront the carer first.
2. Management: single named GP/coordinator, shared care record/alert (with MDT/legal advice re: confidentiality), minimise iatrogenic harm (no unnecessary tests/opioids/surgery), non-confrontational acknowledgement of distress, liaison psychiatry referral (may decline), treat comorbidity; GMC guidance on disclosure; avoid 'catching out'.
3. Acute agitation (NG10): de-escalation first — calm voice, space, one speaker, acknowledge feelings, offer choices/food/drink/phone, remove audience/triggers, treat pain/urinary retention/hypoglycaemia/delirium cause; check for weapons/exit; call police if imminent danger. Oral medication if needed and accepted: lorazepam 1–2 mg or promethazine 25–50 mg (benzodiazepine-naive/respiratory risk) ± oral haloperidol 2–5 mg (ECG; avoid in Parkinson's/dementia with Lewy bodies/QT) or olanzapine 10 mg orodispersible; IM rapid tranquillisation (lorazepam IM, or haloperidol + promethazine) ONLY in a setting with monitoring/resuscitation (hospital/crisis team) — not GP surgery. Mental Health Act assessment (AMHP/s136 police) when illness and risk; document capacity; debrief.

cough-chronic.title: Cough – acute bronchitis, post-viral and chronic cough

options.label: Acute cough / bronchitis (<3 weeks)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Usually viral; self-care — honey (>1 year), fluids, paracetamol/ibuprofen, pelargonium/guaifenesin optional; cough lasts 3–4 weeks. NG120: NO antibiotic for acute bronchitis in otherwise well adults/children; consider immediate or back-up antibiotic if systemically very unwell, high risk of complications (≥65 with ≥2 of hospitalisation last year, diabetes, heart failure, oral steroids; or ≥80 with ≥1), or symptoms worsening rapidly: doxycycline 200 mg day 1 then 100 mg od for 5 days (adults); amoxicillin 500 mg tds 5 days (children/pregnancy); clarithromycin/erythromycin if allergic. CRP point-of-care if available (<20 no antibiotic; 20–100 back-up; >100 immediate).
2. Pneumonia (CRB-65, focal signs, saturations <95%, RR >24, HR >100, fever >38 with crackles) → amoxicillin 500 mg–1 g tds 5 days (doxycycline/clarithromycin if allergic); admit if CRB-65 ≥2, saturations <92%, or unable to cope. Whooping cough (paroxysms, whoop, vomiting, ≥2 weeks; contact with cases; infants) → notify, PCR/serology, clarithromycin/azithromycin if within 3 weeks of onset (limits spread), exclude 48 h; vaccinate pregnant contacts.
3. Safety-net: haemoptysis, chest pain, breathlessness, weight loss, cough >3 weeks → reassess.

options.label: Chronic cough (>8 weeks) — work-up
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Red flags → CXR and 2WW lung cancer if ≥40 with ≥2 of (or ≥1 if smoker): cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss; haemoptysis ≥40 → 2WW regardless; persistent chest infection, finger clubbing, supraclavicular/persistent cervical nodes, thrombocytosis → urgent CXR (NG12).
2. All chronic cough: CXR, spirometry with reversibility (± FeNO), stop ACE inhibitor (switch to ARB — cough resolves within 4 weeks), stop smoking/vaping, review occupational/environmental exposure, assess for the 'big three': asthma/eosinophilic bronchitis (variable, nocturnal, FeNO/eosinophils → ICS trial 8 weeks), upper airway cough syndrome/rhinitis (post-nasal drip, throat clearing → intranasal steroid + antihistamine 4–8 weeks), GORD (heartburn, worse after meals/lying → PPI 8-week trial only if reflux symptoms; lifestyle). Also: bronchiectasis (sputum — HRCT), TB (risk factors, sputum AFB), OSA, heart failure (BNP), interstitial lung disease (crackles, clubbing — HRCT), pertussis.
3. Trial treatments sequentially for 4–8 weeks each; stop if no effect.

options.label: Refractory / unexplained chronic cough
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. If CXR, spirometry normal and treatment trials fail: 'cough hypersensitivity syndrome' (often women 50–60, laryngeal irritation, triggers — talking, cold air, perfume). Refer respiratory/specialist cough clinic (HRCT, bronchoscopy, methacholine challenge, oesophageal pH/manometry as needed).
2. Non-drug: speech and language therapy cough-suppression/laryngeal hygiene programme (first line, good evidence), hydration, avoid throat clearing, honey/lozenges.
3. Neuromodulators (specialist-led/off-label): low-dose morphine MR 5–10 mg bd (best evidence, constipation), gabapentin 300 mg → up to 1800 mg/day or pregabalin, amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte; gefapixant (P2X3 antagonist — NICE TA1024 approved 2024 for refractory chronic cough after specialist assessment). Avoid codeine linctus/dextromethorphan long term.

pleural-effusion.title: Pleural effusion and pneumothorax

options.label: Pleural effusion — assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Breathlessness, dull chest ache, stony-dull percussion, reduced breath sounds/vocal resonance; CXR shows blunted costophrenic angle (>200 mL) — PA + lateral; USS more sensitive. Unilateral effusion in adult = needs diagnosis (BTS 2023: urgent respiratory/pleural clinic referral — 2WW if cancer suspected: smoker, weight loss, age >40, asbestos exposure).
2. Bilateral effusions with heart failure/cirrhosis/nephrotic syndrome/hypoalbuminaemia → treat cause (diuretics; BNP, LFT, albumin, U&E, urine ACR, TFT); aspirate only if atypical (fever, chest pain, unilateral, not resolving with treatment).
3. Pleural aspiration (secondary care, USS-guided): Light's criteria — exudate if pleural:serum protein >0.5, LDH >0.6, or pleural LDH >2/3 upper limit; send protein, LDH, pH, glucose, cytology, microbiology (incl. AFB), differential cell count. Exudate causes: malignancy (lung, breast, mesothelioma, lymphoma), parapneumonic/empyema (pH <7.2 → chest drain), TB, PE, pancreatitis, RA/SLE, drugs (methotrexate, amiodarone), post-cardiac injury, chylothorax.

options.label: Pleural effusion — management
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Parapneumonic/empyema: admit — antibiotics (co-amoxiclav or per culture, 2–6 weeks), chest drain if pH <7.2/pus/loculated; intrapleural tPA/DNase; surgery (VATS) if failure.
2. Malignant effusion (specialist): therapeutic aspiration for symptoms; definitive — indwelling pleural catheter (IPC, home drainage, hospice-compatible) or talc pleurodesis (slurry via drain or thoracoscopic); treat primary (chemotherapy/targeted); mesothelioma — pleural MDT, compensation (Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit, Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme — notify, Mesothelioma UK).
3. GP role: breathlessness management (fan, positioning, opioids in palliative setting), recognise re-accumulation (repeat CXR/USS if symptoms return), IPC care via community nurses, anticipatory care planning; ensure safety-netting for drain site infection. TB effusion: standard 6-month anti-TB therapy (TB team).

options.label: Pneumothorax
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Sudden pleuritic chest pain + breathlessness; reduced breath sounds, hyper-resonance; tall thin young men (primary spontaneous), COPD/asthma/ILD/CF (secondary), trauma, iatrogenic; TENSION (hypotension, tracheal deviation, distended neck veins, severe distress) → 999, needle decompression (2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular, or 4th/5th anterior axillary) by trained clinician, high-flow oxygen.
2. Any suspected pneumothorax → same-day ED for CXR. BTS 2023 (adult, non-tension): minimal symptoms → conservative (ambulatory) regardless of size; symptomatic — high-risk features (secondary, >50 with smoking history, hypoxia, haemopneumothorax, bilateral) → chest drain; otherwise ambulatory device (Rocket pleural vent) or needle aspiration or conservative by patient preference; review 2–4 days, CXR follow-up until resolved.
3. After: no flying until 7 days after CXR confirms resolution (CAA/BTS), NO scuba diving ever (unless bilateral pleurectomy), stop smoking (recurrence risk), avoid heavy exertion 2–4 weeks; recurrence 30–50% → thoracic surgery (VATS pleurodesis/bullectomy) after second ipsilateral episode, first contralateral, or high-risk occupation (pilot, diver).

pleural-effusion.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

pulmonary-nodule.title: Lung cancer pathway – incidental nodules, mediastinal mass, metastases, mesothelioma

options.label: Incidental pulmonary nodule (BTS)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Solid nodule <5 mm (or <80 mm³) → no follow-up (very low risk); 5–6 mm (80–300 mm³) → CT at 1 year (then discharge if stable volume); 6–8 mm or ≥300 mm³ → CT at 3 months then 1 year (volumetry — volume doubling time); ≥8 mm (≥300 mm³) → Brock risk model: <10% → CT surveillance; ≥10% → PET-CT ± biopsy via lung MDT. Sub-solid/ground-glass nodules: CT at 3 months, then annually for 4 years if persistent (slow-growing adenocarcinoma spectrum).
2. In practice: the reporting radiologist usually states the BTS pathway — ensure the follow-up CT is booked (safety-net tracker); refer lung MDT/respiratory for any nodule ≥8 mm, growth, spiculation, upper-lobe location with risk factors, or patient anxiety needing discussion. Explain risk honestly (most nodules benign — granuloma, hamartoma, intrapulmonary node).
3. Multiple nodules (≥5) in a patient with known cancer → metastases until proven otherwise (oncology); in infection/immunosuppressed → fungal/septic emboli/TB (respiratory).

options.label: Suspected lung cancer, mediastinal mass, metastases
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: 2WW if CXR suggests lung cancer or age ≥40 with unexplained haemoptysis. Urgent CXR (within 2 weeks) if ≥40 with ≥2 of cough, fatigue, breathlessness, chest pain, weight loss, appetite loss (≥1 if ever-smoker), or persistent/recurrent chest infection, clubbing, supraclavicular/persistent cervical nodes, thrombocytosis, chest signs. Normal CXR does not exclude cancer — persistent symptoms → CT/2WW.
2. Mediastinal mass on CXR (widened mediastinum, hilar enlargement): CT chest with contrast urgently; anterior — thymoma/teratoma/thyroid/lymphoma ('4 Ts'), middle — lymphadenopathy (lymphoma, sarcoid, TB, metastatic), posterior — neurogenic; superior vena cava obstruction (facial/arm swelling, distended neck veins, headache) → same-day oncology/ED (steroids, stenting, radiotherapy). Myasthenia symptoms → thymoma.
3. Lung metastases (cannonball/multiple nodules): common primaries — colorectal, breast, renal, bladder, melanoma, sarcoma, germ cell, thyroid, head & neck; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, tumour markers as indicated, refer to the relevant site MDT (or acute oncology if unknown primary — 2WW 'non-specific symptoms' pathway). Targeted Lung Health Checks (England): low-dose CT for ever-smokers 55–74 — encourage uptake; eligibility via GP record search.

options.label: Mesothelioma
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Asbestos exposure (shipyards, construction, plumbing, electricians, laggers — often 20–50 years prior, including secondary/household exposure): chest pain (often dull, non-pleuritic), breathlessness, unilateral pleural effusion, weight loss, pleural thickening/plaques on CXR. Any pleural effusion/thickening + asbestos history → 2WW respiratory/pleural MDT (CT, thoracoscopic biopsy).
2. Specialist: chemotherapy (pemetrexed + platinum; nivolumab + ipilimumab first line — NICE TA818), IPC/pleurodesis for effusion, radiotherapy for pain/tract sites, surgery rarely; median survival ~12–18 months; early palliative care; Mesothelioma UK nurse.
3. GP: breathlessness/pain management (opioids, neuropathic agents for chest wall invasion), psychological support, notify (reportable to coroner at death — industrial disease), help with compensation: Industrial Injuries Disablement Benefit (100% automatic), Diffuse Mesothelioma Payment Scheme/2008 scheme (DWP), civil claim via specialist solicitor (time limits — 3 years from diagnosis), War Pension if forces; document exposure history carefully.

pulmonary-nodule.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

sarcoidosis.title: Less common respiratory diagnoses – sarcoidosis, aspergillosis, CTEPH, diaphragm paralysis, neuromuscular respiratory failure

options.label: Sarcoidosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Presentations: incidental bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) on CXR; Löfgren's syndrome (BHL + erythema nodosum + ankle arthritis + fever — excellent prognosis, no biopsy needed); dry cough/breathlessness; skin (lupus pernio, papules, scar sarcoid); eyes (uveitis — urgent ophthalmology); cardiac (palpitations, syncope, heart block — ECG/Holter/MRI); neuro (facial palsy, meningitis); hypercalcaemia/renal stones; fatigue.
2. Work-up: CXR (Scadding stage), FBC, U&E, calcium, LFT, serum ACE (non-specific), ECG, urinalysis, spirometry/gas transfer, TB screen (IGRA — exclude mimic), HRCT; refer respiratory for diagnosis (EBUS lymph node biopsy — non-caseating granulomas) and staging; ophthalmology slit-lamp for all at diagnosis.
3. Treatment (BTS 2020): most stage I–II need observation only (resolves in 60–80% within 2–5 years). Prednisolone 20–40 mg daily tapering over 6–12 months for: symptomatic/progressive pulmonary disease, cardiac, neuro, ocular (not responding to topical), hypercalcaemia, severe skin, renal; methotrexate/azathioprine as steroid-sparing; infliximab refractory (specialist). GP: bone protection with steroids, monitor calcium (avoid vitamin D supplements unless deficient — hypercalcaemia), vaccinations, fatigue management, NSAIDs for Löfgren's; monitor CXR/spirometry 3–6 monthly in first 2 years.

options.label: Aspergillosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ABPA (asthma/CF with worsening control, brown plugs, fleeting infiltrates, eosinophilia, total IgE >1000 IU/mL, Aspergillus-specific IgE/IgG, bronchiectasis central): refer respiratory; prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg 2 weeks then taper over 3–6 months ± itraconazole 200 mg bd 16 weeks (steroid-sparing; LFT/ECG QT, many interactions — statins, DOACs, some antihistamines); monitor IgE; optimise asthma (biologics — omalizumab/mepolizumab — in severe cases).
2. Aspergilloma (fungal ball in a pre-existing cavity — old TB, sarcoid, emphysema; CXR 'air crescent'): often asymptomatic; HAEMOPTYSIS can be massive → same-day admission if significant; options — observation, itraconazole/voriconazole (limited benefit), bronchial artery embolisation for bleeding, surgical resection if fit and recurrent haemoptysis. Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis (cavitation, weight loss, Aspergillus IgG) — long-term azole via respiratory/ID.
3. Invasive aspergillosis (neutropenia, transplant, ITU/COVID/flu): fever + nodules/halo on CT → urgent haematology/ID (voriconazole IV).

options.label: CTEPH, diaphragm paralysis, neuromuscular respiratory failure
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. CTEPH: persistent breathlessness/exercise intolerance ≥3 months after PE on anticoagulation (or history of VTE, pacemaker, splenectomy, thrombophilia); loud P2, RV heave, raised JVP; echo (RVSP >35–40 mmHg) + V/Q scan (preferred screening) → refer pulmonary hypertension centre (Papworth/Hammersmith/Sheffield/Newcastle/Glasgow/Great Ormond St/Royal Free — right heart catheter, CT pulmonary angiography). Treatment: lifelong anticoagulation (warfarin preferred by many centres; DOAC acceptable), pulmonary endarterectomy (potentially curative), balloon pulmonary angioplasty, riociguat (NICE TA). GP: avoid pregnancy (high mortality — contraception advice), oxygen if hypoxic, vaccinations, avoid high altitude.
2. Diaphragm paralysis: orthopnoea, breathlessness on bending/immersion, paradoxical abdominal movement; causes — phrenic nerve (tumour, trauma/surgery, neuralgic amyotrophy, cervical spondylosis, MND, viral), idiopathic. CXR (raised hemidiaphragm) → sniff test (fluoroscopy/USS), spirometry sitting vs supine (>20–25% fall), CT chest for cause. Unilateral: often tolerated — reassure, weight loss, treat cause; bilateral → respiratory failure (nocturnal hypoventilation — overnight oximetry/capnography) → NIV via home ventilation service; diaphragm plication (thoracic surgery) if symptomatic unilateral.
3. Neuromuscular respiratory failure (MND, muscular dystrophy, myasthenia, GBS, post-polio, SMA, high spinal cord injury): symptoms — orthopnoea, morning headache, daytime sleepiness, poor cough, recurrent chest infections, unexplained weight loss; monitor FVC (sitting and supine) and SNIP every 3 months in MND; refer home ventilation/respiratory neuromuscular service when FVC <80% predicted, orthopnoea, or symptomatic for NIV, cough assist (mechanical insufflation-exsufflation), secretion management; vaccinations; early palliative/advance care planning; ACUTE deterioration (FVC <1–1.5 L, cannot count to 20, swallowing failure) → 999 (ITU).

obstructive-sleep-apnoea.title: Obstructive sleep apnoea – assessment, CPAP and driving
niceRefs: NICE NG202 Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome and obesity hypoventilation syndrome 2021
NICE CKS Obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome

options.label: Assessment and referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect: loud snoring, witnessed apnoeas/choking, unrefreshing sleep, excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth ≥11), morning headache, nocturia, resistant hypertension, AF, type 2 diabetes, obesity (BMI ≥35), large neck (>17 in/43 cm men), retrognathia, Down's syndrome, acromegaly, hypothyroidism, pregnancy. STOP-Bang ≥3 = at risk (≥5 high). Children: snoring + behaviour/growth/enuresis → ENT (adenotonsillectomy).
2. Check: BP, BMI/neck circumference, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, TFT, HbA1c, FBC (polycythaemia), oxygen saturation (daytime <94% or bicarbonate >27 suggests obesity hypoventilation — urgent referral), ECG; examine airway (Mallampati).
3. NG202: refer sleep service (respiratory/ENT) for home sleep study (respiratory polygraphy/oximetry) — URGENT (within 4 weeks) if: vocational driver (HGV/PCV/taxi), safety-critical job (pilot, machinery), Epworth ≥16/excessive sleepiness with risk, unstable cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, pre-operative, obesity hypoventilation (daytime hypercapnia/hypoxia), or falls asleep driving. Pre-referral: advise not to drive if sleepy.

options.label: Treatment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. All: weight loss (≥10% improves AHI; consider tier 3 weight management/GLP-1 — tirzepatide licensed for OSA in obesity 2025; bariatric surgery), stop smoking, reduce alcohol (especially evening), avoid sedatives/opioids/benzodiazepines, side-sleeping (positional therapy/tennis-ball), treat nasal obstruction (intranasal steroid), sleep hygiene/regular hours.
2. Mild OSA (AHI 5–14) with symptoms: lifestyle ± mandibular advancement splint (custom, via dentist/sleep service) or CPAP if symptomatic/wants; moderate–severe (AHI ≥15): CPAP first line (fixed or auto-titrating with humidification; telemonitoring; mask fitting support — adherence ≥4 h/night on ≥70% nights; manage nasal symptoms, claustrophobia, pressure intolerance); MAS if CPAP declined/not tolerated; hypoglossal nerve stimulation (NICE IPG598) or upper airway surgery selected cases via ENT. Obesity hypoventilation: CPAP or NIV + weight management; avoid oxygen alone.
3. Follow-up: sleep service annual review (download compliance, Epworth); GP — BP control (OSA causes resistant hypertension; CPAP lowers BP modestly), CVD risk, driving reassessment, pre-operative notification (anaesthetic risk), review sedatives; CPAP in all patients with AF ablation/cardiac surgery planning.

options.label: Driving and occupational rules
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. DVLA: patients with suspected/confirmed OSA with EXCESSIVE SLEEPINESS must not drive and must notify DVLA (Group 1 cars; Group 2 lorries/buses — stricter). Moderate/severe OSAS: must notify; may resume when symptoms controlled on treatment (CPAP compliance confirmed by specialist, usually within 4 weeks), Group 2 needs annual specialist review. Mild OSA without sleepiness: no need to notify. Advise in writing and document; GP has GMC duty to inform DVLA if patient continues to drive against advice.
2. Occupational: safety-critical roles — inform occupational health; HGV/PCV licence reviewed with treatment evidence; shift work worsens.
3. Patient advice: no driving when sleepy, avoid long drives/night driving until treated, Sleep Apnoea Trust (SATA); family — CPAP adherence support.

type-2-diabetes-new.title: Type 2 diabetes – diagnosis, targets, drug intensification, SGLT2i/GLP-1, sick-day rules
niceRefs: NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults (2022 update)
NHS Type 2 Diabetes Path to Remission

options.label: Diagnosis, targets and lifestyle
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnose: HbA1c ≥48 mmol/mol (repeat within 2 weeks if asymptomatic; one result if symptomatic), or fasting glucose ≥7.0, or random ≥11.1 with symptoms. HbA1c invalid in haemoglobinopathy, haemolysis, iron deficiency (falsely high), pregnancy, recent transfusion, CKD 4–5 — use glucose. Prediabetes 42–47 → NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme (refer), annual HbA1c. Consider type 1/LADA (ketones, weight loss, <50, lean, rapid onset — see Type 1 tool), MODY (strong family history, young, non-obese), pancreatic/steroid-induced diabetes.
2. Targets (individualised): HbA1c 48 if lifestyle/metformin alone; 53 if on drugs causing hypoglycaemia (sulfonylurea/insulin); relax (58–64) if frail/multimorbid/limited life expectancy/hypo risk. Intensify when HbA1c ≥58. BP (NG28 → NG136): clinic <140/90 (home <135/85) if under 80; clinic <150/90 (home <145/85) if 80 or over; <130/80 only when CKD with ACR ≥70 mg/mmol; statin — atorvastatin 20 mg if QRISK ≥10% or age >40/established complications (80 mg secondary prevention); aspirin ONLY for established CVD.
3. Structured education (DESMOND/X-PERT), diet (Mediterranean/low-calorie), 150 min/week activity, weight loss ≥5–15% (remission possible — NHS Path to Remission soups-and-shakes 800 kcal/day 12 weeks for BMI ≥27, diagnosed <6 years), stop smoking, alcohol limits. Annual: HbA1c (3–6 monthly), U&E/eGFR + urine ACR, lipids, BP, weight, foot check (risk stratify, podiatry), retinal screening (NHS DESP), review of injection sites, mood/sexual dysfunction, flu/pneumococcal/COVID vaccines, dental. Severe mental illness: same targets, extra support — antipsychotic weight gain (metformin/switch to aripiprazole), adherence, link with mental health team.

options.label: Drug treatment (NG28 2022)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. First line: metformin 500 mg od → 1 g bd (MR if GI intolerance; stop if eGFR <30, review <45; hold during AKI/contrast/sick days; check B12 annually/if neuropathy). PLUS, at diagnosis regardless of HbA1c, an SGLT2 inhibitor if: established CVD/heart failure, or high CVD risk (QRISK ≥10% or age ≥40 with risk factors), or CKD (ACR ≥3 and eGFR ≥20–25 — dapagliflozin/empagliflozin have renal/HF licences) — dapagliflozin 10 mg od, empagliflozin 10 mg od, canagliflozin 100 mg. Counsel: genital thrush, UTI/Fournier's (rare), volume depletion (reduce diuretics), DKA (euglycaemic — stop if unwell/nil by mouth/ketotic; sick-day rules; avoid in very low-carb diets/type 1), foot care (canagliflozin amputation signal), check ketones if vomiting.
2. Intensification (HbA1c ≥58 after 3–6 months at tolerated dose): add one of — DPP-4 inhibitor (sitagliptin 100 mg, linagliptin 5 mg in CKD; weight-neutral), pioglitazone 15–30 mg (avoid HF, bladder cancer, fractures, macular oedema; cheap, durable), sulfonylurea (gliclazide 40–80 mg bd; hypoglycaemia — driving advice, weight gain), or SGLT2i if not already. GLP-1 receptor agonist (semaglutide 0.25 → 1 mg weekly SC, dulaglutide 1.5 mg, liraglutide, oral semaglutide) when triple therapy fails/not tolerated with BMI ≥35 (or ≥32.5 South Asian/other) or <35 with occupational hypo issue/weight benefit; continue only if HbA1c falls ≥11 mmol/mol AND weight ≥3% at 6 months. Tirzepatide (GIP/GLP-1, NICE TA924 for diabetes) alternative. Warn: nausea, pancreatitis, gallstones, diabetic retinopathy progression if rapid HbA1c fall — ensure screening; hold around surgery/GI illness.
3. Insulin when oral/injectable options fail or symptomatic hyperglycaemia (HbA1c >75 with osmotic symptoms): NPH basal (Humulin I/Insulatard) at bedtime 10 units, titrate 2 units every 3 days to fasting 5–7; or long-acting analogue (glargine/degludec) if nocturnal hypos/twice-daily NPH needed/carer-administered; continue metformin/SGLT2i; stop sulfonylurea when prandial insulin starts; DVLA notification for insulin (Group 1: check glucose <2 h before driving, every 2 h; Group 2 stricter); hypo education (glucagon for household); DAFNE-style skills.

options.label: Sick-day rules, hypoglycaemia, hyperglycaemic emergencies
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Sick-day rules (give written card): keep taking/adjusting insulin — NEVER stop basal insulin; check glucose every 2–4 h and ketones (blood ketones if on SGLT2i or insulin); drink 100 mL water/sugar-free fluid every hour; if not eating, replace meals with sugary fluids (if glucose <13); TEMPORARILY STOP (SADMANS): SGLT2 inhibitors, ACE-i/ARB, Diuretics, Metformin, Aldosterone antagonists (spironolactone), NSAIDs, Sulfonylureas (if not eating — hypo risk) — restart 24–48 h after eating and drinking normally; GLP-1 hold if vomiting. Seek urgent help: vomiting >4 h/unable to keep fluids down, glucose >25 persistently or ketones ≥1.5 mmol/L (urine 2+) or ≥3.0 (DKA — 999), drowsy/confused/breathless/abdominal pain, not improving in 24 h.
2. Hypoglycaemia (<4 mmol/L): 15–20 g fast carbohydrate (4–5 glucose tablets, 150–200 mL fruit juice/full-sugar drink, GlucoGel), recheck 10–15 min, repeat up to 3×, then long-acting carbohydrate; unconscious → IM glucagon 1 mg (household trained) or 999; recurrent hypos → review sulfonylurea/insulin dose, renal function, alcohol, missed meals; impaired awareness → DVLA (must not drive Group 1 if severe hypo requiring help while awake ×2 in 12 months; Group 2 one episode), refer diabetes team (CGM — flash/Libre now available for type 2 on insulin with hypo risk/multiple daily injections).
3. Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (elderly, glucose >30, dehydration, drowsiness, no/low ketones, osmolality >320) → 999. Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia: monitor glucose/HbA1c when starting prednisolone ≥20 mg; gliclazide morning dose or insulin per JBDS guidance; reduce as steroids taper.
