type-1-diabetes-adults.title: Type 1 diabetes, LADA, MODY and gestational diabetes – what primary care must do
niceRefs: NICE NG17 Type 1 diabetes in adults (2022 update)
NICE NG18 Diabetes in children and young people

options.label: New type 1 — recognise and act same day
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Any age (peak childhood/young adult, but 40% diagnosed >30): polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue, blurred vision, thrush, days–weeks; DKA features — vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath, drowsiness. Children with 4 Ts (Toilet, Thirsty, Thinner, Tired) → finger-prick glucose IMMEDIATELY — do not send for lab tests/urine and wait.
2. Random glucose ≥11.1 with symptoms = diabetes; ketones (blood ≥1.5 mmol/L or urine ≥2+) → SAME-DAY referral to diabetes team/ED (children ALWAYS same day to paediatrics regardless of ketones); adults with ketones <1.5, well, able to eat → same-day/next-day specialist telephone referral — insulin must start within 24 h. Do not start metformin/gliclazide. Lab: glucose, HbA1c, U&E, bicarbonate, ketones; GAD/IA-2/ZnT8 antibodies and C-peptide (NG17 — measure at diagnosis in all adults to distinguish from type 2/LADA/MODY, especially if ≥50, BMI ≥25, or atypical).
3. LADA (adult-onset, antibody-positive, slow progression — often labelled type 2 that fails oral agents within 3–5 years; lean, no metabolic syndrome, personal/family autoimmunity): check GAD antibodies + C-peptide; early insulin; avoid sulfonylureas; specialist clinic. MODY (autosomal dominant, 3 generations, onset <25, non-obese, antibody-negative, detectable C-peptide, mild fasting hyperglycaemia or sulfonylurea-sensitive): refer for genetic testing (Exeter MODY probability calculator; NHS Genomic Medicine Service) — HNF1A/HNF4A respond to low-dose gliclazide, GCK needs no treatment (except pregnancy); family cascade testing.

options.label: Ongoing type 1 care (NG17)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Specialist-led: basal-bolus (insulin degludec/glargine + rapid-acting aspart/lispro/fiasp) with carbohydrate counting (DAFNE within 6–12 months); HbA1c target ≤48 (individualised); continuous glucose monitoring (real-time CGM or flash — Libre 2/Dexcom) offered to ALL type 1 (NG17 2022); hybrid closed-loop (pump + CGM algorithm) rolled out NHS England 2024–29 (TA943) for HbA1c ≥58, disabling hypos, pregnancy/planning, children; time-in-range 70% target.
2. GP annual/intercurrent: U&E/ACR, lipids, BP (<135/85; <130/80 if albuminuria), statin from 40 (or earlier with risk/duration >10 y), foot check, retinal screening, thyroid (annual TFT — autoimmune), coeliac serology at diagnosis/symptoms, B12 if on metformin adjunct, injection sites (lipohypertrophy — rotate), mental health (diabetes distress, eating disorder — insulin omission), smoking, contraception/pre-conception counselling (folic acid 5 mg, HbA1c <48, stop statin/ACE-i), flu/pneumococcal/COVID. Repeat prescriptions: ensure ketone strips, glucagon, hypo treatment, needles, sharps bin.
3. Hypoglycaemia/driving: same rules as Type 2 tool; recurrent severe hypos or impaired awareness → diabetes team (CGM alarms, HCL). Adjunct: metformin only if BMI ≥25 and specialist advice; SGLT2i NOT recommended (DKA).

options.label: DKA, sick days, pregnancy and gestational diabetes
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. DKA = ketones ≥3.0 mmol/L (or urine 2+) + glucose >11 (or known diabetes) + bicarbonate <15/pH <7.3 → 999/ED; euglycaemic DKA possible on SGLT2i/pregnancy/low carb. Sick days: NEVER stop insulin (basal always; may need 10–20% more); check glucose every 2 h, ketones every 2–4 h if glucose >13/unwell; extra rapid-acting correction doses per ketone level (JBDS/local sick-day plan: ketones 1.5–2.9 → 10% of total daily dose extra every 2 h; ≥3.0 → 20% + urgent advice); fluids 100 mL/h; call diabetes team/999 if ketones ≥3, vomiting, drowsy.
2. Pregnancy with pre-existing diabetes (NG3): pre-conception — HbA1c <48 (avoid pregnancy if >86), folic acid 5 mg from 3 months before, stop ACE-i/ARB/statins, retinal and renal check; from positive test → joint diabetes–antenatal clinic within 1 week; aspirin 75–150 mg from 12 weeks; CGM for all type 1 in pregnancy; metformin/insulin only in type 2.
3. Gestational diabetes (NG3): screen with 75 g OGTT at 24–28 weeks (at booking if previous GDM) for risk factors — BMI ≥30, previous GDM/macrosomia ≥4.5 kg, first-degree relative, South Asian/Black Caribbean/Middle Eastern; diagnose fasting ≥5.6 or 2-h ≥7.8. Management (joint clinic): diet/exercise 1–2 weeks; metformin if targets (fasting <5.3, 1-h post-meal <7.8) not met; insulin if fasting ≥7.0 at diagnosis, macrosomia, or metformin fails; glibenclamide alternative; fetal growth scans; delivery by 40+6. Postnatal: stop treatment at delivery; fasting glucose at 6–13 weeks (or HbA1c after 13 weeks) then ANNUAL HbA1c for life (50% develop type 2 within 10 years) — code 'history of GDM'; NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme; breastfeeding; contraception; next pregnancy — early OGTT/CGM.

hypothyroidism-management.title: Hypothyroidism – when to treat, levothyroxine, subclinical disease, pregnancy

options.label: Diagnosis and who to treat (NG145)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Test TSH (+ free T4 if TSH abnormal or pituitary disease suspected) for: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, bradycardia, menorrhagia, depression, cognitive slowing, goitre, hyperlipidaemia, type 1 diabetes/autoimmune disease, Down's/Turner's, post-neck radiotherapy, amiodarone/lithium, infertility, unexplained hyponatraemia/raised CK. Do not test in acute illness (sick euthyroid — repeat 6 weeks after recovery).
2. Overt (TSH >10 with low fT4, or TSH above range with low fT4): treat. Subclinical (TSH raised, fT4 normal) — repeat with TPO antibodies at 3 months (exclude transient — recovery from thyroiditis, non-adherence): TSH ≥10 on 2 occasions ≥3 months apart → treat; TSH 4–10 → treat if <65 with symptoms (6-month trial, stop if no benefit), TPO-positive (higher progression), planning pregnancy/pregnant/infertility, goitre; >65–80 asymptomatic → observe (TSH annually, or 6-monthly if TPO+). Central hypothyroidism (low/normal TSH with low fT4) → endocrinology (pituitary).
3. Amiodarone: check TFT before and every 6 months; lithium: 6-monthly; immune checkpoint inhibitors: thyroiditis common — oncology protocol.

options.label: Levothyroxine — starting, titrating, problems
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Start levothyroxine 1.6 micrograms/kg/day (≈ 100 micrograms for 65 kg; round to 25) if <65 and no cardiac disease; 25–50 micrograms if ≥65, ischaemic heart disease, or severe/long-standing hypothyroidism (titrate every 4–6 weeks). Take on an empty stomach 30–60 min before breakfast (or at bedtime ≥3 h after food), consistently; separate from calcium, iron, PPIs, soya, coffee by 4 h; same brand if sensitive (Teva/Mercury-pharma differences — MHRA 2021: prescribe by brand if symptoms recur on switching). Recheck TSH every 3 months until stable (TSH 0.4–4; symptom-based within range, some feel best <2.5), then annually.
2. Dose change: increase/decrease by 25 micrograms (12.5 in elderly/cardiac) and recheck in 6–8 weeks; raised TSH on treatment — check adherence FIRST (most common), timing/absorbers, new drugs (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin, sertraline, oestrogen/HRT ↑ requirement; weight change), coeliac/H. pylori/PPI (malabsorption), pregnancy. Suppressed TSH (over-replacement) → reduce (AF, osteoporosis risk); do NOT treat to symptoms with TSH suppressed.
3. Persistent symptoms despite normal TSH: check fT4/fT3, FBC, ferritin, B12, HbA1c, coeliac, calcium, cortisol (Addison's co-exists — treat adrenal first), sleep apnoea, depression, menopause; NG145 — do NOT routinely offer liothyronine (T3) or desiccated thyroid; combination therapy only via endocrinology (BTA position) in selected cases. Weight loss supplements/T3 online — advise against.

options.label: Pregnancy, fertility and special situations
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Pre-conception: optimise TSH <2.5 mU/L; TPO-positive women or subclinical hypothyroidism trying to conceive → treat (levothyroxine 25–50 micrograms) and refer early. On confirming pregnancy: INCREASE levothyroxine by 25–50 micrograms (≈25–30%) immediately, check TSH/fT4 every 4–6 weeks in first half of pregnancy then at 20–24 and 32 weeks (trimester-specific ranges: TSH <2.5 first trimester, <3.0 later); refer to joint endocrine–obstetric clinic; return to pre-pregnancy dose after delivery, check at 6 weeks postnatal. Untreated maternal hypothyroidism → fetal neurodevelopment risk, miscarriage, pre-eclampsia.
2. Postpartum thyroiditis (within 12 months of delivery; TPO+ women; hyper- then hypothyroid phase; 'postnatal depression' mimic): check TFT in postnatal fatigue/depression; hypothyroid phase — levothyroxine if symptomatic/planning pregnancy/TSH >10, trial withdrawal at 6–12 months (50% permanent); annual TFT thereafter; beta-blocker for hyper phase (not antithyroid drugs).
3. Myxoedema coma (hypothermia, bradycardia, confusion, hyponatraemia — elderly, untreated, precipitated by infection/sedatives) → 999. Elderly starting treatment: look for angina. Children/congenital: paediatric endocrinology (newborn screening). Thyroid nodules/cancer: see Thyroid nodules tool.

thyroid-nodule.title: Thyroid nodules, goitre and thyroid cancer
niceRefs: BTA thyroid cancer guideline 2014/BTA nodule guidance
NICE CKS Thyroid cancer – recognition and referral

options.label: Assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Palpable nodule/goitre: history — rapid growth, pain, hoarseness, dysphagia, stridor, compressive symptoms, family history (medullary/MEN2, papillary), childhood neck irradiation; examine — fixation, hardness, cervical lymphadenopathy, tracheal deviation, retrosternal extension (Pemberton's sign).
2. TSH first: suppressed TSH → thyroid uptake scan (toxic nodule — rarely malignant; treat hyperthyroidism); normal/raised TSH → thyroid USS (U1–U5 classification) ± FNA for U3–U5 (one-stop neck lump clinic). Calcitonin only if medullary suspected (family history/MEN2). Do not order routine thyroid USS for diffuse goitre with normal TSH and no nodule/compression.
3. NG12: 2WW ENT/thyroid clinic for an unexplained thyroid LUMP (nodule) — all; URGENT same-day/2WW if stridor (anaplastic/compression — ED), rapidly enlarging, hoarse voice/cord palsy, hard fixed mass, lymphadenopathy, age <20 or >70 with new nodule, prior irradiation. Incidental USS/CT nodules: follow radiology U-grading (U2 benign — discharge; U3 indeterminate — FNA; U4/5 — 2WW).

options.label: Thyroid cancer types and treatment (specialist)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Differentiated (papillary 80%, follicular 10% — good prognosis >95% 10-year survival): hemi/total thyroidectomy ± central neck dissection, radioactive iodine ablation for intermediate/high risk, TSH-suppressive levothyroxine (target per risk: TSH <0.1 high risk; 0.1–0.5 low risk, relaxed to normal range after years of no evidence of disease), thyroglobulin + antibodies surveillance, neck USS; lifelong follow-up via thyroid cancer MDT (increasingly shared with primary care for low-risk). Hürthle/oncocytic — follicular variant.
2. Medullary (5%; calcitonin-producing C cells; 25% hereditary — RET mutation/MEN2 — screen family, phaeochromocytoma BEFORE surgery): total thyroidectomy + central/lateral dissection; calcitonin/CEA monitoring; no RAI/TSH suppression (replace to normal TSH); selpercatinib/vandetanib for advanced RET-driven disease; genetics referral for all.
3. Anaplastic (1–2%, elderly, rapidly enlarging hard mass, stridor, dysphagia; median survival 3–6 months): urgent MDT — airway (tracheostomy/stent), palliative radiotherapy, BRAF-targeted (dabrafenib/trametinib) if V600E, early palliative care. Lymphoma (Hashimoto's background, rapid growth) — chemotherapy, not surgery.

options.label: GP role after thyroid cancer and benign nodules
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. After thyroidectomy: levothyroxine dose per MDT target (do not 'normalise' suppressed TSH without checking the plan); calcium/PTH post-op (hypoparathyroidism — alfacalcidol/calcium; check calcium with symptoms of tingling/cramps); voice (recurrent laryngeal nerve — SLT/ENT); RAI — no pregnancy for 6–12 months, avoid close contact with children/pregnant women for days after dose per instructions, salivary problems; long-term: second cancer surveillance low; psychological support (Butterfly Thyroid Cancer Trust); DS1500 not usually needed (good prognosis).
2. Benign nodule (U2/FNA Thy2): discharge or USS at 12 months if >1 cm/patient concern; no TSH suppression; surgery only for compressive symptoms/cosmesis/toxic nodule.
3. Multinodular goitre with normal TSH and no compression: reassure; annual TSH; refer if growth, new dominant nodule, hoarseness, dysphagia/stridor, retrosternal extension (CT/flow-volume loop → thyroidectomy).

thyroid-nodule.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

adrenal-insufficiency.title: Adrenal insufficiency – Addison's, steroid-induced, sick-day rules and crisis
niceRefs: Society for Endocrinology adrenal crisis guidance 2016/2024

options.label: Recognise and diagnose
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Primary (Addison's — autoimmune 80%, TB, adrenal haemorrhage/metastases, congenital adrenal hyperplasia): fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, abdominal pain, salt craving, postural dizziness, HYPERPIGMENTATION (palmar creases, buccal, scars), vitiligo/other autoimmunity (thyroid, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia), hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, eosinophilia, raised TSH (can be transient). Secondary (pituitary disease, or STEROID-INDUCED after prednisolone ≥5 mg >4 weeks, inhaled high-dose steroids, intra-articular/topical potent steroids, opioids, immune checkpoint inhibitors): no pigmentation, no hyperkalaemia, normal aldosterone.
2. Test: 9 am serum cortisol (off any steroid; hydrocortisone 24 h, prednisolone 24–48 h; oestrogen/COC raises cortisol) — <100 nmol/L highly suggestive (start treatment and refer same day if unwell); 100–350 indeterminate → short Synacthen test (250 micrograms IM, cortisol at 0/30/60 min — ≥420 nmol/L excludes primary; assay-dependent); >450 unlikely. Plus ACTH (high in primary), renin/aldosterone, adrenal antibodies (21-hydroxylase), U&E, glucose, TFT, coeliac. Refer endocrinology urgently (within 2 weeks) for confirmation — same day if hyponatraemia/hyperkalaemia/hypotension.
3. ADRENAL CRISIS (hypotension/shock, vomiting, confusion, severe abdominal pain, hypoglycaemia — often triggered by infection/surgery/missed doses/stopping steroids): 999 — give hydrocortisone 100 mg IM/IV IMMEDIATELY if available (patient's emergency kit), IV saline; do not wait for tests.

options.label: Maintenance treatment (specialist-initiated)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in 2–3 divided doses mimicking circadian rhythm (e.g. 10 mg on waking, 5 mg lunch, 5 mg mid-afternoon; last dose before 6 pm); or prednisolone 3–5 mg once daily (alternative); Plenadren (modified-release) selected cases. Primary AI: add fludrocortisone 50–200 micrograms daily (monitor BP incl. postural, U&E, renin — adjust; increase in heat/exercise); DHEA for women with low libido (specialist). Dose adequacy judged clinically (weight, BP, energy, pigmentation) — cortisol day curves rarely needed.
2. Patient must have: NHS Steroid Emergency Card + MedicAlert jewellery; written sick-day rules; home hydrocortisone injection kit (100 mg) with training for patient AND family; spare oral supply; Addison's Disease Self-Help Group (ADSHG) membership. Annual review: BP, weight, U&E, HbA1c, TFT, B12 (pernicious anaemia), coeliac, bone (DEXA if over-replaced), osteoporosis prevention, vaccinations, mental health; check inhaled/topical steroid use elsewhere.
3. Enzyme inducers (rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin) → double hydrocortisone; HRT/COC raise CBG (no change needed); pregnancy — hydrocortisone dose +50% in third trimester, 100 mg IM at labour (obstetric/endocrine plan); hypothyroidism — start steroids BEFORE levothyroxine (crisis risk).

options.label: Sick-day rules and steroid withdrawal
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Sick-day rules (Society for Endocrinology): fever/infection needing bed rest or antibiotics → DOUBLE oral hydrocortisone (or prednisolone to ≥10 mg) until recovered (then 2 days extra); vomiting (within 30 min of dose) or severe diarrhoea → repeat dose; vomiting twice/unable to keep tablets → 100 mg IM hydrocortisone and call 999/attend ED (IV fluids/hydrocortisone 200 mg/24 h); minor procedures (dental with LA — extra 20 mg beforehand), major surgery/colonoscopy prep/labour → 100 mg IM/IV then infusion (anaesthetist informed — Steroid Emergency Card); severe stress/trauma → extra dose; avoid missing doses (set alarms); antiemetic (ondansetron) and glucose advice. Fludrocortisone unchanged.
2. Steroid-induced suppression (anyone on prednisolone ≥5 mg for ≥4 weeks or equivalent): issue Steroid Emergency Card (NHS 2020) and sick-day advice while on treatment and for 12 months after high-dose courses; never stop long-term steroids abruptly; taper — reduce to physiological (prednisolone 5 mg/hydrocortisone 20 mg) by 2.5–5 mg steps every 1–2 weeks, then 1 mg per month (or switch to hydrocortisone and check 9 am cortisol before stopping: <100 continue, >350–420 stop, in between Synacthen/endocrinology); watch for withdrawal symptoms (fatigue, arthralgia, nausea) vs adrenal insufficiency (hypotension, hyponatraemia).
3. Emergency: carry injection kit at all times/travel; paramedics give IM hydrocortisone 100 mg; relatives trained; schools/workplaces informed.

adrenal-insufficiency.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS / BNF / named guideline)

aortic-stenosis-severity.title: Heart valve disease – murmurs, aortic stenosis, mitral and tricuspid disease
aortic-stenosis-severity.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG208 Heart valve disease 2021; NICE CKS; BNF)

options.label: Murmur — who needs an echo
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG208: refer for echocardiography any adult with a murmur AND symptoms (exertional breathlessness, chest pain, syncope/presyncope, palpitations), or an ejection systolic murmur that radiates/is loud (≥3/6), or any diastolic murmur, or a murmur with an abnormal ECG. Asymptomatic soft systolic murmur with normal ECG in a young adult: echo still reasonable if any doubt.
2. Before referral: ECG, BNP/NT-proBNP if breathless, FBC, U&E, TFTs, chest X-ray if symptoms.
3. Signs of severity: slow-rising pulse, narrow pulse pressure, soft/absent S2, heaving apex (AS); displaced apex, S3 (MR); loud S1, opening snap, mid-diastolic rumble, AF, malar flush (MS).

options.label: Aortic stenosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Severity by echo: severe = valve area <1.0 cm², mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, peak velocity ≥4 m/s. Symptomatic severe AS has 50% 2-year mortality untreated — do NOT wait.
2. Any symptom (angina, syncope, breathlessness) with moderate–severe AS → urgent cardiology; severe AS with LVEF <50% even if asymptomatic → cardiology for intervention (SAVR or TAVI; NG208 recommends TAVI for high surgical risk, shared decision otherwise).
3. Asymptomatic: mild — echo every 3–5 years; moderate — every 1–2 years; severe — 6–12 monthly with cardiology.
4. Primary care: control BP (ACE-i/ARB acceptable), statin for CV risk (statins do not slow AS), avoid vasodilators/nitrates and dehydration in severe AS, treat anaemia, warn against heavy exertion if severe; endocarditis prophylaxis not routinely (NICE CG64) but good dental hygiene.

options.label: Mitral and tricuspid disease, referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Mitral regurgitation: echo; symptomatic severe MR, LVEF <60%, LV end-systolic dimension ≥40 mm, new AF or pulmonary hypertension → cardiology/surgical (repair preferred over replacement; MitraClip for high-risk). Asymptomatic moderate: annual echo. Treat heart failure per NG106 (ACE-i, beta-blocker, diuretic for congestion).
2. Mitral stenosis (rheumatic): symptoms, AF (anticoagulate with WARFARIN — DOACs not licensed for moderate–severe MS), pulmonary hypertension, valve area <1.5 cm² → cardiology (balloon valvotomy). Rate control with beta-blocker/diltiazem; diuretics.
3. Tricuspid regurgitation: usually secondary (pulmonary hypertension, left-sided disease); treat the cause and congestion (loop diuretic); severe with symptoms/RV dysfunction → cardiology (repair at time of left-sided surgery).
4. Refer urgently if: new murmur with fever (endocarditis — blood cultures ×3 before antibiotics, same-day admission), syncope, heart failure, haemodynamic instability.

ecg-st-elevation.title: ECG findings in primary care – what needs action
ecg-st-elevation.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG185 Acute coronary syndromes 2020; NICE CKS Bradycardia/Palpitations; ESC pacing 2021; BHRS; BNF)

options.label: ST changes and bundle branch block
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ST elevation ≥1 mm in two contiguous limb leads or ≥2 mm chest leads WITH chest pain = STEMI: 999, aspirin 300 mg chewed, GTN, oxygen only if sats <94%, do not delay for troponin. New LBBB with chest pain = treat as STEMI.
2. ST elevation without pain: early repolarisation (young, concave, J-point notching), pericarditis (saddle-shaped, PR depression, widespread), LV aneurysm (old MI), Brugada (see below), LBBB/LVH strain — compare with old ECG; same-day cardiology advice if new.
3. ST depression/T-wave inversion with symptoms → NSTEMI/unstable angina: 999 if ongoing pain; if pain-free and stable, same-day ED/ACS pathway with troponin. Asymptomatic lateral T inversion → check BP, echo (LVH/HCM), cardiology routine.
4. RBBB: common, benign if asymptomatic with normal heart — no action unless new with symptoms (PE, RV strain) or with left axis deviation/1st-degree block (trifascicular → cardiology). LBBB: always abnormal — echo + cardiology referral (ischaemia, cardiomyopathy, AS); new LBBB with breathlessness → urgent.

options.label: Bradycardia and heart block
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Heart rate <50: review drugs (beta-blocker incl. timolol eye drops, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin, amiodarone, ivabradine, donepezil), TFTs, U&E, potassium, Lyme/sarcoid if young. Athletic sinus bradycardia asymptomatic — no action.
2. SAME DAY (999 if unstable): rate <40 with symptoms (syncope, presyncope, breathlessness, confusion), complete (3rd-degree) heart block, Mobitz II (dropped beats without PR lengthening), pauses >3 s, bradycardia with hypotension or heart failure.
3. 1st-degree block (PR >200 ms) and Mobitz I (Wenckebach): benign if asymptomatic — no referral; review if PR >300 ms or symptoms.
4. Pacing indications (cardiology): symptomatic sinus node disease, Mobitz II or 3rd-degree block (even asymptomatic), tachy-brady syndrome, AF with slow ventricular response + symptoms. Advise DVLA rules (no driving until symptoms controlled/paced; HGV stricter).

options.label: Long QT, Brugada and inherited arrhythmia
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. QTc (Bazett) >450 ms men / >470 ms women is prolonged; >500 ms high risk of torsades. Causes: drugs (citalopram/escitalopram, amitriptyline, haloperidol, quetiapine, domperidone, ondansetron, clarithromycin/erythromycin, fluconazole, hydroxychloroquine, methadone, sotalol, amiodarone — check crediblemeds.org), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, hypocalcaemia, bradycardia, congenital.
2. Action: stop/replace QT-prolonging drugs; correct electrolytes (K >4.0, Mg >0.8); repeat ECG. QTc >500 ms or syncope/family history of sudden death <40 → urgent cardiology/inherited cardiac conditions clinic; avoid strenuous swimming/exertion in congenital LQT1; beta-blocker (nadolol/propranolol) started by specialist.
3. Brugada pattern (coved ST elevation ≥2 mm V1–V3 with T inversion): refer cardiology/ICC clinic (urgent if syncope, nocturnal agonal breathing, family history); avoid fever untreated (paracetamol promptly), avoid flecainide, propafenone, tricyclics, lithium, excess alcohol (brugadadrugs.org).
4. Family screening: first-degree relatives of anyone with inherited arrhythmia or sudden cardiac death <40 → ICC clinic referral.

cvd-risk-qrisk3.title: Cardiovascular risk and statins – QRISK3, primary and secondary prevention, intolerance
cvd-risk-qrisk3.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG238 Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction 2023; NICE CKS Lipid modification 2024; NHS AAC lipid pathway 2024; BNF)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Lipid modification – CVD prevention
NHS England AAC lipid management pathway

options.label: Assess risk (primary prevention)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. QRISK3 for adults 25–84 without CVD; do NOT use QRISK in: established CVD, type 1 diabetes, CKD eGFR <60 or albuminuria, familial hypercholesterolaemia (total cholesterol >7.5 or LDL >4.9, or family history of premature CHD → Simon Broome/DLCN, refer lipid clinic), age ≥85 — these all get a statin anyway (NG238).
2. Lipid profile (non-fasting): total, HDL, non-HDL, triglycerides; plus HbA1c, U&E, LFT, TFTs, CK only if muscle symptoms; BP, BMI, smoking.
3. Offer atorvastatin 20 mg if QRISK3 ≥10% over 10 years (shared decision; NG238 also allows statin below 10% if the person wants it after informed discussion). Lifestyle for all: Mediterranean diet, 150 min activity/week, smoking cessation, alcohol ≤14 units, weight.
4. Severe hypertriglyceridaemia >10 mmol/L → repeat fasting, exclude alcohol/diabetes, urgent lipid clinic (pancreatitis risk); 4.5–9.9 → address causes, consider fibrate only on specialist advice.

options.label: Statin choice, targets and monitoring
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Primary prevention: atorvastatin 20 mg nocte/any time. Secondary prevention (any CVD, incl. PAD, TIA/stroke): atorvastatin 80 mg (20 mg if CKD eGFR <30 then specialist, or interactions e.g. clarithromycin — withhold statin during course; ciclosporin, HIV protease inhibitors).
2. Targets: primary — non-HDL reduction ≥40% at 3 months; secondary (NICE 2023/AAC) — LDL ≤2.0 mmol/L (non-HDL ≤2.6). If not at target on maximal tolerated statin: add ezetimibe 10 mg; then bempedoic acid 180 mg + ezetimibe (TA694) or injectables via lipid clinic — inclisiran (TA733, LDL ≥2.6 on max therapy, GP can prescribe in many ICBs), alirocumab/evolocumab (TA393/394, LDL ≥3.5–4.0).
3. Monitoring: lipids + LFT at 3 months and 12 months, then annually; stop statin if ALT >3× ULN (continue if <3×). CK only if muscle symptoms. HbA1c at baseline/annually (small diabetes risk — benefit outweighs).
4. Pregnancy/breastfeeding: stop statin 3 months before conception.

options.label: Muscle symptoms and intolerance
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Muscle pain on statin: check CK, TFTs, vitamin D, U&E; ask about exertion, hypothyroidism, interacting drugs (fibrates, macrolides, azoles, amiodarone, diltiazem/verapamil, grapefruit).
2. CK >10× ULN or rhabdomyolysis symptoms (dark urine, severe weakness) → STOP, same-day U&E/CK, admit if AKI. CK 4–10× ULN: stop, recheck in 2–4 weeks, rechallenge at lower dose. CK <4× with tolerable symptoms: continue or reduce dose.
3. Intolerance pathway (AAC): statin holiday 2–4 weeks → rechallenge same statin lower dose, or switch to rosuvastatin 5–10 mg or pravastatin 40 mg (hydrophilic), or alternate-day/ twice-weekly rosuvastatin; placebo-controlled (SAMSON) shows most symptoms are nocebo — explain and persist.
4. True intolerance to ≥3 statins: ezetimibe 10 mg ± bempedoic acid; refer lipid clinic for PCSK9 inhibitor/inclisiran if LDL above thresholds. Document intolerance accurately (adverse reaction vs preference) for QOF exception.

palpitations-no-red-flags.title: Palpitations and tachycardia – assessment, SVT, broad complex
palpitations-no-red-flags.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Palpitations 2024; NICE NG196 AF; Resuscitation Council UK ALS tachycardia algorithm 2021; BNF)

options.label: Assessment and red flags
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Red flags → same-day/999: palpitations with syncope or presyncope, chest pain, breathlessness, haemodynamic compromise, during exertion, structural heart disease, family history of sudden death <40, known WPW/long QT.
2. History: onset/offset (abrupt = SVT; gradual = sinus), regularity ('thumping' pauses = ectopics; irregularly irregular = AF), triggers (caffeine, alcohol, stimulants, decongestants, salbutamol, thyroxine), anxiety/panic (palpitations with hyperventilation, paraesthesia — but still exclude arrhythmia).
3. Tests: 12-lead ECG (pre-excitation, QTc, LVH, Q waves), FBC, U&E, Mg, TFTs, glucose; ambulatory monitoring matched to frequency — 24-h Holter if daily, 7-day patch/event recorder if weekly, implantable loop via cardiology if rare with syncope; echo if ECG abnormal, murmur, heart failure or family history.
4. Benign ectopics (<10% burden, normal heart): reassure, reduce caffeine/alcohol, treat anxiety; bisoprolol 2.5–5 mg if troublesome; cardiology if >10% burden on Holter or symptoms persist.

options.label: Narrow complex tachycardia / SVT
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Acute SVT (regular, narrow, 150–220/min) in surgery: if unstable → 999. Stable: modified Valsalva (strain 15 s then lie flat, legs raised — REVERT, 43% success), carotid sinus massage if no bruit and age <65; if persists → ED for adenosine 6 → 12 → 18 mg (contra-indicated in asthma — verapamil instead) or verapamil 2.5–5 mg IV.
2. Irregular narrow complex = AF/flutter → see AF tool (rate control, anticoagulation by CHA2DS2-VASc).
3. Recurrent SVT: teach vagal manoeuvres; 'pill in pocket' or regular bisoprolol 2.5–5 mg / verapamil 40–120 mg tds (NOT if WPW on ECG — delta wave, short PR — verapamil/digoxin can precipitate VF; refer); cardiology/EP referral for catheter ablation (AVNRT/AVRT >95% cure) if frequent, drug-intolerant, WPW, or patient preference. Avoid flecainide without specialist (structural disease).

options.label: Broad complex tachycardia
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Broad complex (QRS >120 ms) at rate >100 = VT until proven otherwise, especially with ischaemic heart disease, previous MI or cardiomyopathy. 999 immediately; unstable (shock, syncope, chest pain, heart failure) → synchronised DC cardioversion; stable → amiodarone 300 mg IV in hospital.
2. SVT with aberrancy/bundle branch block can mimic VT — do not attempt to distinguish in primary care; adenosine only in hospital with monitoring.
3. After VT: cardiology for ICD assessment (secondary prevention), ischaemia work-up, beta-blocker; driving stops (DVLA 6 months private, bar HGV); avoid QT-prolonging drugs; correct K/Mg.
4. Torsades (polymorphic VT with long QT): magnesium sulfate 2 g IV in ED; stop causative drugs (see ECG tool).

hirsutism.title: Skin signs of systemic disease and rarer dermatoses
hirsutism.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Hirsutism 2024; NICE CKS Coeliac; BAD guidelines; PCDS; NICE NG12; BNF)

options.label: Hirsutism
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Male-pattern terminal hair in a woman (Ferriman–Gallwey ≥8). PCOS in 70–80%. Red flags for tumour: rapid onset, virilisation (voice, clitoromegaly, male-pattern balding), testosterone >5 nmol/L → urgent endocrinology ± adrenal/ovarian imaging.
2. Tests: testosterone (and SHBG, free androgen index), 17-OH progesterone (late-onset CAH if high), prolactin, TSH, HbA1c/lipids if PCOS; DHEAS if adrenal source suspected.
3. Management: weight loss (PCOS); cosmetic — shaving, waxing, electrolysis, laser (NHS-funded in some ICBs for PCOS/ transgender care); eflornithine 11.5% cream bd (facial, 8 weeks to judge, NHS prescribable); combined oral contraceptive (co-cyprindiol/Dianette for 3–4 months after hair improves then switch — VTE risk; or any COC) first-line hormonal; spironolactone 50–200 mg daily (off-label, contraception needed, check K) or finasteride 2.5–5 mg (specialist) if COC unsuitable. Response takes 6 months.

options.label: Dermatomyositis, lupus, pyoderma, DH
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Dermatomyositis: heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules over knuckles, shawl sign, nailfold changes, proximal weakness, raised CK — URGENT rheumatology/dermatology; 15–25% have underlying cancer (NG12 — age-appropriate cancer screen: CT chest/abdo/pelvis, CA125, mammography, PSA). Treatment: high-dose prednisolone + methotrexate/azathioprine (specialist), sun protection.
2. Discoid lupus: scaly red plaques with scarring/alopecia on face/scalp/ears; ANA, dsDNA, FBC, U&E, urinalysis (5% progress to SLE). Treat: SPF50 daily, potent topical steroid (betamethasone valerate 0.1% or clobetasol on face short term) or tacrolimus 0.1%, intralesional triamcinolone; hydroxychloroquine 200–400 mg (specialist, baseline eye screen); stop smoking (reduces response).
3. Pyoderma gangrenosum: rapidly enlarging painful ulcer with violaceous undermined border, often after trauma (pathergy); associated IBD, RA, haematological malignancy — SAME-DAY/urgent dermatology; do NOT debride; potent topical/ intralesional steroid for small lesions, prednisolone 0.5–1 mg/kg or ciclosporin for larger (specialist); investigate for associated disease (FBC, CRP, faecal calprotectin, protein electrophoresis).
4. Dermatitis herpetiformis: intensely itchy grouped vesicles/excoriations on elbows, knees, buttocks, scalp; tTG-IgA + total IgA (coeliac in >90%); dermatology for skin biopsy (direct IF). Treat: strict gluten-free diet for life (rash takes months to clear), dapsone 50–100 mg (specialist; check G6PD, FBC, LFT; haemolysis) for rapid control; gastroenterology for coeliac work-up.

options.label: Granulomatous, lymphoma, Kaposi, morphoea, photosensitivity
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Granuloma annulare: smooth skin-coloured/pink annular plaques, dorsal hands/feet; self-limiting in 50% within 2 years; check HbA1c/lipids (weak association), potent topical/intralesional steroid; dermatology if generalised. Cutaneous sarcoidosis (lupus pernio, papules in scars, erythema nodosum) → chest X-ray, calcium, ACE, dermatology/respiratory.
2. Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides): persistent 'eczema/psoriasis' not responding to treatment, in sun-protected areas (buttocks, trunk), poikiloderma, plaques/tumours → 2WW dermatology for biopsy; Sézary if erythroderma + lymphadenopathy.
3. Kaposi sarcoma: purple-brown macules/plaques/nodules, often legs, mouth; HIV test (AIDS-defining) and consider in transplant/immunosuppressed; 2WW dermatology; treatment via HIV/oncology (ART, radiotherapy, chemotherapy).
4. Morphoea (localised scleroderma): indurated ivory plaques with lilac border; no systemic sclerosis features (no Raynaud's/sclerodactyly); dermatology — potent topical steroid/tacrolimus/calcipotriol, phototherapy, methotrexate for linear/deep forms (especially children — growth impairment).
5. Photosensitivity: polymorphic light eruption (itchy papules hours after sun, spring — SPF50, hardening phototherapy, short prednisolone course for holidays); drug-induced (doxycycline, thiazides, amiodarone, NSAIDs, chlorpromazine — stop/replace); lupus (ANA, Ro/La); porphyria (blistering, fragility — urine/plasma porphyrins); chronic actinic dermatitis in older men → dermatology.

stevens-johnson.title: Drug eruptions, erythema multiforme, SJS/TEN and erythema nodosum
stevens-johnson.curatedBy: Claude draft (BAD SJS/TEN guideline 2016; NICE CKS; PCDS; BNF)

options.label: Drug eruption — assessment
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Timing: morbilliform/exanthematous (commonest) 4–14 days after new drug (antibiotics — amoxicillin esp. with EBV, sulfonamides, allopurinol, anticonvulsants, NSAIDs); urticarial within hours–days; fixed drug eruption (recurrent same-site round plaque — paracetamol, NSAIDs, tetracyclines); DRESS 2–8 weeks (rash + fever + facial oedema + eosinophilia + LFT/renal derangement — allopurinol, carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine, vancomycin → ADMIT).
2. DANGER signs → same-day admission: mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals), skin pain, blistering/skin detachment, Nikolsky positive, fever, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, purpura, eosinophilia >1.5, deranged LFTs/creatinine.
3. Management of simple exanthem: stop the likeliest culprit (and any started in previous 2–3 weeks), emollients, moderate topical steroid (betamethasone valerate 0.1% bd 1–2 weeks), non-sedating antihistamine for itch (cetirizine 10 mg, up to qds); resolves 1–2 weeks after stopping. Document the allergy clearly (drug, reaction type, date); Yellow Card report; consider allergy clinic if the drug is important (penicillin de-labelling).

options.label: SJS / TEN — emergency
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Prodrome of fever/flu-like symptoms then painful dusky macules/targets with blisters and sheet-like epidermal detachment, mucositis (≥2 sites), conjunctivitis. SJS <10% BSA, overlap 10–30%, TEN >30%; mortality 10–50% (SCORTEN).
2. Culprits: allopurinol, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, phenytoin, sulfonamides, nevirapine, oxicam NSAIDs, usually within 4–28 days of starting. HLA-B*15:02 (carbamazepine, Han Chinese/Thai — test before starting), HLA-B*58:01 (allopurinol).
3. Action: 999/immediate admission (burns unit/ITU-level care); stop ALL possible culprits immediately — the single most important intervention; do not give steroids/antibiotics prophylactically in primary care.
4. Aftercare: lifelong avoidance and documentation, MedicAlert; ophthalmology (dry eye, symblepharon), genital/urethral strictures, nail/skin pigmentation, PTSD screening; first-degree relatives avoid the same drug class.

options.label: Erythema multiforme and erythema nodosum
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Erythema multiforme: typical target lesions (3 zones) on acral sites, symmetrical, ± oral lesions (EM major); 90% infection-triggered — HSV (recurrent EM), Mycoplasma (children, with pneumonia/mucositis), not usually drugs. Self-limiting 2–4 weeks: emollients, topical steroid, antihistamine, mouthwash (benzydamine 0.15%); treat HSV (aciclovir 400 mg tds 5 days); recurrent EM (≥6/year) → prophylactic aciclovir 400 mg bd for 6 months; dermatology if severe/mucosal. Distinguish from SJS (truncal, dusky, detachment, drug-related).
2. Erythema nodosum: tender red subcutaneous nodules on shins, no ulceration, lasting 3–6 weeks, bruise-like fading; causes — streptococcal infection (ASOT, throat swab), sarcoidosis (chest X-ray — bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy = Löfgren's), IBD (faecal calprotectin), TB (IGRA if risk), pregnancy/COC, drugs (sulfonamides, penicillins), Behçet's, lymphoma; 50% idiopathic.
3. EN management: treat cause; rest, leg elevation, compression; NSAID (naproxen 500 mg bd); potassium iodide or short prednisolone course (specialist) if severe; refer if persisting >8 weeks, ulcerating (not EN — consider vasculitis/panniculitis → biopsy), or systemic features.

tinea-pedis.title: Fungal skin infections – tinea, pityriasis versicolor, seborrhoeic dermatitis/dandruff
tinea-pedis.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Fungal skin infection – body and groin / foot / scalp / Pityriasis versicolor / Seborrhoeic dermatitis 2024; BAD; BNF)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Fungal skin infection – foot
NICE CKS Fungal skin infection – body and groin
NICE CKS Fungal skin infection – scalp

options.label: Tinea pedis, corporis, cruris
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnosis clinical (annular scaly plaque with active edge and central clearing; interdigital maceration; moccasin scaling); skin scrapings for mycology if atypical, extensive, treatment failure, or before oral therapy. Beware tinea incognito after topical steroid.
2. Topical first line 2–4 weeks (continue 1–2 weeks after clearing): terbinafine 1% cream od–bd (foot 1 week), or clotrimazole 1%/miconazole 2% bd–tds; for inflamed lesions, combined hydrocortisone 1% + antifungal for ≤7 days then antifungal alone.
3. Oral if extensive, failed topical, moccasin-type or immunosuppressed: terbinafine 250 mg od for 2–4 weeks (body/groin), 2–6 weeks (foot); check LFTs if pre-existing liver disease; alternative itraconazole 100 mg od 15 days or 200 mg od 7 days.
4. Nails (onychomycosis): confirm with clippings first; terbinafine 250 mg od 6 weeks (fingers) / 12–24 weeks (toes); amorolfine 5% lacquer weekly 6–12 months for mild distal disease; treat tinea pedis concurrently to prevent recurrence. Foot hygiene, dry between toes, antifungal powder in shoes, avoid shared towels.

options.label: Tinea capitis and pityriasis versicolor
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Tinea capitis (children, Afro-Caribbean esp.): scaly patches with broken hairs/black dots, kerion (boggy mass — do not incise), occipital nodes. Send scalp scrapings/plucked hairs. ALWAYS oral: griseofulvin 10–20 mg/kg od (max 1 g) 6–8 weeks (licensed in children; Microsporum) or terbinafine 62.5–250 mg by weight od 4 weeks (Trichophyton tonsurans — commonest in UK; off-label in children). Ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly for patient and household; check siblings; no school exclusion once treated.
2. Pityriasis versicolor: fine scaly hypo/hyperpigmented macules on trunk/upper arms, Malassezia; worse in heat/humidity. Ketoconazole 2% shampoo to affected skin daily 5 days (leave 5 min) or selenium sulfide 2.5% shampoo 7 days; small areas — clotrimazole/terbinafine cream bd 2 weeks. Extensive/failed: itraconazole 200 mg od 7 days or fluconazole 300 mg weekly ×2. Warn pigmentation takes months; recurrence common — monthly prophylactic shampoo.

options.label: Seborrhoeic dermatitis / dandruff
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Scalp: ketoconazole 2% shampoo twice weekly for 4 weeks then weekly maintenance; alternatives coal tar, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione, salicylic acid for thick scale (Sebco/Cocois ointment overnight); short course mometasone 0.1% scalp lotion for itch/inflammation.
2. Face/body: ketoconazole 2% cream or clotrimazole bd + hydrocortisone 1% for ≤2 weeks; eyelids — lid hygiene; chest — antifungal shampoo as wash. Severe/widespread — think HIV (test) or Parkinson's.
3. Infantile (cradle cap): emollient/olive oil softening, gentle brushing, baby shampoo; usually clears by 12 months; hydrocortisone 1% for inflamed areas short term; no ketoconazole under 12 (off-label use acceptable if needed).
4. Refer dermatology: diagnostic doubt (psoriasis, tinea, lupus), failure of adequate treatment, severe disease in immunosuppressed.

consent-child.title: Consent and capacity – adults, children, minor surgery
consent-child.curatedBy: Claude draft (Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice; GMC Decision making and consent 2020; GMC 0–18 years; RCGP/BMA; NICE NG108 Decision-making and mental capacity 2018)
niceRefs: Mental Capacity Act 2005 Code of Practice

options.label: Capacity assessment (adults, England & Wales)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. MCA principles: presume capacity; support the person to decide (time, place, communication aids, interpreter — not family as interpreter for key decisions); an unwise decision is not incapacity; best interests; least restrictive option.
2. Two-stage test, decision- and time-specific: (a) impairment/disturbance of mind or brain (dementia, delirium, learning disability, intoxication, mental illness, brain injury); (b) because of it, unable to UNDERSTAND the relevant information, RETAIN it long enough, USE OR WEIGH it, or COMMUNICATE the decision. Failure on any one = lacks capacity for THIS decision.
3. Document: the decision in question, information given, the person's own words, which limb failed and why, who was present, steps taken to support capacity. Reassess if condition fluctuates (delirium — treat and retry).
4. If lacking capacity: check for valid Advance Decision (refusal of treatment — binding if valid and applicable; life-sustaining refusal must be written, signed, witnessed), Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare (verify on OPG register — a finance LPA does NOT cover health), court-appointed deputy; otherwise best-interests decision consulting family/carers; IMCA if no one to consult and serious treatment/accommodation decision. Deprivation of liberty → DoLS/LPS application (care home/hospital). Scotland: Adults with Incapacity Act — s47 certificate.

options.label: Children and young people
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. 16–17: presumed competent to consent (Family Law Reform Act 1969); MCA applies; refusal of life-saving treatment can be overridden by a parent or court — seek advice.
2. Under 16: Gillick competent if they understand the nature, purpose and consequences of the treatment and the alternatives, including of not treating — assess and document per decision; a competent child's consent is valid without parental knowledge; encourage parental involvement unless this risks harm. If not competent, a person with parental responsibility consents (mother always; father if married to mother at birth or on birth certificate from 2003; step-parent only with court order/agreement).
3. Fraser guidelines (contraception/sexual health specifically): understands the advice, cannot be persuaded to tell parents, likely to continue sexual activity, health would suffer without treatment, best interests. Under 13: cannot in law consent to sexual activity — safeguarding referral always; 13–15: assess exploitation (age gap, coercion, substances, grooming) and refer if concerns.
4. Disputes between parents or parent and child: do not proceed with elective treatment; involve safeguarding lead, medical defence organisation, and court if necessary (life-saving treatment given in an emergency regardless).

options.label: Consent for minor surgery and procedures
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Montgomery standard: disclose material risks THIS patient would attach significance to — not just what a doctor thinks important. Cover: diagnosis and uncertainty, options including no treatment, benefits, risks (common and serious), who will do it, histology plan, scarring, infection (~2–5%), bleeding, pain, recurrence, nerve damage for specific sites (e.g. temporal branch of facial nerve, spinal accessory in posterior triangle), need for further surgery.
2. Written consent for all excisions, joint injections and cryotherapy of lesions where scarring/pigment change possible; verbal (documented) for simple procedures; the person doing the procedure takes consent; allow time to decide; interpreter for non-English speakers.
3. Safety checklist (RCGP minor surgery): identity, site marked and agreed, allergies, anticoagulants/antiplatelets (continue warfarin if INR <3 checked within 72 h; DOACs — omit morning dose for higher-risk sites), pacemaker (bipolar diathermy only), lidocaine max dose 3 mg/kg plain / 7 mg/kg with adrenaline (avoid adrenaline in digits only if peripheral vascular disease), send ALL excised lesions for histology, specimen labelled before leaving room, aftercare and suture removal written.
4. Do not excise in primary care: suspected melanoma (2WW), lesions on face/high-risk BCC sites unless accredited, lesions >2 cm, deep lumps, sarcoma concern. Record capacity if any doubt; a competent refusal must be respected.

zinc-deficiency.title: Micronutrient deficiencies – zinc, magnesium, vitamin C, vitamin K, multiple
zinc-deficiency.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CG32 Nutrition support 2006/2017; NICE CKS Malnutrition; BNF; SPS hypomagnesaemia guidance)

options.label: Magnesium
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hypomagnesaemia (<0.7 mmol/L; severe <0.5): causes — PPIs (long-term; stop/switch to H2RA), diuretics (loop/thiazide), alcohol, diarrhoea/malabsorption, diabetes, refeeding, drugs (cisplatin, ciclosporin, EGFR inhibitors), renal wasting (Gitelman/Bartter). Symptoms: cramps, tremor, arrhythmia, seizures; causes refractory hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia — check K, Ca, PTH, ECG.
2. Severe (<0.4) or symptomatic/arrhythmia → same-day admission for IV magnesium sulfate 20 mmol over 12–24 h.
3. Mild–moderate asymptomatic: oral magnesium aspartate 10 mmol sachet od–bd (Magnaspartate — licensed) or magnesium glycerophosphate 4 mmol tablets 1–2 tds (unlicensed/'special'); diarrhoea limits dose; recheck 1–2 weeks and after cause addressed; if PPI needed and Mg stays low despite supplements → stop PPI.

options.label: Zinc and vitamin C
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Zinc: suspect in alcohol excess, malabsorption (coeliac, IBD, bariatric), CKD, anorexia, vegan diets, long-term diuretics, acrodermatitis-type rash (periorificial, acral), alopecia, taste loss, poor wound healing, recurrent infection, diarrhoea. Serum zinc <11 micromol/L (fasting, interpret with albumin/CRP — low in inflammation). Treat: zinc sulfate 125 mg (45 mg elemental) od–tds (Solvazinc) for 3 months then reassess; take away from iron/calcium; long-term use depletes copper — check if >6 months.
2. Vitamin C (scurvy): dietary restriction, alcohol, elderly living alone, eating disorder, 'tea and toast'; perifollicular haemorrhage, corkscrew hairs, gum bleeding/swelling, bruising, poor healing, anaemia; plasma ascorbate <11 micromol/L (take on ice) but treat on clinical suspicion. Treat: ascorbic acid 500 mg–1 g daily for 1–2 weeks then 100 mg daily until diet corrected; symptoms improve within days; dietary advice (fruit, peppers, potatoes); dietitian/social support.

options.label: Vitamin K and multiple deficiencies / refeeding
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Vitamin K: prolonged PT with normal APTT/fibrinogen and bleeding (bruising, gum/GI); causes — fat malabsorption (coeliac, cholestasis, pancreatic insufficiency, bariatric), prolonged antibiotics, warfarin, poor intake. Adults: phytomenadione 10 mg orally (Konakion MM) or IV if bleeding/malabsorption, recheck PT 24–48 h; neonates — IM 1 mg at birth (vitamin K deficiency bleeding; oral regimen if parents refuse IM). Warfarin-related high INR — see Anticoagulation tool.
2. Multiple deficiencies (alcohol dependence, bariatric surgery, eating disorders, elderly malnourished, homeless): screen FBC, ferritin, B12, folate, vitamin D, calcium, phosphate, magnesium, zinc, LFT, albumin, PT; MUST score. Alcohol: thiamine 100 mg tds (or 200–300 mg daily) + vitamin B co-strong 1–2 tablets tds; Pabrinex IV in hospital if Wernicke risk (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus) — give BEFORE glucose. Bariatric: lifelong multivitamin (Forceval od), iron, B12 injections 3-monthly, calcium/vitamin D, annual bloods per BOMSS.
3. REFEEDING risk (CG32): BMI <16, >15% weight loss in 3–6 months, little intake >10 days, low K/PO4/Mg before feeding — start feeding at ≤10 kcal/kg/day, thiamine 200–300 mg before and during first 10 days, monitor K, phosphate, Mg daily; admit if high risk or needs enteral support; dietitian referral for all.

achalasia.title: Dysphagia and oesophageal motility disorders – achalasia, spasm
achalasia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG12; NICE CKS Dyspepsia – unidentified cause; BSG/ACG achalasia 2020; BNF)

options.label: Dysphagia — first step
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG12: ANY dysphagia in an adult → 2WW upper GI endoscopy (oesophageal cancer); do not wait for a barium swallow. Also 2WW: age ≥55 with weight loss + dyspepsia/reflux/upper abdominal pain.
2. Features pointing to motility rather than stricture: dysphagia for BOTH solids and liquids from onset, intermittent, regurgitation of undigested food, chest pain, long history, weight loss modest. Oropharyngeal dysphagia (coughing, choking, nasal regurgitation, neurological disease) → SLT and neurology rather than endoscopy first.
3. Red flags for admission: complete obstruction (cannot swallow saliva — food bolus; ED), aspiration pneumonia, severe weight loss/dehydration.

options.label: Achalasia
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Endoscopy normal or dilated oesophagus with retained food ('pseudo-achalasia' from tumour at GOJ must be excluded). Diagnosis: high-resolution oesophageal manometry (gold standard, gastroenterology); barium swallow 'bird's beak'.
2. Definitive treatment via upper GI surgery/gastroenterology: pneumatic dilatation (graded, repeated), Heller myotomy + fundoplication, or POEM (NICE IPG; best for type III); botulinum toxin injection for frail/unfit (lasts 6–12 months).
3. Bridging/primary care: nifedipine 10–20 mg SL 30 min before meals or isosorbide dinitrate 5 mg SL (modest effect; hypotension); eat upright, small meals, fluids with meals, sleep head-up; PPI after myotomy/dilatation for reflux. Lifelong cancer risk slightly raised — report new dysphagia/weight loss.

options.label: Oesophageal spasm / hypercontractile oesophagus
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Intermittent retrosternal chest pain ± dysphagia, often triggered by hot/cold food or stress; exclude cardiac cause first (ECG, troponin/cardiology if risk), then endoscopy (2WW if dysphagia) and manometry.
2. Treat reflux first (frequently co-exists): omeprazole 20–40 mg od 8 weeks trial. Eosinophilic oesophagitis (young, atopic, food impaction) — endoscopy with biopsies; PPI, swallowed fluticasone/budesonide (Jorveza), elimination diet.
3. Spasm: smooth-muscle relaxants — diltiazem 60 mg tds or nifedipine; low-dose amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte for visceral hypersensitivity; peppermint oil capsules; reassurance; refer gastroenterology if refractory (botox, POEM for type III).

anal-fissure.title: Anorectal conditions – fissure, haemorrhoids, fistula, pilonidal sinus
anal-fissure.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CKS Anal fissure / Haemorrhoids / Pilonidal sinus 2024; ACPGBI; NICE NG12; BNF)

options.label: Anal fissure
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Severe sharp pain on defecation lasting minutes–hours, bright red blood on paper; posterior midline tear (lateral/multiple fissures → Crohn's, HIV, TB, cancer → refer). Examine gently; DRE may be impossible — do not force.
2. First 1–2 weeks: soften stool — fibre 25–30 g/day, fluids, ispaghula or macrogol daily; sitz baths; lidocaine 5% ointment before defecation for a few days; paracetamol/ibuprofen (avoid codeine — constipation).
3. Chronic (>6 weeks) or persistent: GTN 0.4% rectal ointment (Rectogesic) 2.5 cm bd for 6–8 weeks (headache common — start pea-sized); or topical diltiazem 2% bd 6–8 weeks (unlicensed/'special', fewer headaches; first line in many areas). Continue laxative throughout.
4. Refer colorectal (routine) if not healed after 8 weeks of topical therapy, recurrent, or atypical: botulinum toxin injection, lateral internal sphincterotomy (continence risk — not first choice in women post-childbirth), anal advancement flap. Children: fissure common with constipation — treat constipation (NG99); consider abuse if other features.

options.label: Haemorrhoids (including thrombosed)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Painless bright red bleeding, prolapse, itch; classify I–IV. NG12 — do NOT attribute rectal bleeding to piles without assessment: FIT (≥10 micrograms/g → 2WW), 2WW if age ≥50 with unexplained bleeding, or ≥40 with bleeding + change in bowel habit/weight loss/abdominal pain, or any age with a rectal/abdominal mass; iron deficiency anaemia → investigate.
2. Conservative: fibre/ispaghula, fluids, avoid straining/prolonged sitting, toilet position; topical — Anusol or short course (≤7 days) of a steroid-containing preparation (Anusol HC, Scheriproct) for symptoms; simple analgesia.
3. Thrombosed external haemorrhoid: very painful tense blue perianal lump — if <72 h, same-day surgical referral for excision gives fastest relief; otherwise analgesia (ibuprofen/paracetamol, NOT opioids), ice, laxative, topical GTN/lidocaine; resolves 7–10 days leaving a skin tag.
4. Refer colorectal: grade II–IV persisting despite conservative care (rubber band ligation, injection sclerotherapy, HALO/THD, haemorrhoidectomy for grade IV), acutely prolapsed irreducible/strangulated piles (same day), diagnostic uncertainty.

options.label: Anal fistula, perianal abscess, pilonidal sinus
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Perianal abscess: painful swelling, fever, unable to sit — SAME-DAY surgical referral for incision and drainage (antibiotics alone inadequate; give co-amoxiclav 625 mg tds only if cellulitis/immunosuppressed while awaiting). Diabetes, Crohn's, immunosuppression increase risk.
2. Anal fistula: persistent discharge/recurrent abscess with an external opening; ask about Crohn's symptoms (faecal calprotectin), TB, HIV. Refer colorectal (routine; urgent if recurrent abscesses): MRI pelvis to map, seton, fistulotomy for simple low fistulas, LIFT/advancement flap for complex; Crohn's fistula → gastroenterology for anti-TNF. Keep area clean, pad; no role for long-term antibiotics except in Crohn's (metronidazole 400 mg tds/ciprofloxacin on specialist advice).
3. Pilonidal sinus: natal cleft pits ± abscess in hirsute young adults, drivers, sitting occupations. Acute abscess → same-day/urgent incision and drainage. Chronic/recurrent: hair removal (laser/shaving weekly), hygiene, weight loss; refer surgery for off-midline excision/flap (Karydakis, Bascom) if recurrent or persistent discharge; asymptomatic pits need no surgery.
4. Pruritus ani: exclude threadworm (children/family — mebendazole), dermatitis, psoriasis, lichen sclerosus, fungal, piles/fissure/fistula, diabetes; treat with hygiene (water not wipes, pat dry), avoid scratching/irritants, short-course hydrocortisone 1%, zinc barrier, fibre; refer if persistent >6 weeks or any suspicious lesion (anal cancer — 2WW for unexplained anal mass or ulceration).

ascites.title: Gallstones, cholestatic liver disease and cirrhosis complications
ascites.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CG188 Gallstone disease 2014; NICE NG50 Cirrhosis 2016; NICE CKS Gallstones / Cirrhosis; BSG; BASL; BNF)

options.label: Gallstones — asymptomatic, biliary colic, cholecystitis, cholangitis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Asymptomatic gallstones (incidental on USS): no treatment (CG188) — reassure; no low-fat diet needed; cholecystectomy only if stones in the common bile duct (ERCP/surgery even if asymptomatic), porcelain gallbladder, or large polyps ≥10 mm.
2. Biliary colic (RUQ/epigastric pain >30 min, often after fatty meal, no fever, normal inflammatory markers): LFTs, lipase, USS; analgesia — diclofenac 75 mg IM/50 mg PR or ibuprofen; paracetamol; if severe, morphine; low-fat diet until surgery; refer for laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 6 weeks of first episode (CG188) — urgent if recurrent attendances. Pregnancy: conservative, surgery 2nd trimester if needed.
3. Acute cholecystitis (pain >6 h + fever + Murphy's positive + raised WCC/CRP): same-day admission — IV antibiotics (co-amoxiclav) and cholecystectomy within 1 week (CG188 'hot gallbladder').
4. Ascending cholangitis (Charcot's triad: fever/rigors, jaundice, RUQ pain ± hypotension/confusion = Reynolds' pentad): EMERGENCY admission — IV antibiotics, ERCP decompression within 24–48 h. Obstructive jaundice without pain → think malignancy (NG12: 2WW pancreatic cancer for age ≥40 with jaundice; CT).

options.label: PBC and PSC
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Primary biliary cholangitis: middle-aged women, fatigue, pruritus, raised ALP ± GGT, AMA positive (95%), raised IgM; USS to exclude obstruction. Refer hepatology. Treat: ursodeoxycholic acid 13–15 mg/kg/day (GP can initiate per shared care); if ALP not <1.67× ULN at 12 months → obeticholic acid (NICE TA443; withdrawn/restricted 2024 — check) or specialist options; pruritus — colestyramine 4 g od–bd (separate from other drugs by 4 h), rifampicin 150–300 mg (specialist), naltrexone; fatigue — exclude thyroid/anaemia/depression; bone protection (DEXA, calcium/vitamin D); fat-soluble vitamin check if jaundiced; annual LFT, platelets; cirrhosis surveillance as below.
2. Primary sclerosing cholangitis: younger men, 70% have ulcerative colitis (do colonoscopy if not known IBD), cholestatic LFTs, pANCA; MRCP shows beading. Refer hepatology — no proven disease-modifying drug (UDCA not recommended at high dose); manage pruritus; annual MRCP/CA19-9 (cholangiocarcinoma risk 10–15%), annual colonoscopy for colorectal cancer surveillance if IBD, gallbladder USS yearly (polyps), bone density; cholangitis episodes → antibiotics; transplant for end-stage.

options.label: Cirrhosis — surveillance, ascites, encephalopathy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnose/stage (NG50): transient elastography (FibroScan) for NAFLD/alcohol/hepatitis; cirrhosis = refer hepatology; 6-monthly USS ± AFP for HCC surveillance; endoscopy for varices if clinically significant portal hypertension (FibroScan >20 kPa or platelets <150) — carvedilol 6.25–12.5 mg od for primary prophylaxis of bleeding; vaccinate hepatitis A/B, pneumococcal, influenza; avoid NSAIDs, aspirin, excess paracetamol (≤2–3 g/day), sedatives; alcohol abstinence; nutrition — 1.2–1.5 g/kg protein, late evening snack, no protein restriction.
2. Ascites: new ascites → urgent hepatology/admission for diagnostic tap (SAAG, neutrophils >250 = SBP). Treat: no added salt (<5–6 g), spironolactone 100 mg od increasing to 400 mg (± furosemide 40 → 160 mg, ratio 100:40), monitor U&E weekly initially (stop if Na <125, K >6, creatinine rising); fluid restriction only if Na <125; large-volume paracentesis with albumin for tense ascites; SBP prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin 500 mg od / co-trimoxazole) after an episode or if protein <15 g/L; refractory → TIPS/transplant assessment. Any fever/abdominal pain/encephalopathy in ascites = SBP until proven otherwise (admit).
3. Hepatic encephalopathy: confusion, flap, reversed sleep; find precipitant — infection, GI bleed, constipation, dehydration/diuretics, sedatives, hypokalaemia, high protein load. Admit if new/grade ≥2. Maintenance: lactulose 20–30 mL bd–tds titrated to 2–3 soft stools/day; add rifaximin 550 mg bd (NICE TA337) after a second episode; do not drive (DVLA) if recurrent; carers' education; consider palliative care planning in decompensated disease (Child-Pugh C).

gist.title: Inflammatory bowel disease, rectal bleeding and other GI conditions
gist.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG129 Crohn's 2019; NICE NG130 Ulcerative colitis 2019; NICE NG12; NICE CKS; BSG IBD 2019; BSG haemochromatosis 2018; BNF)

options.label: IBD — suspected, flare, maintenance
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect: diarrhoea >6 weeks, blood/mucus, urgency, nocturnal symptoms, weight loss, abdominal pain, perianal disease, extra-intestinal (uveitis, arthritis, erythema nodosum), age <45 (over 45 with new bowel symptoms → NG12 FIT/2WW colorectal first). Tests: FBC, CRP, ferritin, B12, LFT, coeliac serology, stool culture + C. difficile, faecal calprotectin (>100–150 → urgent gastroenterology for colonoscopy; <50 and no red flags → IBS pathway).
2. UC flare (known patient, Truelove–Witts): mild–moderate — optimise mesalazine: oral to 4–4.8 g/day (e.g. Octasa 2.4 g bd) plus topical mesalazine 1 g enema/suppository nocte for 4–8 weeks (NG130); if no response in 2 weeks → prednisolone 40 mg od tapering by 5 mg/week over 8 weeks + calcium/vitamin D ± bone protection; SEVERE (≥6 bloody stools + fever/tachycardia/anaemia/raised CRP) → same-day admission (IV steroids, VTE prophylaxis, rescue infliximab/ciclosporin, colectomy). Crohn's flare: prednisolone 40 mg or budesonide 9 mg (ileocaecal) — contact IBD team; never give loperamide/opioids in severe colitis (toxic megacolon); stop NSAIDs.
3. Maintenance: mesalazine 2–2.4 g od (UC; also reduces cancer risk) — annual U&E; thiopurines (azathioprine 2–2.5 mg/kg — TPMT first; FBC/LFT monitoring per shared care), methotrexate, biologics (infliximab, adalimumab, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, JAK inhibitors) via IBD team. GP: vaccinations (no live vaccines on biologics/thiopurines; pneumococcal, influenza, COVID, HPV, VZV status), smoking cessation (Crohn's), bone health, skin cancer surveillance (thiopurines), colonoscopy surveillance from 8–10 years after onset (extensive colitis), iron, B12, folate, mental health, contraception/pregnancy planning (continue most IBD drugs; stop methotrexate 3–6 months before).

options.label: Rectal bleeding, faecal impaction, mesenteric adenitis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Rectal bleeding: examine (PR, proctoscopy if available); FIT for all unless 2WW criteria already met (NG12: ≥40 with bleeding + change in bowel habit/weight loss/abdominal pain; ≥50 unexplained bleeding; any age rectal/abdominal mass; FIT ≥10); FIT-negative with persisting symptoms → still refer if clinical concern. Large-volume/haemodynamically significant bleeding (dizziness, Hb drop) → admit. Under 40 with FIT-negative bleeding and anal source (fissure/piles) → treat; faecal calprotectin if diarrhoea.
2. Faecal impaction (overflow diarrhoea in elderly/opioid users/children): confirm by PR ± abdominal X-ray; disimpaction — macrogol (Laxido/Movicol) 8 sachets/day in 1 L for up to 3 days (NICE CG99/NG99 for children — escalating macrogol), or in frail patients sodium phosphate/arachis oil enema (not if nut allergy) then bisacodyl 10 mg suppository; manual evacuation only under supervision; then maintenance macrogol daily, review opioids/anticholinergics, fluids, mobility; admit if obstruction, vomiting, severe abdominal pain.
3. Mesenteric adenitis (child/teen with RIF pain after URTI, low-grade fever, no peritonism): diagnosis of exclusion — do NOT label without excluding appendicitis (same-day surgical review if guarding, worsening, high CRP); analgesia, fluids, safety-net review 12–24 h; USS where available.

options.label: Haemochromatosis, autoimmune hepatitis, Wilson's
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Haemochromatosis: transferrin saturation >45% (fasting) + ferritin >300 (men)/>200 (women) → HFE genotype (C282Y homozygous or compound heterozygote); exclude alcohol/NAFLD/inflammation as cause of high ferritin alone. Refer hepatology: venesection 450–500 mL weekly until ferritin 20–30 then every 2–4 months maintenance (many areas via blood service); MRI/FibroScan if ferritin >1000 (cirrhosis risk — HCC surveillance); screen diabetes, cardiac (ECG/echo), arthropathy, pituitary/testosterone; avoid vitamin C supplements, raw shellfish; alcohol moderation; offer first-degree relatives HFE testing + iron studies at 18–30 (not children).
2. Autoimmune hepatitis: raised ALT/AST ± jaundice, raised IgG, ANA/SMA (type 1) or LKM (type 2, young), other autoimmune disease; exclude viral/drug/alcohol/NAFLD. URGENT hepatology (acute severe AIH can progress to failure): liver biopsy; prednisolone 40–60 mg then azathioprine 1–2 mg/kg (TPMT); budesonide if non-cirrhotic; lifelong monitoring; bone protection; pregnancy possible on azathioprine.
3. Wilson's disease: consider in ANY liver disease age <40, unexplained neurological/psychiatric symptoms (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia), haemolysis; low caeruloplasmin (<0.2 g/L), 24-h urinary copper, Kayser–Fleischer rings (slit lamp), ATP7B genetics; urgent hepatology — penicillamine/trientine chelation, zinc maintenance, transplant for fulminant failure; screen siblings.

options.label: Gastroparesis, SIBO, lactose intolerance, microscopic colitis, Whipple's, GIST
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Gastroparesis: early satiety, nausea, bloating, vomiting undigested food, usually diabetes (optimise glucose; stop GLP-1 agonists/pramlintide), post-viral, opioids (stop), post-surgical. Gastric emptying scintigraphy via gastroenterology after normal endoscopy. Small frequent low-fat, low-fibre meals; liquid calories; metoclopramide 10 mg tds max 5 days (MHRA) or domperidone 10 mg tds max 7 days (QT — ECG; avoid >60 years/with QT drugs) for acute symptoms; erythromycin 250 mg tds short term; refer for gastric electrical stimulation/G-POEM if refractory.
2. SIBO: bloating, diarrhoea, B12 low/folate high, risk factors (surgery, strictures, scleroderma, PPIs, diabetes); glucose/lactulose hydrogen breath test; rifaximin 550 mg tds 14 days (unlicensed; gastroenterology) or co-amoxiclav; address cause; recurrence common.
3. Lactose intolerance: symptoms within hours of dairy; trial 2–4 week lactose-free diet with rechallenge or hydrogen breath test; secondary after gastroenteritis resolves in weeks; ensure calcium 700–1000 mg/day (lactose-free dairy, fortified alternatives, supplements) — children: dietitian; do not confuse with cow's milk protein allergy in infants.
4. Microscopic colitis: chronic watery non-bloody diarrhoea in women >60, normal colonoscopy — biopsies needed; associated NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, statins (stop if possible), coeliac (test), smoking. Treat: budesonide 9 mg od 6–8 weeks then taper; loperamide for symptom control; relapse common — low-dose budesonide maintenance (gastroenterology).
5. Whipple's disease: rare — middle-aged men with arthralgia for years, then diarrhoea, weight loss, lymphadenopathy, neurological signs; PAS-positive macrophages on duodenal biopsy/T. whipplei PCR; refer — ceftriaxone 2 weeks then co-trimoxazole 12 months.
6. GIST: incidental submucosal gastric/small-bowel mass on endoscopy/CT or GI bleeding; refer upper GI MDT (EUS, biopsy for KIT/CD117); surgery ± imatinib; lesions <2 cm may be surveilled.

barrett-s-surveillance.title: GI cancer referral (2WW), Barrett's, peptic ulcer and gastritis
barrett-s-surveillance.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG12 Suspected cancer 2015/2023; NICE CG184 Dyspepsia/GORD 2014/2019; NICE CKS; BSG Barrett's 2014/2023; UKHSA H. pylori; BNF)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Dyspepsia – proven peptic ulcer

options.label: 2WW criteria — oesophageal, gastric, pancreatic, colorectal
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Upper GI 2WW endoscopy (NG12): dysphagia at any age; age ≥55 with weight loss AND any of upper abdominal pain, reflux, dyspepsia. Non-urgent direct-access endoscopy: ≥55 with treatment-resistant dyspepsia, or upper abdominal pain with low Hb, or raised platelets with nausea/vomiting/weight loss/reflux/dyspepsia/pain, or nausea/vomiting with weight loss/reflux/dyspepsia/pain. Upper abdominal mass → 2WW gastric cancer. Haematemesis → admit (Glasgow–Blatchford).
2. Pancreatic 2WW: age ≥40 with jaundice (also urgent LFT/USS/CT); consider urgent direct-access CT (or USS) in ≥60 with weight loss AND any of diarrhoea, back pain, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, constipation, new-onset diabetes. CA19-9 is not a screening test.
3. Colorectal 2WW (NG12 2023 FIT-first): FIT ≥10 micrograms/g with any symptom; any age with abdominal or rectal mass, or unexplained anal mass/ulceration; FIT not required before referral if these. Offer FIT for: abdominal pain, change in bowel habit, weight loss, iron deficiency anaemia, age ≥40 with bleeding+pain or ≥50 with bleeding, ≥60 with anaemia even if not iron deficient. FIT-negative with ongoing concern → safety-net/refer anyway. Bowel screening (FIT every 2 years from 50–74 in England) — encourage uptake.
4. After a cancer diagnosis (GP role): fitness for treatment, nutrition (dietitian, oral supplements), VTE awareness, stoma/pain/psychological support, cancer care review, treatment summary; colorectal survivors — colonoscopy at 1 and 3–5 years, CEA 6-monthly for 3 years, late effects (bowel function, neuropathy from oxaliplatin).

options.label: Barrett's oesophagus
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnosis on endoscopy with biopsies (columnar-lined ≥1 cm). Cancer risk ~0.3%/year without dysplasia. Lifelong PPI (omeprazole 20–40 mg od; lansoprazole 30 mg) controls reflux — no proven chemoprevention beyond that; AspECT trial suggests high-dose PPI ± aspirin may help (discuss).
2. Surveillance (BSG): no dysplasia and <3 cm → endoscopy every 3–5 years; ≥3 cm → every 2–3 years; indefinite for dysplasia → repeat 6 months after PPI optimisation; low-grade dysplasia (confirmed by 2 pathologists) → radiofrequency ablation offered; high-grade/intramucosal cancer → endoscopic resection + ablation (NICE IPG). Stop surveillance if comorbidity makes treatment of cancer inappropriate (shared decision).
3. Red flags between scans → 2WW: new dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, anaemia. Lifestyle: weight, smoking cessation, alcohol, head of bed elevation.

options.label: Peptic ulcer, H. pylori, gastritis, oesophagitis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. H. pylori test (CG184): urea breath test or stool antigen — stop PPI 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks before; serology only if never previously treated. Eradication 7 days: PPI bd (omeprazole 20 mg/lansoprazole 30 mg) + amoxicillin 1 g bd + clarithromycin 500 mg bd OR metronidazole 400 mg bd (use metronidazole if clarithromycin given in past year for any reason). Penicillin allergy: PPI + clarithromycin 500 mg bd + metronidazole 400 mg bd. Second line: swap the unused antibiotic; or PPI + amoxicillin + levofloxacin 250 mg bd 7 days (if no quinolone in past year); third line → gastroenterology for bismuth quadruple (Pylera) 10 days. Retest only (breath/stool, ≥4 weeks after antibiotics, 2 weeks off PPI) if: ulcer, MALT lymphoma, ongoing symptoms, family history of gastric cancer, or patient wishes.
2. Peptic ulcer on endoscopy: eradicate H. pylori; PPI full dose 4 weeks (DU) / 8 weeks (GU) then repeat endoscopy for GASTRIC ulcer (6–8 weeks) to confirm healing/exclude cancer; stop NSAIDs/aspirin where possible (if aspirin essential — PPI long term); bleeding ulcer → admit. Alarm symptoms after treatment → 2WW.
3. Gastritis (endoscopic/histological): H. pylori-associated → eradicate; NSAID/alcohol → stop; atrophic gastritis/intestinal metaplasia (autoimmune — check B12, anti-parietal/IF antibodies, treat pernicious anaemia; or H. pylori-related) → BSG: extensive atrophy/IM → endoscopic surveillance every 3 years (gastric cancer risk), consider NET risk in autoimmune type.
4. Reflux oesophagitis (LA grade): PPI full dose 8 weeks (grade A/B) — then lowest effective dose/on demand; severe (C/D) — maintain full-dose PPI long term, repeat endoscopy to exclude Barrett's; add alginate (Gaviscon Advance) for breakthrough; eosinophilic oesophagitis if young/atopic (biopsies); refer for fundoplication if PPI-dependent with volume reflux or intolerance. Long-term PPI: annual review, check magnesium if >1 year, B12 if symptoms, bone health; step down where possible.

nafld-in-diabetes.title: Fatty liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) and hepatitis C – assessment and referral
nafld-in-diabetes.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG49 NAFLD 2016; BSG abnormal LFTs 2017; EASL MASLD 2024; NICE CKS NAFLD; NHS England hepatitis C elimination; BNF)
niceRefs: BSG abnormal liver blood tests guideline
NICE CKS Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

options.label: Find fibrosis — the question that matters
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect MASLD in: raised ALT/GGT, fatty liver on USS, or type 2 diabetes/obesity/metabolic syndrome even with normal LFTs (NG49 suggests case-finding in T2DM; EASL 2024 recommends FIB-4 in all with T2DM/obesity + metabolic risk). Alcohol history (<14 units/week = non-alcoholic; AUDIT-C); exclude other causes — hepatitis B/C serology, ferritin/TSAT, autoantibodies/immunoglobulins, coeliac, TFTs, drugs (methotrexate, amiodarone, tamoxifen, steroids).
2. Risk-stratify: FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets): <1.3 (<2.0 if age >65) = low risk — repeat in 3 years (1–2 years if diabetes); ≥1.3 → ELF test (NG49: ≥10.51 = advanced fibrosis) or transient elastography (FibroScan): <8 kPa low risk; 8–12 indeterminate → hepatology or repeat; ≥12 kPa likely advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis → hepatology. FIB-4 >2.67 → refer directly.
3. Advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis: hepatology — HCC surveillance (6-monthly USS), varices screening, vaccinations, avoid hepatotoxins; the liver, not the LFTs, decides — normal ALT does not exclude cirrhosis.

options.label: Management of MASLD
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Weight loss is the treatment: ≥5% improves steatosis, ≥7–10% resolves steatohepatitis and improves fibrosis — Mediterranean diet, 500–750 kcal/day deficit, minimise sugar-sweetened drinks/fructose, coffee allowed (protective), 150–300 min moderate exercise/week + resistance training; refer tier 3 weight management/bariatric surgery (BMI ≥35 with MASLD — resolves NASH in most).
2. Diabetes: pioglitazone 15–45 mg (improves NASH — weigh against weight gain, fluid, fracture, bladder cancer signal; NG49 'consider' in advanced fibrosis via specialist); GLP-1 agonists — semaglutide (NICE TA875 for weight; ESSENCE trial shows NASH resolution) and tirzepatide preferred where eligible; SGLT2 inhibitors reduce liver fat; metformin neutral. Statins are SAFE and indicated for CV risk (cardiovascular disease is the commonest cause of death) — continue unless ALT >3× ULN. Resmetirom (first licensed NASH drug, US 2024) — not yet NICE-approved; check.
3. Alcohol: ideally abstain if fibrosis; certainly within 14 units. Vitamin E 800 IU/day in non-diabetic biopsy-proven NASH (specialist). Monitor LFTs/FIB-4 annually; HbA1c, lipids, BP; sleep apnoea screening.

options.label: Hepatitis C — test, refer, treat
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Test (anti-HCV antibody with reflex RNA) anyone with: ever injected drugs, received blood/products before 1991/organs before 1992 in UK, born/medical treatment where HCV is common (Pakistan, Egypt, E. Europe, S. Asia), prison, tattoos/piercings in unregulated settings, HIV, MSM, sexual partner/household of case, unexplained raised ALT, on dialysis. Opportunistic testing — NHS England aims to eliminate HCV by 2025–30; free postal self-test kits (hepctest.nhs.uk).
2. RNA positive = active infection → refer to the hepatitis C operational delivery network (ODN) — all genotypes now cured in >95% with 8–12 weeks of pan-genotypic direct-acting antivirals (sofosbuvir/velpatasvir, glecaprevir/pibrentasvir); no interferon; treatment is given regardless of fibrosis stage; drug–drug interactions (statins, PPIs, amiodarone, some antiepileptics) — check hep-druginteractions.org.
3. Before/after: FibroScan at diagnosis (cirrhosis needs lifelong HCC surveillance even after cure), hepatitis A/B vaccination, HIV test, alcohol advice, harm reduction (needle exchange, OST), contact tracing; SVR12 (RNA negative 12 weeks post-treatment) = cure; reinfection possible — re-test annually if ongoing risk. Antibody positive/RNA negative = past cleared infection, no treatment, no immunity.

gord-pregnancy.title: Dyspepsia and GORD – uninvestigated, PPI use, refractory, pregnancy
gord-pregnancy.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CG184 Dyspepsia and GORD 2014/2019; NICE CKS Dyspepsia – unidentified cause / proven GORD 2024; NICE NG12; BNF)

options.label: Uninvestigated dyspepsia — red flags then stepwise
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Red flags → 2WW/urgent endoscopy: dysphagia; age ≥55 with weight loss + dyspepsia/reflux/pain; upper abdominal mass; haematemesis/melaena (admit); persistent vomiting; iron deficiency anaemia; treatment-resistant dyspepsia in ≥55 (non-urgent endoscopy). Chest pain — consider cardiac.
2. Review drugs causing dyspepsia: NSAIDs, aspirin, bisphosphonates, steroids, calcium antagonists, nitrates, theophylline, SSRIs, doxycycline, potassium — stop/switch where possible.
3. Lifestyle: weight loss, smaller meals, avoid eating <3 h before bed, raise bed head, reduce alcohol/caffeine/fatty foods/smoking, avoid trigger foods.
4. Then (CG184): either test-and-treat for H. pylori (see GI cancer/peptic ulcer tool) OR full-dose PPI 4 weeks (omeprazole 20 mg, lansoprazole 30 mg, esomeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg od) — whichever first by local pathway, then the other if no response; H2RA (famotidine 20–40 mg bd) if PPI inadequate/unsuitable; alginate (Gaviscon Advance 10 mL after meals/nocte) for breakthrough; review at 4–8 weeks; step down to lowest effective/on-demand dose.

options.label: Proven GORD, refractory symptoms, long-term PPI
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
