1. Endoscopy-negative reflux or mild oesophagitis: PPI full dose 4–8 weeks → then on-demand/lowest dose; severe oesophagitis (LA C/D)/Barrett's/stricture → long-term full-dose PPI (see Barrett's tool).
2. Refractory (no response to 8 weeks full-dose PPI): check adherence and timing (30–60 min before breakfast); double dose (bd) for 4–8 weeks; switch PPI (esomeprazole 40 mg); add famotidine 40 mg nocte for nocturnal acid; consider non-acid causes — functional heartburn/hypersensitive oesophagus (amitriptyline 10–25 mg nocte, CBT), eosinophilic oesophagitis (biopsies), achalasia/spasm, rumination, gallstones, cardiac. Endoscopy if not already done; gastroenterology for pH-impedance study/manometry; anti-reflux surgery (laparoscopic fundoplication) or LINX if PPI-dependent with objective reflux, volume regurgitation, or intolerance.
3. Long-term PPI review (annual): confirm ongoing indication (Barrett's, severe oesophagitis, NSAID/aspirin gastroprotection in high-risk, Zollinger–Ellison); otherwise attempt step-down/stop with alginate cover (rebound acid 1–2 weeks); risks of long-term use — hypomagnesaemia (check Mg if >1 year or on diuretics/digoxin), B12 deficiency, C. difficile/enteric infection, fracture (bone health), possible CKD/gastric polyps — discuss; use lowest dose; deprescribing per NICE/Bruyère algorithm.

options.label: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Reflux affects 40–80% of pregnancies; usually resolves after delivery. Lifestyle first (small meals, avoid lying flat after eating, left lateral sleep, elevate bed head, avoid triggers).
2. Step 1: antacids/alginates — Gaviscon Advance (sodium alginate/potassium bicarbonate) or calcium carbonate (Rennie) as needed; avoid high-sodium or magnesium trisilicate long term and aluminium-containing in large doses.
3. Step 2: famotidine 20 mg od–bd (ranitidine withdrawn; famotidine has reassuring data) — or Step 3: omeprazole 20 mg od (most pregnancy data; safe) if persistent; lansoprazole also used. Avoid metoclopramide beyond 5 days.
4. Red flags in pregnancy: epigastric pain with hypertension/proteinuria/headache (pre-eclampsia/HELLP — same-day obstetric review), haematemesis, dysphagia, severe vomiting (hyperemesis — see Women's health). Breastfeeding: omeprazole, famotidine, alginates all compatible.

ankle-osteoarthritis.title: Osteoarthritis – hip, knee, hand, shoulder, ankle
ankle-osteoarthritis.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG226 Osteoarthritis 2022; NICE CKS Osteoarthritis 2024; BNF)

options.label: Diagnosis — no imaging needed
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. NG226: diagnose clinically WITHOUT X-ray if age ≥45, activity-related joint pain, and morning stiffness ≤30 min (or none). Image only if atypical (rapid worsening, hot joint, night pain, trauma, age <45) — X-ray severity does not match symptoms.
2. Exclude: inflammatory arthritis (prolonged stiffness, swelling, raised CRP, RF/anti-CCP → rheumatology), gout/pseudogout, septic arthritis (hot, unwell — same day), referred pain (hip → knee; spine → hip), avascular necrosis (steroids, alcohol, sickle), stress fracture.
3. Assess: function, sleep, mood, falls, work, BMI, comorbidities limiting drug choice; use shared decision tools.

options.label: Core treatment and drugs
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. CORE (all patients, NG226): therapeutic exercise — muscle strengthening + aerobic, supervised initially (physio, ESCAPE-pain, Versus Arthritis programmes), 'hurt not harm' message; weight loss if overweight (≥10% gives large benefit); education and self-management plan; appropriate footwear, walking stick in contralateral hand, hand splints for thumb-base OA.
2. Drugs (adjuncts only): topical NSAID (ibuprofen 5%/diclofenac 1% gel tds–qds) FIRST for knee/hand; oral NSAID (ibuprofen 400 mg tds, naproxen 250–500 mg bd) at lowest dose for shortest time with PPI; paracetamol and weak opioids NOT routinely (NG226 — minimal benefit) — paracetamol only short-term infrequent use; do not offer strong opioids, glucosamine, chondroitin, acupuncture, arthroscopic lavage.
3. Intra-articular corticosteroid (methylprednisolone 40 mg/triamcinolone 40 mg ± lidocaine) for short-term relief (2–10 weeks) when other options failed or to enable exercise; not more than every 3 months; hyaluronic acid not recommended.
4. Sleep/mood: CBT-informed approaches, pain management programme; duloxetine not recommended by NICE for OA (off-label option in some pathways).

options.label: Joint-specific points and referral
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Knee: patellofemoral vs tibiofemoral; valgus/varus brace or insoles may help; degenerative meniscal tear = OA (no arthroscopy). Hip: groin pain, limited internal rotation; stress fracture of femoral neck in osteoporotic/runner → urgent. Hand: DIP (Heberden's), PIP (Bouchard's), thumb CMC — splint, topical NSAID, steroid injection to CMC. Shoulder (glenohumeral): loss of external rotation, crepitus; X-ray distinguishes from frozen shoulder; physio, injection, arthroplasty if severe. Ankle: usually post-traumatic; rocker-sole shoes, ankle-foot orthosis, injection, arthrodesis/arthroplasty via foot & ankle surgeon.
2. Refer for joint replacement (NG226): symptoms substantially affecting quality of life AND core treatments tried — do NOT withhold referral on grounds of age, BMI, smoking or comorbidities alone (optimise but refer); use Oxford hip/knee score locally. Give realistic expectations: 80–90% satisfied, 10–15% persistent pain after TKR; recovery 3–6 months.
3. Review: within 12 months if on NSAIDs/drugs, otherwise as needed; multimorbidity — review analgesic burden annually.

soft-tissue-infection.title: Inflammatory, infective and regional MSK conditions – spondyloarthritis, reactive arthritis, vasculitis, osteomyelitis, CRPS and others
soft-tissue-infection.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG65 Spondyloarthritis 2017; NICE CKS; BSR ANCA vasculitis 2014/2024; BSR reactive arthritis; RCP CRPS 2018; BOAST; BNF)
niceRefs: RCP Complex regional pain syndrome guidelines 2018

options.label: Spondyloarthritis and reactive arthritis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Axial SpA (NG65): low back pain >3 months starting <45 years with ≥4 of — onset <35, waking in second half of night, buttock pain, improves with movement, improves within 48 h of NSAIDs, first-degree relative with SpA, current/past arthritis/enthesitis/psoriasis → refer rheumatology (do not wait for X-ray changes; HLA-B27 and MRI arranged by specialist). Treat: NSAID at full dose (naproxen 500 mg bd) for 2–4 weeks with PPI, physio/exercise (NASS), smoking cessation; biologics (anti-TNF, IL-17, JAK) for persistent high disease activity (BASDAI ≥4) via rheumatology.
2. Peripheral SpA (psoriatic, IBD-related, reactive): dactylitis ('sausage digit'), enthesitis (Achilles, plantar), asymmetric oligoarthritis, nail changes → rheumatology (urgent if ≥3 joints or synovitis — early DMARD window).
3. Reactive arthritis: 1–4 weeks after GI (Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, Yersinia) or GU (Chlamydia) infection; asymmetric lower-limb oligoarthritis ± conjunctivitis/urethritis/keratoderma. Tests: CRP, FBC, HLA-B27, STI screen (NAAT; treat chlamydia and partners), stool culture if diarrhoea, aspirate if septic doubt. NSAID (naproxen 500 mg bd) + PPI; intra-articular steroid; sulfasalazine/methotrexate if >3–6 months (rheumatology); most settle in 3–12 months; recurrence in HLA-B27+.

options.label: Vasculitis — ANCA and IgA
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. ANCA-associated (GPA/Wegener's, MPA, EGPA): consider in adults with unexplained systemic symptoms + any of: persistent sinusitis/crusting/epistaxis, haemoptysis, palpable purpura, mononeuritis multiplex, red eye/scleritis, haematuria/proteinuria/rising creatinine, late-onset asthma + eosinophilia (EGPA). Tests SAME DAY: urine dip + protein:creatinine ratio, U&E, FBC, CRP/ESR, ANCA (PR3/MPO), chest X-ray. Active urinary sediment or rising creatinine or lung haemorrhage = EMERGENCY → same-day renal/rheumatology; otherwise urgent rheumatology (within 1–2 weeks). Treatment: high-dose steroids + rituximab or cyclophosphamide induction, then maintenance (specialist); GP — PJP prophylaxis awareness, bone protection, vaccination, infection vigilance, BP.
2. IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura): children 3–10 (adults rarer, worse renal outcomes) — palpable purpura on legs/buttocks, arthralgia, abdominal pain, haematuria. Check BP, urinalysis, U&E, FBC (platelets normal — distinguishes from ITP/meningococcus), clotting. Usually self-limiting 4–6 weeks: paracetamol/ibuprofen (avoid NSAID if renal involvement); refer same day if severe abdominal pain (intussusception), GI bleeding, nephrotic/nephritic (proteinuria >1 g, hypertension, rising creatinine), testicular pain. Follow-up: BP + urinalysis weekly for 1 month, 2-weekly to 3 months, then at 6 and 12 months; persistent haematuria/proteinuria → paediatric nephrology.

options.label: Bone and joint infection, AVN, CRPS
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Osteomyelitis: localised bone pain, swelling, fever (may be absent in diabetic foot/vertebral); risk — diabetes, open fracture, prosthesis, IVDU, immunosuppression, sickle cell (Salmonella). Tests: FBC, CRP/ESR, blood cultures ×2, X-ray (changes late, 10–14 days), MRI. Diabetic foot with probe-to-bone positive/ulcer >2 cm → same-day diabetic foot MDT. Vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis (back pain + fever/raised CRP ± neurology) → same-day admission (MRI, cultures, 6 weeks IV/oral antibiotics; epidural abscess = emergency). Do NOT start antibiotics before cultures unless septic. Soft-tissue infection (cellulitis/abscess) → see Dermatology cellulitis tool; necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, systemic toxicity) = 999.
2. Avascular necrosis (hip): groin pain, often night, in steroids (≥20 mg prednisolone for weeks), alcohol excess, sickle cell, SLE, HIV, chemotherapy, divers; X-ray may be normal early → MRI; urgent orthopaedics (core decompression before collapse; THR after); stop/reduce steroids where possible; bisphosphonates not proven.
3. Complex regional pain syndrome (Budapest criteria): continuing regional pain disproportionate after injury/surgery, with sensory (allodynia), vasomotor (colour/temperature), sudomotor/oedema, and motor/trophic changes. EARLY recognition matters: start physiotherapy/OT immediately (graded motor imagery, mirror therapy, desensitisation, keep moving), amitriptyline 10–75 mg nocte or gabapentin/pregabalin (NICE CG173), short course prednisolone 30–40 mg tapered over 2–3 weeks in early CRPS (specialist), bisphosphonate (pamidronate/neridronate — pain clinic), avoid immobilisation and repeated surgery; refer pain clinic within 1–2 months if not improving (RCP). Psychological support; sleep; return-to-work planning.

options.label: Regional conditions — labral tear, patellar tendinopathy, AC joint, metatarsalgia, sarcoid
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Hip labral tear/femoroacetabular impingement: young active adult, anterior groin pain/clicking/catching, positive FADIR test; X-ray (cam/pincer morphology), MR arthrogram via specialist; physiotherapy (hip stabiliser strengthening, avoid deep flexion/pivoting) 3 months; image-guided steroid injection; refer young-adult hip surgeon for arthroscopy if persistent and no OA (NICE IPG408); FAI with established OA → OA pathway.
2. Patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee): inferior pole pain on loading; relative rest, isometric then heavy slow resistance/decline-squat eccentric programme 12 weeks, patellar strap, avoid steroid injection into tendon; ESWT; refer if >6 months.
3. AC joint arthritis/osteoarthritis: pain at the top of the shoulder, high-arc (>150°) pain, cross-body adduction positive, tender over ACJ; X-ray; activity modification, NSAID, ACJ steroid injection (small volume, USS-guided ideally), refer orthopaedics for distal clavicle excision if persistent.
4. Metatarsalgia: forefoot pain under metatarsal heads — causes: high heels, hallux valgus transfer, plantar plate tear (2nd MTP — drawer test), Morton's neuroma, stress fracture, Freiberg's (adolescent 2nd MT head — X-ray), RA (check), diabetes/neuropathy; footwear (wide, low heel, cushioned), metatarsal dome/orthoses, calf stretches, NSAID, weight; podiatry; refer if persistent >6 months or plantar plate rupture (progressive toe deviation).
5. Sarcoid arthropathy: Löfgren's syndrome (acute ankle periarthritis + erythema nodosum + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy) — self-limiting, NSAIDs, chest X-ray, calcium, ACE; refer respiratory/rheumatology; chronic sarcoid arthritis → rheumatology (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine).

anxiety-child.title: Paediatrics – gastroenteritis, limp, scarlet fever, inguinal hernia, TB contact, anxiety
anxiety-child.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG143 Fever under 5 2019; NICE CG84 Diarrhoea and vomiting under 5 2009; NICE CKS Gastroenteritis / Scarlet fever / Inguinal hernia / TB; UKHSA scarlet fever 2023; NICE NG33 TB; BSPAR limp; NICE CG159 social anxiety/anxiety; BNF/BNFc)

options.label: Gastroenteritis and dehydration
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Assess hydration (CG84): red flags — altered consciousness, sunken eyes, tachycardia/tachypnoea, reduced skin turgor, cold extremities, prolonged CRT, hypotension (shock). Risk: <1 year (esp. <6 months), low birth weight, ≥6 stools or ≥3 vomits in 24 h, unable to tolerate fluids, stopped breastfeeding, malnourished.
2. No dehydration: continue breast/formula/normal diet, extra fluids, offer ORS (Dioralyte) 5 mL/kg after each loose stool if at risk; avoid fruit juice/fizzy drinks. Clinical dehydration: ORS 50 mL/kg over 4 h PLUS maintenance, little and often (syringe/spoon 5 mL every 1–2 min); continue breastfeeding; NG tube/admit if refusing or vomiting persistently; shock → 999/IV fluids.
3. Drugs: no antidiarrhoeals in children; ondansetron 0.15 mg/kg single oral dose (off-label, often used in ED) can enable oral rehydration; antibiotics only for specific pathogens (Salmonella <6 months/immunocompromised, Shigella, Campylobacter severe, C. difficile, giardia) — stool culture if blood/mucus, recent travel, immunocompromised, >7 days, or outbreak.
4. Safety-net: diarrhoea usually 5–7 days (stops by 2 weeks), vomiting 1–2 days (stops by 3 days); return if signs of dehydration, blood in stool, bilious vomiting, severe abdominal pain, fever persisting. Exclusion from school/nursery 48 h after last episode; no swimming 2 weeks; hand hygiene; notify if outbreak/E. coli O157/bloody diarrhoea. Post-gastroenteritis lactose intolerance — temporary.

options.label: Limping child
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. SAME DAY referral (paediatrics/orthopaedics): any limp with fever or unwell (septic arthritis/osteomyelitis — Kocher: non-weight-bearing, temp >38.5, ESR >40, WCC >12), non-weight-bearing, limp in child <3 years, pain at rest/night, history of trauma with inability to weight bear, suspected non-accidental injury, limp >1 week without diagnosis, systemic signs (weight loss, bruising, pallor — leukaemia).
2. Transient synovitis (irritable hip): 3–10 years, after viral URTI, mild limp, afebrile/low-grade, can weight-bear, well — if Kocher criteria 0 and bloods normal (FBC, CRP/ESR): ibuprofen, rest, review 48 h and at 1 week; USS shows effusion; must resolve within 1–2 weeks — if not, re-refer (Perthes).
3. Perthes disease: 4–8 years, boys, insidious limp, hip/knee pain, restricted abduction/internal rotation → X-ray AP + frog-lateral (may be normal early → MRI), orthopaedic referral (urgent). SUFE: 10–16 years, often overweight, hip/knee/thigh pain, externally rotated leg, loss of internal rotation → SAME-DAY orthopaedics, non-weight-bearing (frog-lateral X-ray — never miss; bilateral in 20–40%). Also: DDH in toddlers (Trendelenburg gait, leg-length discrepancy — X-ray after 6 months), JIA (morning stiffness, swelling — rheumatology), reactive arthritis, malignancy (osteosarcoma/Ewing's — night pain, mass → 2WW/X-ray within 48 h per NG12), discitis, psoas abscess, appendicitis, testicular torsion (examine).

options.label: Scarlet fever, inguinal hernia, TB, anxiety
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Scarlet fever (group A strep): sandpaper rash starting trunk, flushed cheeks with perioral sparing, strawberry tongue, fever, sore throat; Centor/FeverPAIN. Treat ALL suspected cases: phenoxymethylpenicillin — 1–11 months 62.5 mg qds, 1–5 years 125 mg qds, 6–11 years 250 mg qds, ≥12 years 500 mg qds for 10 days (UKHSA 2023: amoxicillin liquid acceptable if penicillin V unavailable; clarithromycin if allergic). NOTIFIABLE — notify UKHSA. Exclude from school until 24 h of antibiotics. Safety-net: invasive GAS (iGAS) signs — drowsiness, breathing difficulty, poor feeding, rash not fading, persistent fever >48 h on antibiotics, limb pain/swelling (necrotising fasciitis) → 999/same day. Complications: quinsy, otitis media, rheumatic fever, post-strep glomerulonephritis (urinalysis if oedema/haematuria 2–3 weeks later).
2. Inguinal hernia: groin swelling that may extend to scrotum, worse crying/straining, reducible; infants <1 year — URGENT paediatric surgical referral (herniotomy within weeks; incarceration risk 30% in first year); irreducible/tender/vomiting → EMERGENCY (incarceration — attempt to reduce only if trained, do not delay transfer). Hydrocele: transilluminates, cannot get above it is false — can get above; most resolve by 2 years; refer if persists >2 years. Umbilical hernia: wait until 4–5 years unless large/symptomatic.
3. TB in children: contact of smear-positive case → notify/refer to TB service (Mantoux or IGRA ≥2 years; chest X-ray; latent TB — 3 months rifampicin + isoniazid or 6 months isoniazid; <2 years exposed → immediate chemoprophylaxis). Active TB: persistent cough >3 weeks, fever, weight loss/faltering growth, lymphadenopathy, from high-incidence country/contact → urgent chest X-ray + TB service (NG33); notifiable; BCG for eligible infants (high-incidence areas/parents from countries ≥40/100,000).
4. Anxiety in children: screen (RCADS, SCARED), explore school, bullying, family, neurodevelopment (ASD/ADHD), sleep, screen time, physical symptoms (abdominal pain/headache). First line: psychoeducation, parent-led CBT (books/online — e.g. 'Helping your child with fears and worries'), school support/ELSA, guided self-help via Mental Health Support Teams; CBT via CAMHS/CYP-IAPT for moderate–severe or functional impairment (school refusal); sertraline (CAMHS-initiated, 25 mg → 50–100 mg) for severe/unresponsive; safeguarding and self-harm/suicide screen always; refer CAMHS urgently if self-harm, eating restriction, psychosis.

nocturia.title: Urinary incontinence, overactive bladder and nocturia
nocturia.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG123 Urinary incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse in women 2019; NICE CG97 LUTS in men 2010/2015; NICE CKS Incontinence / LUTS; BAUS; BNF)
niceRefs: NICE CKS Incontinence – urinary, in women

options.label: Assessment (all)
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Categorise: stress (leak on cough/exertion), urge/OAB (urgency ± leak, frequency >8/day, nocturia), mixed (treat the dominant symptom first), overflow (poor stream, retention — check post-void residual), functional (mobility/cognition). 3-day bladder diary (volumes, times, fluid intake); urinalysis ± MSU; post-void residual (bladder scan) if voiding symptoms, recurrent UTI, neurological disease, men; examine abdomen, pelvic floor strength (women), prolapse, prostate (men), neurology; medication review (diuretics, alpha-blockers in women → stress incontinence, antimuscarinic burden, sedatives, lithium, SGLT2i).
2. Red flags → refer: visible haematuria (2WW ≥45), microscopic haematuria with dysuria/raised WCC in ≥60 (2WW), recurrent UTI with haematuria ≥60 (2WW), palpable bladder/pelvic mass, suspected fistula, neurological disease (new), persistent pain, previous pelvic surgery/radiotherapy complications, faecal incontinence, voiding difficulty/retention.
3. Lifestyle for all: caffeine reduction, fluid 1.5–2 L/day (not restricted unless excessive), avoid fizzy/alcohol/artificial sweeteners, weight loss if BMI >30, stop smoking, treat constipation, bladder training (urge), timed voiding, containment products (NHS continence service), pelvic floor exercises.

options.label: Stress and urge/OAB — women
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Stress: supervised pelvic floor muscle training ≥3 months (8 contractions ×3/day; physio/continence nurse; apps/pessary as adjunct); duloxetine 40 mg bd only if surgery declined/unsuitable (nausea; second line); refer urogynaecology if not improved — options (NG123, after MDT): colposuspension, autologous fascial sling, urethral bulking; mid-urethral mesh tape currently under high-vigilance restriction — specialist shared decision.
2. OAB/urge: bladder training ≥6 weeks FIRST; then antimuscarinic with lowest anticholinergic burden — solifenacin 5 mg od (→10 mg), tolterodine 2 mg bd/4 mg MR, trospium 20 mg bd (does not cross BBB — preferred in elderly/cognitive impairment); AVOID oxybutynin IR in frail older women (NG123, cognitive decline). Review at 4 weeks then 12 months (6 months if >75). If ineffective/not tolerated: mirabegron 50 mg od (25 mg if renal/hepatic impairment; check BP — contraindicated if uncontrolled hypertension ≥180/110) — may combine with antimuscarinic; vibegron (newer beta-3, NICE 2024 — check).
3. Nocturia specifically: evening fluid/caffeine/alcohol restriction, leg elevation afternoon (oedema), treat sleep apnoea/heart failure/diabetes, review diuretic timing (midday); desmopressin 25 micrograms (women)/50 micrograms (men) sublingual (Noqdirna) at bedtime for nocturnal polyuria (>33% of 24-h output at night) if age <65 or Na checked (baseline, day 3–7, 1 month; avoid if Na <135, heart failure, age >65 without specialist).
4. Refractory OAB: urology/urogynaecology — botulinum toxin A 100 units intravesical (NG123; teach self-catheterisation risk 5–10%), percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, sacral neuromodulation; vaginal oestrogen (estriol 0.1% cream/estradiol 10 microgram pessary) for post-menopausal women with OAB/atrophy — safe long term.

options.label: Men — incontinence and post-prostatectomy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Urge/OAB in men: exclude obstruction (IPSS, flow, PVR >200 mL → treat BPH first — see LUTS tool); bladder training; antimuscarinic (solifenacin/tolterodine) or mirabegron — safe to combine with alpha-blocker (tamsulosin) if PVR <200 mL; review retention risk.
2. Stress incontinence after prostatectomy: pelvic floor training (physio-led) started before and continued after surgery for ≥6–12 months — most improve by 12 months; containment; refer urology at 6–12 months if persistent: male sling or artificial urinary sphincter (NG123/BAUS); duloxetine off-label.
3. Overflow/retention: PVR >300 mL, dribbling, palpable bladder → catheterise/urology; chronic retention with hydronephrosis or renal impairment → urgent.
4. Functional incontinence (dementia, immobility): timed toileting, commode, clothing adaptations, continence products, treat constipation, avoid antimuscarinics where possible, OT/continence service, carer support.

bph-medical.title: Male LUTS, BPH and prostate cancer – assessment, PSA, treatment, referral
bph-medical.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE CG97 LUTS in men 2010/2015; NICE NG131 Prostate cancer 2019/2024; NICE NG12; NICE CKS LUTS in men / Prostate cancer; PCRMP 2022; BNF)

options.label: LUTS assessment and PSA
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Assess (CG97): IPSS score and bother, 3-day frequency–volume chart, urinalysis, DRE (size, consistency, nodules), PVR if voiding symptoms, U&E if chronic retention suspected; medication review (anticholinergics, decongestants, diuretics). Red flags: haematuria (2WW ≥45), retention (catheterise), palpable bladder, renal impairment, recurrent UTI, stones, neurological symptoms.
2. PSA: offer counselling (PCRMP) before testing any man ≥50 who asks, or earlier if Black ethnicity/family history/BRCA; no screening programme. Do not test within 6 weeks of UTI/prostatitis, 48 h of ejaculation/vigorous exercise, 1 week of DRE. Age-specific referral thresholds (NG12 2024/PCRMP): 40–49 >2.5; 50–59 >3.5; 60–69 >4.5; 70–79 >6.5 micrograms/L; ≥80 use clinical judgement — refer 2WW if above threshold OR prostate feels malignant on DRE (regardless of PSA). Finasteride/dutasteride halve PSA — double the result after 6 months.
3. Mild symptoms (IPSS ≤7) or not bothered: reassure, lifestyle — reduce evening fluids, caffeine, alcohol; bladder training; double voiding; treat constipation; review annually.

options.label: BPH drug treatment and when to refer
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Moderate–severe voiding LUTS: alpha-blocker — tamsulosin 400 micrograms od MR (alfuzosin 10 mg MR, doxazosin 4 mg MR alternatives); benefit within 1–2 weeks; warn postural hypotension, ejaculatory dysfunction, floppy-iris (tell ophthalmologist before cataract surgery).
2. Prostate >30 g (or PSA >1.4 micrograms/L as proxy) and risk of progression: add 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor — finasteride 5 mg od or dutasteride 500 micrograms od (combination capsule Combodart); takes 3–6 months; reduces retention/surgery risk; sexual side effects, breast changes (report lumps), MHRA depression/suicidal ideation warning; halves PSA.
3. Storage symptoms persisting on alpha-blocker with PVR <200 mL: add antimuscarinic (tolterodine 4 mg MR/solifenacin 5 mg) or mirabegron 50 mg (CG97/NG123). Nocturnal polyuria: desmopressin 50 micrograms (Noqdirna) with Na monitoring. PDE5 inhibitor (tadalafil 5 mg od) if co-existing erectile dysfunction (licensed for BPH-LUTS).
4. Refer urology (routine): symptoms bothersome despite drugs, PVR >200–300 mL, recurrent UTI, bladder stones, haematuria, renal impairment from obstruction, patient preference for surgery — options TURP, HoLEP, UroLift (NICE MTG58; preserves ejaculation), Rezum, prostate artery embolisation. Acute retention → same-day catheter + alpha-blocker 2–3 days before trial without catheter.

options.label: Prostate cancer — after diagnosis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Pathway: 2WW → multiparametric MRI (Likert ≥3 → targeted biopsy) → Gleason/ISUP grade, PSA, staging (CAPRA/NICE risk groups); bone scan/PSMA-PET if intermediate/high risk.
2. Low risk (PSA <10, Gleason 6, T1–2a): ACTIVE SURVEILLANCE (NG131) — PSA every 3–4 months year 1, DRE, repeat MRI at 12–18 months, biopsy if change; GP: reassure, support, avoid unnecessary PSA outside protocol. Intermediate: surveillance (favourable), radical prostatectomy or radiotherapy (external beam ± brachytherapy) with 6 months ADT; high risk/locally advanced: radiotherapy + 2–3 years ADT, or prostatectomy + nodes; metastatic: ADT (GnRH agonist leuprorelin/goserelin/triptorelin 3-monthly, or antagonist degarelix/relugolix oral) PLUS docetaxel or abiraterone/enzalutamide/apalutamide (NICE TAs), bone protection (zoledronate/denosumab) for bone metastases.
3. GP role on ADT: cardiovascular risk (BP, lipids, HbA1c annually), osteoporosis — DEXA at baseline, calcium/vitamin D, bisphosphonate if T ≤−2.5 or fracture; hot flushes (medroxyprogesterone 20 mg od, cyproterone 50 mg bd, venlafaxine, gabapentin); fatigue (exercise programme), sexual dysfunction, gynaecomastia (prophylactic tamoxifen/radiotherapy), mood, anaemia, metabolic syndrome. Post-treatment: PSA at 6 weeks then 6-monthly for 2 years then annual; biochemical recurrence (PSA >0.2 post-surgery or nadir +2 post-radiotherapy) → oncology. Spinal cord compression (back pain + leg weakness/numbness/retention) = EMERGENCY — dexamethasone 16 mg + same-day MRI whole spine (NG75).

uti-pregnancy.title: Urinary tract infection – women, men, pregnancy, recurrent, and painful bladder syndrome
uti-pregnancy.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG109 UTI lower 2018; NG111 pyelonephritis 2018; NG112 recurrent UTI 2018; NICE CKS UTI (lower) women / men / Recurrent / Bladder pain syndrome 2024; UKHSA diagnosis of UTI 2024; BAUS/EAU BPS; BNF)
niceRefs: UKHSA Diagnosis of UTI quick reference 2024
NICE CKS Urinary tract infection (lower) – women

options.label: Women (non-pregnant) — acute and recurrent
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Diagnose on symptoms (UKHSA 2024): ≥2 of dysuria, new nocturia, cloudy urine = treat empirically (dipstick adds little in <65s; NO dipstick in >65s or catheterised — asymptomatic bacteriuria is common and not treated). Send MSU if: pregnancy, men, recurrent, treatment failure, resistance risk (care home, recent antibiotics, travel), haematuria, age >65 with symptoms. Exclude vaginal cause (discharge/irritation → STI/candida), urethritis, atrophic vaginitis.
2. Uncomplicated cystitis: back-up/delayed prescription or immediate; self-care — paracetamol/ibuprofen, fluids; NOT cranberry/alkalinisers as treatment. First line 3 days: nitrofurantoin MR 100 mg bd (if eGFR ≥45) or trimethoprim 200 mg bd (if low resistance risk/not used in past 3 months); second: pivmecillinam 400 mg stat then 200 mg tds (3 days), fosfomycin 3 g single dose. Pyelonephritis (loin pain, fever, rigors, vomiting): cefalexin 500 mg bd–tds 7–10 days or co-amoxiclav 625 mg tds/ciprofloxacin 500 mg bd 7 days; admit if septic, pregnant, vomiting, no improvement 48 h.
3. Recurrent (≥2 in 6 months / ≥3 in 12 months, NG112): MSU each episode, review contraception (switch from spermicide/diaphragm), post-coital voiding, fluids; post-menopausal — vaginal oestrogen (estriol 0.1% cream twice weekly) FIRST; D-mannose 2 g od and cranberry (no strong evidence; may try); methenamine hippurate 1 g bd (ALTAR trial — as effective as prophylactic antibiotics; avoid eGFR <10/alkalinising agents); single-dose post-coital antibiotic (trimethoprim 100 mg/nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg) if coital trigger; otherwise 3–6 months prophylaxis trimethoprim 100 mg nocte or nitrofurantoin 50–100 mg nocte (review at 6 months; nitrofurantoin long-term lung/liver risk, FBC/LFT/pulmonary symptoms). Refer urology: haematuria, recurrent despite prophylaxis, stones, structural abnormality, poor emptying (USS KUB + PVR).

options.label: Men, catheters, pregnancy
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Men: always send MSU before antibiotics; treat 7 days — trimethoprim 200 mg bd or nitrofurantoin MR 100 mg bd (only if no prostatic involvement suspected); if prostatitis features (perineal/low back pain, fever, tender prostate, systemically unwell) → ciprofloxacin 500 mg bd 14 days (or trimethoprim 200 mg bd 14 days if quinolone unsuitable; MHRA restrictions) — do NOT massage prostate; admit if septic. Investigate ALL men with UTI: PVR, consider USS renal tract/flexible cystoscopy via urology if recurrent, haematuria, retention, or age >60 (NG12 2WW if visible haematuria ≥45 or unexplained non-visible haematuria + dysuria/raised WCC ≥60). STI screen if <35 or risk.
2. Catheter-associated UTI: do not dipstick/culture or treat bacteriuria without symptoms; symptoms = fever, rigors, new flank/suprapubic pain, new confusion/delirium, visible haematuria; change the catheter (if in >7 days) and send CSU from the new one; 7 days antibiotics (NG113) — nitrofurantoin/trimethoprim/amoxicillin per sensitivities, or if upper tract/septic → cefalexin/co-amoxiclav/ciprofloxacin; consider removing catheter; no prophylactic antibiotics for long-term catheters.
3. Pregnancy: send MSU at booking and treat ASYMPTOMATIC bacteriuria (confirmed on a second sample) — reduces pyelonephritis/preterm birth; symptomatic or bacteriuria → 7 days nitrofurantoin MR 100 mg bd (AVOID at term ≥36 weeks — neonatal haemolysis), amoxicillin 500 mg tds (only if sensitive), cefalexin 500 mg bd; AVOID trimethoprim in first trimester (folate antagonist — if unavoidable give folic acid 5 mg) and quinolones throughout; test of cure MSU 7 days after; group B strep in urine → inform maternity (intrapartum prophylaxis). Pyelonephritis in pregnancy → ADMIT.

options.label: Bladder pain syndrome / interstitial cystitis
options.guidance:
MANAGEMENT PLAN:
1. Suspect: suprapubic pain related to bladder filling, relieved by voiding, frequency/urgency/nocturia >6 weeks with repeatedly NEGATIVE MSU and no other cause (UTI, stones, OAB, endometriosis, prostatitis, cancer — cystoscopy to exclude carcinoma in situ in >40s/smokers/haematuria). Often co-exists with IBS, fibromyalgia, vulvodynia, anxiety/depression.
2. First line (BAUS/EAU/AUA): education, bladder diary, dietary modification (avoid caffeine, alcohol, acidic/spicy foods, artificial sweeteners — individual triggers), stress management/CBT, pelvic floor physiotherapy (down-training — NOT Kegels), analgesia (paracetamol; amitriptyline 10 mg nocte titrating to 25–75 mg; or gabapentin/pregabalin via pain clinic), antihistamine (cimetidine 400 mg bd, hydroxyzine 25–50 mg nocte — modest evidence), avoid repeated antibiotic courses without positive cultures.
3. Refer urology (routine; urgent if haematuria) for cystoscopy ± hydrodistension (Hunner lesions → fulguration/triamcinolone), intravesical treatments (hyaluronic acid/chondroitin — Cystistat/iAluRil; DMSO; lidocaine cocktails), botulinum toxin A, pentosan polysulfate (Elmiron — NICE TA; MHRA pigmentary maculopathy warning, eye checks), neuromodulation; multidisciplinary pain service; patient support (Bladder Health UK).

triage-burns.title: GP Triage – common urgent presentations: 999 / same day / 24–48 h / self-care
triage-burns.curatedBy: Claude draft (NICE NG143 Fever in under 5s 2019; NICE CG176/NG232 Head injury; NICE NG88 HMB; NICE CG134 Anaphylaxis; Resuscitation Council UK 2021; NICE CKS Burns and scalds / Dental abscess / Foreign body; TOXBASE; NHS 111 pathways; UK Sepsis Trust; JRCALC)

options.label: Breathlessness, allergic reaction, choking, severe bleeding
options.guidance:
TRIAGE:
• BREATHLESSNESS — 999: unable to speak in sentences, cyanosis/blue lips, drowsy/confused, chest pain, stridor, new sudden onset at rest, sats <92% if measured, known asthma not responding to 10 puffs salbutamol, anaphylaxis. SAME DAY: worsening over hours, fever + productive cough + unwell (pneumonia), asthma/COPD exacerbation responding partly to inhaler, calf swelling (PE), new ankle oedema/orthopnoea (heart failure). 24–48 h: gradual onset over days, exertional only, no red flags. SELF-CARE: mild URTI with cough, anxiety-related with normal observations — safety-net.
• ALLERGIC REACTION — 999 (ANAPHYLAXIS, CG134/RCUK): airway swelling (lips/tongue/throat tightness, hoarse voice), wheeze/breathlessness, dizziness/collapse/pale/floppy, rapidly spreading rash WITH any of these → use adrenaline auto-injector immediately if available (adult 500 micrograms IM, child 150–300 micrograms), lie flat, legs raised, second dose after 5 min. SAME DAY: urticaria/angioedema without airway or breathing symptoms but spreading, first reaction to a new food/drug/sting, ACE-inhibitor angioedema (stop drug). 24–48 h/SELF-CARE: localised urticaria, mild itch — cetirizine 10 mg (child by age), avoid trigger; refer allergy clinic after any anaphylaxis/systemic reaction (prescribe 2 auto-injectors + training before leaving).
• CHOKING — 999 if cannot cough/speak/breathe (give 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts — chest thrusts in infants <1 year; CPR if unresponsive); after any abdominal thrusts → same-day medical review; SAME DAY if persisting cough/wheeze/stridor after choking episode (inhaled foreign body — chest X-ray; children with peanuts/small objects → paediatrics even if well); SELF-CARE if cleared fully, well, normal breathing.
• SEVERE BLEEDING — 999: bleeding not controlled by 10 min firm direct pressure, spurting/pooling, amputation, bleeding with pallor/faintness/sweating, haematemesis, melaena with dizziness, on anticoagulant with any significant bleed, pregnancy >20 weeks with bleeding, post-partum haemorrhage. SAME DAY: nosebleed >20 min despite pinching soft part leaning forward (ED for packing), rectal bleeding large volume/on anticoagulant, wound needing closure (within 12–24 h — minor injury unit), haematuria with clots. 24–48 h: small rectal bleed, bruising on anticoagulant (INR/FBC). SELF-CARE: minor cut controlled with pressure, small nosebleed stopped.

options.label: Abdominal pain, heavy vaginal bleeding, diabetic unwell, overdose/poisoning
options.guidance:
TRIAGE:
• ABDOMINAL PAIN — 999: collapse/shock, rigid abdomen, pain + vomiting blood, suspected AAA (>50, severe back/abdominal pain, pulsatile mass, known aneurysm), testicular pain sudden onset (torsion — within 6 h; same-day surgical if not 999), pregnancy with severe pain/shoulder-tip pain/faintness (ectopic). SAME DAY: severe constant pain >6 h, RIF pain (appendicitis), fever + pain, bilious/persistent vomiting, unable to pass stool or wind with distension, pain in child <5 with lethargy/drawing up legs (intussusception) or in known diabetic (DKA), first-trimester pain/bleeding (EPAU), loin pain with fever, pain with jaundice, elderly/immunosuppressed with new pain. 24–48 h: colicky intermittent pain, dyspepsia, change in bowel habit without red flags, suspected UTI with mild symptoms. SELF-CARE: mild cramps, known IBS pattern, gastroenteritis tolerating fluids — safety-net.
• HEAVY VAGINAL BLEEDING — 999: soaking a pad every 30–60 min for >2 h with dizziness/fainting/pallor, pregnancy >12 weeks with heavy bleeding, bleeding with severe pain and collapse (ectopic). SAME DAY: heavy bleeding in early pregnancy (EPAU/gynaecology), bleeding + fever/offensive discharge (sepsis), post-menopausal bleeding with large volume, bleeding on anticoagulant, passing large clots and symptomatic (FBC). 24–48 h/ROUTINE: heavy periods without acute symptoms (NG88 — FBC, tranexamic acid 1 g tds during menses, consider LNG-IUS; 2WW if post-menopausal bleeding, ≥55 with unexplained vaginal discharge or thrombocytosis, intermenstrual/post-coital bleeding with pelvic mass/abnormal cervix). SELF-CARE: slightly heavier period, no symptoms of anaemia — book routine review.
• DIABETIC UNWELL / HYPO — 999: unconscious or fitting (give IM glucagon 1 mg if available, do not give oral), unable to swallow, hypo not responding to 3 cycles of 15–20 g fast glucose at 15-min intervals, DKA features (vomiting, abdominal pain, Kussmaul breathing, drowsy, ketones ≥3 mmol/L / 'high'), hyperglycaemia with reduced consciousness. SAME DAY: ketones 1.5–2.9 with hyperglycaemia or unable to keep fluids down (sick-day rules failing), recurrent hypos in last 24 h, hypo on sulfonylurea/long-acting insulin (prolonged — observe), infection in diabetic with foot ulcer/cellulitis, glucose persistently >25 mmol/L. 24–48 h: raised glucose with no ketones and well (medication review; increase monitoring), single explained mild hypo. SELF-CARE: sick-day rules (never stop insulin, check glucose/ketones 2–4 hourly, 100 mL fluid/hour, pause SGLT2i/metformin if vomiting), hypo treated with 15–20 g glucose then long-acting carbohydrate.
• OVERDOSE / POISONING — 999/ED for ALL deliberate overdoses regardless of amount or apparent wellness (paracetamol is silent for 24 h; antidote window), any ingestion with drowsiness/vomiting/arrhythmia, button battery or magnet ingestion in children (EMERGENCY — oesophageal burn within 2 h), caustic/petroleum ingestion, carbon monoxide exposure. SAME DAY: accidental ingestion of medicines in a child (check TOXBASE — many need ED observation, e.g. iron, tricyclics, calcium-channel blockers, sulfonylureas, opioids), plant/mushroom ingestion with symptoms, iron tablets. 24–48 h: accidental minor ingestion confirmed non-toxic on TOXBASE/NPIS 0344 892 0111 (clinician line) — observe at home. Mental health: all deliberate self-harm → same-day psychosocial assessment (liaison psychiatry/crisis team); do not use this tool to decide against assessment.

options.label: Child fever, ear pain, dental emergency, limb injury, burns, swallowed object
options.guidance:
TRIAGE:
• CHILD WITH FEVER (NG143 traffic light) — 999: non-blanching rash, unresponsive/difficult to rouse, grunting/severe respiratory distress, seizure >5 min, mottled/blue/pale with cold extremities, bulging fontanelle with drowsiness, <3 months with temp ≥38 and unwell. SAME DAY (within hours; face-to-face): any infant <3 months with fever ≥38 °C; 3–6 months ≥39 °C; any amber feature — pallor, not responding normally, reduced activity, nasal flaring, tachypnoea/tachycardia, CRT ≥3 s, reduced urine output, fever ≥5 days, limb/joint swelling or not weight-bearing, rigors; parent concern. 24–48 h: fever <5 days, green features, feeding >50%, wet nappies, playful between doses of antipyretic. SELF-CARE: fluids, paracetamol OR ibuprofen (alternate only if distress persists), light clothing, no tepid sponging; check for rash with a glass; return if worse or new symptoms; do not send to nursery.
• EAR PAIN — SAME DAY: severe pain with fever and bulging drum in child <2 (consider antibiotics if bilateral <2 years or discharging — amoxicillin 5–7 days), discharge with mastoid swelling/tenderness or ear pushed forward (MASTOIDITIS — ED), facial weakness, vertigo/severe headache/neck stiffness, diabetic/immunosuppressed with severe otalgia (malignant otitis externa), post-ear-surgery, foreign body in ear with pain/button battery (999). 24–48 h: otitis media without red flags not settling after 3 days of analgesia, otitis externa (acetic acid/antibiotic-steroid drops), ear wax (olive oil drops 5 days then review). SELF-CARE: mild earache with URTI <3 days — paracetamol/ibuprofen, most resolve in 3 days; delayed antibiotic prescription option.
• DENTAL — 999/ED: facial swelling spreading to eye or neck, trismus (cannot open mouth 2 fingers), difficulty swallowing/breathing, drooling (Ludwig's angina), avulsed permanent tooth (reimplant within 1 h — hold by crown, store in milk, dentist/ED immediately), uncontrolled bleeding after extraction. SAME DAY (urgent dental care — NHS 111 dental): dental abscess with fever/swelling (GP may give phenoxymethylpenicillin 500 mg qds or amoxicillin 500 mg tds 5 days ONLY as a bridge if systemic signs and no dental access — antibiotics do not treat the cause), severe uncontrolled toothache, broken tooth with exposed pulp. 24–48 h: toothache controlled with ibuprofen + paracetamol, lost filling. SELF-CARE: sensitivity, mild pain — ibuprofen 400 mg + paracetamol 1 g, salt-water rinses, book dentist.
• LIMB INJURY — 999: open fracture, deformity with absent pulse/white or blue limb, suspected hip fracture (shortened externally rotated leg, cannot stand), amputation, crush injury, high-energy trauma. SAME DAY (minor injuries/ED): unable to weight-bear 4 steps (Ottawa), bony tenderness at malleoli/navicular/5th metatarsal/patella/fibular head, obvious deformity, wound over joint, suspected scaphoid fracture (snuffbox tenderness after fall on outstretched hand — X-ray even if first negative), hot swollen joint, numbness/weakness distal to injury, tendon rupture (Achilles — cannot plantarflex; biceps 'Popeye'), elderly on anticoagulants with head/limb injury. 24–48 h: sprain with some weight-bearing, soft-tissue swelling without bony tenderness. SELF-CARE: PRICE 48 h, ibuprofen/paracetamol, mobilise early; review if not improving at 1 week.
• BURNS — 999: airway burns (facial burns, singed nasal hair, hoarse voice, soot in sputum), >15% body surface adult (>10% child; palm of patient's hand = 1%), electrical/chemical burns (irrigate 20+ min), full-thickness (white/leathery/painless), circumferential limb/chest burns, burns with other trauma/smoke inhalation. SAME DAY (ED/burns unit): any burn to face, hands, feet, genitals, perineum, flexures or across joints; >1% full/partial thickness in child or >3% adult; all children <5 and >60 years with significant burns; non-accidental injury concern (glove-and-stocking scald, cigarette burns, inconsistent history — safeguarding); diabetic/immunosuppressed. 24–48 h: small partial-thickness burn blistered — cool 20 min running water (within 3 h of injury), cover with cling film/non-adherent dressing, analgesia, review for infection at 48 h, tetanus status. SELF-CARE: superficial erythema (sunburn-like) <1% — cool, moisturise, analgesia.
• SWALLOWED OBJECT — 999/ED immediately: BUTTON BATTERY (any size, even if well — X-ray; oesophageal battery removed within 2 h), 2+ magnets or magnet + metal, sharp objects (needles, open safety pins, fish/chicken bones with pain/drooling), objects >2.5 cm or >6 cm long, choking/drooling/unable to swallow saliva/chest pain (oesophageal impaction — food bolus also), vomiting/abdominal pain after ingestion, known oesophageal disease. SAME DAY: coin in child <5 (X-ray — if in oesophagus needs removal; stomach — can wait), any ingestion with symptoms. 24–48 h/SELF-CARE: small smooth blunt object (coin in older child/adult, bead) in a well, asymptomatic person — normal diet, check stools for 1–2 weeks (no laxatives/induced vomiting), return if abdominal pain, vomiting, fever, blood in stool, or not passed in 2–3 weeks (X-ray).
